definitions.definition: The jīva is a mere semblance of consciousness in the intellect, neither real nor the original; knowing it as semblance, only consciousness remains (Sureśvara; cf. BS 2.3.50).
Everything is a manifestation (ābhāsa) of consciousness within itself, appearing as if external; the world is real as manifestation and unfolded on consciousness's own screen by its will.

relations.note: Advaita's apparent transformation; the Kashmir Śaivas hold manifestation to be real and free

definitions.definition: Letters/words convey word-meanings as an intermediate step, like the flame in cooking; the word-meanings then convey the sentence meaning.

The two means of stilling (1.12): practice is effort toward stability, grounded by long, uninterrupted, devoted cultivation (1.13–14); dispassion dams the stream toward objects while practice opens the stream of discrimination (YBh 1.12).

name: The saving regard of the teacher (ācārya-abhimāna)

definitions.definition: For one who can do nothing, being held as his own by a true teacher is itself enough for salvation; the teacher's embrace is the final means.
The teacher is indispensable as the one who imparts the mantras and may perform surrender on the disciple's behalf.

The Lord and his powers (internal, marginal, external) are simultaneously one and different, in a way reason cannot resolve and revelation affirms; the soul is his marginal power, a 'difference-and-non-difference manifestation'.

name: The three planes: divine, bodily, sacrificial

definitions.definition: Correspondences are drawn in parallel series: in the realm of the gods the sun is the eater and the moon the food; in the realm of the self the breath is the eater and food is its food (ŚB 10.6.2.1–4).
The Āraṇyaka saṃhitā-teachings extend the planes to speech: stops, sibilants and vowels = earth, atmosphere, sky = eye, ear, mind (AA 3.2.5).

Who may perform a rite and receive its fruit: humans, not animals or gods (MS 6.1.4–5); women as well as men, husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17); for Vedic rites, those with Vedic learning, excluding śūdras (MS 6.1.25–38); the eligibility injunction states ownership of the fruit.

relations.note: Vedānta distinguishes the eligible for ritual from the eligible for Brahman-inquiry (P4-stage)

definitions.definition: The Śrauta rites are for human beings able to undertake them, excluding the maimed, the unlearned, eunuchs and śūdras; for the three higher classes, and for women too (KŚS 1.1.1–8).

Seekers are low, middle or highest by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant with sole refuge in Viṣṇu; eligibility for the Veda, the Tantra and the Name differs by class and gender, and the Mahābhārata was composed for those not entitled to the Veda.
The sūtras are commented on in topic-sections, each with subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection; commentators group and count them differently.

name: The adhikaraṇa method of interpretation

definitions.definition: Each topic is set out in five members — subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view, conclusion — and the conclusion becomes a maxim (nyāya) applied elsewhere.

notes: Some later manuals give 'nirṇaya' or 'prayojana' in place of saṅgati; the Nyāyamālā's own list is followed.

relations.note: both treat teachings as means relative to the student

definitions.definition: The teaching method of scripture: provisionally superimpose (creation, sheaths, attributes) and then retract, leaving the substratum; creation-teachings are means (GK 3.15).

relations.note: Śaṅkara: 'the learned call this superimposition avidyā'

definitions.definition: The appearance, like memory, of something previously seen in something else; the mutual superimposition of self and not-self, natural and beginningless, called avidyā, the root of all empirical dealings.

name: The injunction of Vedic study and the transmission of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Veda is learned from a teacher by the injunction 'one's own Veda is to be studied'; after study one stays at the teacher's house to inquire into its sentences; every study presupposes an earlier teacher's study, without beginning.

Merit and demerit (qualities of selves) that cause motions without visible cause — needle and magnet, ascent of sap, upward flame, the first motion of atoms and minds — and the mind's departure at death and entry at birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.8, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C); acts done for the unseen (VS 6.2.2).
A supersensible cause of experience must be admitted (NK stabaka 1); the Lord sets the stores of merit and demerit in motion (NBh 4.1.21).

relations.note: Mīmāṃsā's apūrva

definitions.definition: The lineage recited in the tradition: Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā (Padmabhava), Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śuka, Gauḍapāda, Govinda, Śaṅkara, and his disciples Padmapāda, Hastāmalaka, Toṭaka and the Vārttikakāra (Sureśvara).

name: Āgama as rooted in or continuous with the Veda
notes: Bhāskararāya's statement read in the local Setubandha e-text; no teaching id created (U23).

definitions.definition: The Pāñcarātra is the Lord's own word and of Vedic root; its followers are brahmins.
Vaikhānasa worship follows the path of the śruti in every rite and is performed with Vedic mantras.
Tantras that teach the worship of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Rudra, Paraśiva or Sundarī are rooted in Upaniṣads such as the Rāmatāpanī and are beyond doubt (Bhāskararāya, Setubandha introduction).

name: The Āgamas as the body of Sadāśiva

relations.note: both treat a sacred whole as the Lord's body

definitions.definition: The 28 tantras are the limbs of Sadāśiva's body made of tantras and mantras, from the Kāmika as his feet to the Vātula as his garment; one scripture, manifold through the hearers.

name: The ages, the Manu-periods and the day of Brahmā

definitions.definition: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000, 1,000 divine years with twilights; 12,000 make a divine age; a thousand divine ages a day of Brahmā; seventy-one a Manu-period; creations and dissolutions without number (MDh 1.68–80).
The age-names appear in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa as states of a man — lying, rising, standing, moving (AB 7.15).

name: Agni, the fire in the rite and in all

definitions.definition: Agni is the household priest, messenger and mouth of the gods who carries the oblation (RV 1.1), churned by Atharvan (6.16.13), guardian of ṛta, present as the flesh-eating and the oblation-bearing fire (10.16.9), as Vaiśvānara the light set in the heart (6.9).

The great brick altar built over a year in five layers, typically falcon-shaped, sevenfold to a hundred-and-one-fold (ŚB 10.2.3.18); the builder rebuilds Prajāpati, gains immortality after death and escapes re-death (ŚB 10.4.3); its 'secret' (rahasya) in ŚB 10 interiorizes it as fires built of mind, speech, breath, eye, ear and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3).
Its layout by cord and peg, and the transformation of its shapes with equal area, are the subject of the Śulbasūtras.
The referent of 'I' is the soul itself, not the ego-evolute of prakṛti; the 'I' persists in deep sleep and in release.

relations.note: the self known as 'I'; rejects the Advaita view that the 'I' is a superimposition

definitions.definition: The principle of self-assertion (SK 24), from which the organs and subtle elements proceed in its vaikṛta, bhūtādi and taijasa aspects (SK 25); it, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).

name: Non-injury and ritual action (Mīmāṃsā view)

definitions.definition: Violence is prohibited; a rite stated as a means for one who wishes to harm (the Śyena) is harmful, and the Veda does not enjoin the harming itself.

notes: The Bhāṭṭa position that killing enjoined as part of a rite (e.g. the Agnīṣomīya animal) is not sin is general knowledge, not checked here; see dsp:sacrificial-killing.

name: The unity of Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā (aikaśāstrya)

definitions.definition: Ritual inquiry and inquiry into Brahman are one science; the first prepares for the second, and rightly read presupposes the Lord.

Power is a sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) giving non-obstruction (SK 45); the commentators list becoming minute, great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control and going where one wishes (Gauḍapāda on SK 23). Warnings: attachment to the powers is the error 'delusion', through which gods like Indra fall back (Gauḍapāda on SK 48); gaining the powers is not liberation, since they end (SS 5.82; 4.32). Yogic powers are nonetheless not to be denied (SS 5.128).
The breath's natural sound — ha going out, sa coming in — repeated 21,600 times a day without effort; knowing it gives liberation (Dhyānabindu 61–65; Yogacūḍāmaṇi 31–35; Haṃsa).
From the highest standpoint nothing is ever born — not from itself, another, both or neither; creation-teachings are means to lead the mind (GK 3.15).

name: The mode in the form of the partless (akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti)

definitions.definition: The mental mode arising from the mahāvākya that destroys ignorance and then itself subsides; Brahman is pervaded by the mode but not illumined by the reflected consciousness in it.
'This is silver' is two cognitions, a perception and a memory lacking its 'that', whose difference is not grasped; no cognition as such is false.

That on which space is woven, described only by negations, by whose command sun and moon stand apart; unknown, all rites are finite; the unseen seer (BAU 3.8.8-11); the object of the higher knowledge and source of beings (MuU 1.1.5-7); also the syllable Om.
Contact through the universal (grasping all instances), through a cognition (the presented content of a prior cognition), and born of yoga.

Immortality is prayed for as full life and freedom from death (RV 7.59.12), won by soma ('we have become immortal', 8.48.3), by gifts (10.107.2), and as a place in the immortal world of light and bliss (9.113.7–11); 'knowing the Person one goes beyond death; there is no other path' (VS 31.18); 'knowing the ageless self one does not fear death' (AVŚ 10.8.44).

relations.note: Two strands: immortality as a heavenly world reached by rite and merit, and going beyond death by knowledge (VS 31.18; AVŚ 10.8.44).

definitions.definition: Worship of Viṣṇu is through the fire without form, or in a consecrated image; image worship is praised as best.

Brahman is bliss (TU 3.6); the self made of bliss is the innermost of the five selves (TU 2.5); 'the essence' (raso vai saḥ) — who could live if this bliss were not in space? (TU 2.7); the highest bliss of the brahma-world on a fraction of which beings live (BAU 4.3.32); the knower of brahman's bliss fears nothing (TU 2.4, 2.9).

name: The calculus of bliss (ānanda-mīmāṃsā)

definitions.definition: A graded measure of bliss: the fullest human bliss multiplied a hundredfold at each step through classes of beings up to the bliss of brahman (TU 2.8; BAU 4.3.33 with a different list), with the refrain that the learned one untouched by desire has each of these.

members: TU 2.8: human; human gandharvas; divine gandharvas; fathers of long-lasting world; gods by birth; gods by works; gods; Indra; Bṛhaspati; Prajāpati; brahman
BAU 4.3.33: human; fathers who have won their world; gandharva world; gods by works; gods by birth; Prajāpati's world; brahman's world (moderate)

definitions.definition: Even in liberation bliss is graded: each class of the liberated enjoys a hundredfold more than the one below, up to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Śrī far above and Viṣṇu infinitely above.

relations.note: gradation continues in liberation as graded bliss

definitions.definition: The ancestors eat monthly, drink svadhā and have the moon as light (ŚB 2.4.2.2); the paths of the fathers lead to cremation grounds for those who desired offspring (ĀpDh 2.9.23).
Primeval deities of several classes, satisfied by śrāddha offerings for months or forever (MDh 3.192–199; 3.267–272).

The eternal state of sorrow, without return, reached by the souls fit for darkness; the texts connect it with hatred of Viṣṇu and his devotees and with the conceit 'I am ever the Lord and the world is unreal'.
Jīvas are many, each with its own ignorance; one is liberated while others remain bound.

name: The self (jīva, aṅga, ātman) in the Vīraśaiva view

definitions.definition: The jīva is a part of the formless Śiva through beginningless ignorance, with Śiva abiding in it as fire in the sunstone; the self is eternal and distinct from body, senses and intellect (against Cārvāka and Bauddha), atomic through contact with impurity, yet in truth shining like a lamp in the heart.

Following the six-fold verse of the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā: resolve to do what pleases, avoidance of what displeases, great faith, choosing the Lord as protector, helplessness, and self-offering; Deśika makes the first five limbs and self-offering the principal.
The same qualities are the natural adjuncts of one who knows his dependence, not limbs of a means.

name: The person the size of a thumb

definitions.definition: The inner person dwelling in the heart or the middle of the body, lord of past and future, like a smokeless flame, to be drawn out from the body like the stalk from muñja grass (KU 2.1.12-13, 2.3.17; ŚU 3.13, 5.8).

name: The eight lordly powers (aṇimā and the rest)

definitions.definition: Minuteness, lightness, greatness, reach, irresistible will, control, lordship and settling things at will — arising from mastery of the elements, with perfection and invulnerability of the body; though able, the yogin does not overturn the order set by the earlier-perfected Lord (3.45, YBh 3.45).

name: Error as appearance of the indescribable (anirvacanīya-khyāti)

definitions.definition: In error an indescribable object (neither real nor unreal) is produced by ignorance for the duration of the error; the Advaita alternative to the rival theories of error.
In Sāṃkhya threefold: buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, each with its own function, sharing the five vital winds as their common function (SK 29, 33).
One inner organ functioning as mind (doubt), intellect (decision), citta (memory) and ego (I-sense); the adjunct of the jīva, not the self.
Bhāskara: the intellect and mind are real limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the soul, part of what makes it distinct from Brahman until death.

Vallabha addresses his own mind in the Antaḥkaraṇaprabodha; the mind's flowing toward the Lord is itself service (mānasī sevā), the highest form; identification with the inner organ is one of the five joints of ignorance.
The mind is to be engaged in remembrance while the tongue sings (Upadeśāmṛta 8) and instructed (Raghunātha Dāsa's Manaḥśikṣā); bhāva 'softens' the heart (citta-māsṛṇya).

name: Mind and its parts in Dvaita

definitions.definition: Mahat, ahaṃkāra, buddhi and manas are non-eternal, uncompounded products of prakṛti; manas is the sixth sense; memory arises from mental perception; above all these stands the witness, the soul's own awareness.

name: Mind and its parts in Viśiṣṭādvaita

definitions.definition: Mind (manas), intellect (mahat/buddhi) and ahaṃkāra are evolutes of prakṛti and instruments of the soul; the actual knowing is the soul's attributive consciousness working through them; ahaṃkāra as evolute is distinct from the true 'I', the self.
The last three limbs are inner compared with the first five (3.7), but outer compared with seedless samādhi (3.8).

The self who dwells in each element, faculty and being, other than it, unknown to it, having it as body and controlling it from within — the unseen seer, the immortal (BAU 3.7.3-23); 'the inner controller, the source of all' (MāU 6).

relations.note: the inner controller is the Lord seen as controlling from within

definitions.definition: The bhakti-yogin must remember the Lord at death; for the surrendered the Lord himself remembers and leads them, so no last remembrance is needed (the fourth of Varadarāja's six sayings).
Qualified student, subject, relation and purpose of a teaching.

name: The Anubhava Maṇṭapa

definitions.definition: In the tradition's account, the hall of experience at Kalyāṇa where śaraṇas of every birth, women included, shared and tested their experience under Allama on the throne of the void.

notes: Scholarly account (labeled): known chiefly from the 15th-c. Śūnyasampādane and later hagiography; its form as a formal institution is debated.

name: Non-apprehension as a means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Where no positive means of knowledge arises, non-apprehension makes known absence; absence is real and fourfold.
Not a separate means; the five suffice.
For the most intensely graced, one hearing of the teacher's word reveals one's ever-present nature; nothing is to be done (TĀ 2; Śivadṛṣṭi 7.5-6; Anuttarāṣṭikā).

name: After-cognition (anuvyavasāya): cognition is known by a further cognition

definitions.definition: A cognition does not cognize itself; it is known by a subsequent inner perception 'I know this pot'.
Words are learned from elders' usage in which they occur in action-guiding sentences; hence they express meanings already connected, principally with the 'to-be-done'.
Error apprehends a property where it is absent (Tarkasaṅgraha; Gaṅgeśa).
False cognition is destroyed by knowledge of truth, as dream-notions on waking; it has a real substrate (NS 4.2.33–37).
In extremity the rules may be set aside to preserve life, with later expiation, as in Viśvāmitra's taking the dog's haunch (MBh 12.139).
When livelihood by one's own duty fails, one may live by the next class's means (with limits), as set out in MDh 10.81ff. — though living permanently by another's dharma causes a fall (MDh 10.97).
The Vedas and the Vedāṅgas are 'lower knowledge'; the higher is that by which the imperishable is attained (MuU 1.1.4–5) — the Vedāṅga tradition's own placement of itself below realization.
Correspondingly, self-knowledge is 'the foremost of all sciences' (MDh 12.85).

Direct realization of God, which wins his highest grace; the gods are liberated when Hari becomes directly perceived to them; its scope is limited by fitness — few may see him as all-pervading, most see him within their own body.

relations.note: without knowledge there is no abundant grace

definitions.definition: Dvaita: the Veda has no author, not even God; it is eternal and intrinsically valid.
The Veda has no author: names of recensions come from expounders; apparent persons mentioned are sound-similarities; the unbroken chain of study has no beginning; creator-authorship is unprovable.

relations.note: a creator-author of the Veda is rejected

name: Liberation (apavarga) as the end of pain

definitions.definition: Absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), reached by removing false knowledge (NS 1.1.2). Mainstream view: the liberated self has neither pleasure nor cognition — there is no proof of an eternal pleasure, and seeking it would bind (NBh 1.1.22); liberation is peace in which all pain is cut off (NBh 1.1.2). Minority view (Bhāsarvajña): the cessation of pain is qualified by the experience of eternal bliss.
A destruction of pain not contemporaneous with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).

relations.note: the same state described through adṛṣṭa and the body

definitions.definition: The relation between substance and mode, Brahman and its body, substance and attribute: the second can neither exist nor be known without the first, though distinct from it; it replaces both identity and the Nyāya inherence (samavāya).

name: Apūrva (the unseen potency of ritual action)

definitions.definition: The perishable act produces an unseen potency that yields the enjoined fruit at a later time; its existence is known from the injunction itself (MS 2.1.5, Śabara).
Identified with the injunction's 'what is to be done' (kārya), known only from the Veda.

relations.note: the apūrva brings about heaven for one who desires it
Jaimini: dharma itself gives the fruit, not a lord (as reported in BS 3.2.40)

name: Injunction proper, restriction and exclusive specification

definitions.definition: An injunction enjoins what is otherwise not obtained at all (apūrva-vidhi), restricts to one of optional means (niyama) or, where something is obtained in several ways, excludes the others (parisaṅkhyā).

name: Aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam — the Kuṟaḷ's three aims

definitions.definition: The Kuṟaḷ is 'Muppāl', in three books on virtue, wealth and love; release (vīṭu) is taught within virtue (renunciation, truth, desire's end).

relations.note: dharma, artha, kāma (and mokṣa)

name: New beginning (ārambha): the effect does not pre-exist

definitions.definition: The effect is not existent, non-existent-and-existent etc. before production, but is known to have been non-existent (NS 4.1.48–50); existence does not arise from non-existence (NS 4.1.14–18); an effect is the counterpositive of a prior absence (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's pre-existent effect.

name: The path of light (arcirādi-gati)

definitions.definition: All who reach Brahman travel after death by the path of light — flame, day, bright fortnight, northern course, year, wind, sun, moon, lightning, then Varuṇa, Indra and Prajāpati as escorts — cross the Virajā and enter Vaikuṇṭha.

notes: Order and list of stations recalled; check against Śrībhāṣya 4.3 and the Arcirādi.

name: The five things to be known (artha-pañcaka)

definitions.definition: The self to attain, the Lord to be attained, the means, the goal and the obstacle, each in five kinds.

name: The five things to be known (arthapañcaka, Nimbārka)

definitions.definition: The worshipped, the worshipper, the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, the obstacles.
Supposing an unseen fact without which a seen or heard fact would be impossible — a separate means of knowledge for both Mīmāṃsā schools.

name: Arthavāda (explanatory praise and blame)

definitions.definition: Non-injunctive Vedic passages; without independent purpose, they serve injunctions by praise, forming one sentence with them (MS 1.2.1, 1.2.7); fruits stated for subsidiaries are arthavāda (MS 4.3.1).
Praise or blame; supplementing injunction or prohibition; figurative, restating, or fact-stating; praise, blame, another's deed, ancient narrative.

relations.note: arthavāda is one of the six marks of purport in Vedānta manuals, where it signals the passage's purport

notes: The reconciliation principle P7-arthavada in config/principles.md derives from this concept.

name: The method of pointing out Arundhatī (arundhatī-nyāya)

definitions.definition: Leading from the gross to the subtle step by step, as one points to a faint star by first showing a bright neighbouring one; used for the progressive teaching of the sheaths.

The 'other' samādhi, preceded by practice of the cognition of cessation, with only impressions remaining (1.18); its means is higher dispassion; the mind becomes supportless, as if non-existent (YBh 1.18); nothing is cognized in it (YBh 1.2). Bhoja: reached by rejecting every arising activity 'not this, not this' (RM 1.18).
Relatives within the sapiṇḍa circle are impure for ten days after a death (MDh 5.59) or for periods graded by class (5.83); infants under two are buried without water-offerings (MDh 5.68; YS 3.1).

The affliction of I-am-ness is the seeming identity of the power of seeing (buddhi) with the seer (2.6); in samprajñāta samādhi, asmitā is awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17); 'asmitā-mātra' is the sixth unparticularized principle (YBh 2.19) and the source of created minds (4.4); in the gaps of discernment the thoughts 'I am', 'mine' arise (YBh 4.27). Bhoja distinguishes asmitā (mere being shining in the inward-turned mind) from ahaṃkāra (apprehending objects as 'I') (RM 1.17).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): ChU 2.23.1 names three 'branches of dharma' (sacrifice/study/gift; austerity; the student living in the teacher's house) and says the one established in brahman attains immortality; MaiU 4.3 speaks of proceeding through one's own āśramas; ŚU 6.21 of those beyond the āśramas; the fourfold scheme is formulated in the Jābāla Upaniṣad (U04) and the Dharmasūtras (U02).
Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's pastimes through the eight periods of the day, the object of meditative remembrance.
Mirrored in the eight daily periods of temple service (aṣṭayāma sevā), from maṅgalā to śayana.

Brahman is defined as the source of the world's creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release; Tattvasaṅkhyāna adds happiness, sorrow, covering and light. God is the efficient cause and controller, not the material cause.

Restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samādhi (2.29); their practice destroys impurity until discriminative discernment (2.28); the last three are inner limbs (3.7). Nārāyaṇatīrtha subsumes many named yogas under the eight limbs.
Eight protections enclosing the devotee's life: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra.
The SSM's bhakta-sthala includes initiation, liṅga-wearing, ash, rudrākṣa, the five-syllable mantra and the worship and prasāda of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama among its fifteen sub-sthalas.

name: The inverted aśvattha tree of saṃsāra

definitions.definition: The world-tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, nourished by the guṇas, binding through action, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); the Anugītā's tree of Brahman (14.47).

name: 'Atat tvam asi' — Dvaita's reading of Chāndogya 6.8.7

definitions.definition: The Chāndogya teaching repeated nine times with examples is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), or 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control; it teaches difference, and the conceit of identity is condemned.

relations.note: the reading of 6.8.7 is one plank of the critique of Advaita

definitions.definition: Rites that lack their own procedure take it from an archetype (MS 7.4.1); transferred details are modified (ūha) or cancelled (bādha) where they serve no purpose (MS 10.1.1–2).

Pāśupatas ('beyond the āśramas') and Lākulas ('beyond the world', skull observance) in the Niśvāsamukha; the Svacchanda names skull-observers and Pāśupatas, and levels for Mausulas, Kārukas, Vaimalas and 'Pramāṇa'; the Kūrma lists Pāśupata, Soma and Lākula; some sources and scholars add the Kāpālikas (Somasiddhānta) as a third division.

name: Levels assigned to Atimārga goals by the Mantramārga

definitions.definition: Pāśupatas reach the Aiśvara level; Mausulas and Kārukas the Māyā principle; Vaimalas the level of Tejeśa; the 'Pramāṇa' the Dhruva; skull-observers and Pāśupatas are not re-created.

name: Rival accounts of liberation: transfer, possession, production, manifestation

definitions.definition: Liberation is the manifestation of the soul's own Śiva-nature, not transfer, possession or production of the Lord's qualities.
The Pāśupatas speak of the attainment of the Lord's qualities and powers in liberation.

notes: Which Atimārga school held which of the rejected views is a scholarly attribution, not stated in the passage.

name: Śaivism's two great divisions: Atimārga and Mantramārga

definitions.definition: The Śaiva scriptures distinguish the Atimārga - knowledge 'beyond the world', whose followers are not re-created - from the Mantra path, in whose Śiva-knowledge all Atimārga goals are attained with ease.

Immediately after death the being takes an airy conveyance-body (ātivāhika); over the first ten days the piṇḍas offered by the sons build, limb by limb, a hand-sized body for the preta, which joins the airy body; the preta feels hunger from the tenth day.
The knower who has transcended caste and stage and abides in the Self (Avadhūta 2; Kaivalya 2; Maitreya 1.13).

The innermost self: the seer of seeing, not an object of seeing (BAU 3.4.2); the light of a person when all other lights are gone (BAU 4.3.6); the person made of understanding in the heart (BAU 4.3.7); the inner controller (BAU 3.7); dearer than all (BAU 1.4.8); unborn and undying (KU 1.2.18); free from evil, old age, death, sorrow, hunger and thirst (ChU 8.7.1). It is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated upon (BAU 2.4.5).

relations.note: identity is declared in the mahāvākyas; the later schools read the identity as strict (Advaita), as body-soul relation (Viśiṣṭādvaita) or deny it (Dvaita)

name: The identity of the self and brahman

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads declare that the self is brahman: 'I am brahman' (BAU 1.4.10), 'this self is brahman' (MāU 2; BAU 2.5.19), 'that you are' (ChU 6.8.7 and refrain), 'intelligence is brahman' (AU 3.1.3); 'this self of mine within the heart is brahman' (ChU 3.14.4); 'the person yonder, I am he' (Īśa 16). How this identity is to be understood is disputed by the later schools (dsp:tat-tvam-asi, dsp:souls-one-or-distinct); this entry records only the statements.
The inner self of every being is Brahman; difference is due only to adjuncts produced by ignorance (Kāśakṛtsna's view, accepted by Śaṅkara).

relations.note: the four later-named mahāvākyas are its classic formulations

name: Worship for oneself and worship for others

definitions.definition: Worship is twofold: for oneself, in the liṅga received at initiation or on a ground-altar, for one's own fruit; for others, in temples with installed liṅgas, for the king and realm.

name: The atomic size of the self (aṇu-jīva)

definitions.definition: The soul is atomic, a knower, one per body, infinite in number.
The soul is atomic, a spark of Brahman.
The soul is an infinitesimal particle of consciousness.

notes: Nyāya, Sāṃkhya and Advaita hold the self all-pervading (see dsp:atomic-or-pervasive-self).

definitions.definition: Earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless, imperceptible atoms of spherical size (VS 4.1.1, 4.1.6–7, 7.1.26 C); at creation, atoms set in motion by adṛṣṭa combine into dyads and so on up to the gross elements (Praśastapāda); the triad (trasareṇu) is the smallest visible thing (later manuals).
Division of wholes ends in atoms, beyond the truṭi; atoms are partless, since ākāśa's 'penetration' does not apply to non-products and the alternative is an infinite regress (NS 4.2.16–25).

Renunciation by one in mortal danger (ātura), by mind and speech alone, versus renunciation in due order (krama); ritual renunciation is 'occasioned' or 'unoccasioned' (Jābāla 5; Nāradaparivrājaka 3, 5).
The Pāśupata initiate leaves the rules of his former āśrama for the restraints of a state beyond the four āśramas; open to brahmins of any āśrama.
Yāmuna objects that Śaivas devise āśramas outside the Vedic order.
Non-difference of soul and Brahman is natural; difference is due to real limiting adjuncts (body, senses, intellect), removed at liberation after death.

name: The authority of smṛti, custom and other scriptures

definitions.definition: Smṛti is authoritative as implying a Vedic source, but is set aside when it conflicts with the Veda or shows a worldly motive; customs of the good done without visible motive are authoritative (MS 1.3.1–7).
Texts of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata and the Buddhists have no authority for dharma, even where they agree with the Veda, because the sources of dharma are fixed in number (Tantravārttika).

name: The original relation of word and meaning

definitions.definition: The relation of word and meaning is not established by any person; it is known from the beginningless usage of elders (MS 1.1.5; Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).
The jīva is Brahman delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot; nothing is added or lost.

The property or relation that fixes the scope of another property — e.g. the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot' is delimited by potness and by the relation (conjunction) through which the pot is denied; central to exact definitions such as that of pervasion.

The highest renouncer, 'who has shaken off' saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, living without marks or rules, appearing child-like, mad or ghost-like (Avadhūta 1–2; Turīyātīta; Jābāla 6; Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 5).
The liberated wanderer who has shaken off all ties, behaves like a child, madman or dullard, is untouched by desire and learns from all beings.
The one beyond hope, vāsanā, meditation and ego, defined syllable by syllable in the Avadhūta Gītā.

name: The two powers of ignorance: veiling and projecting

definitions.definition: Ignorance veils the self (āvaraṇa, tamas) and projects the world and the bodies (vikṣepa, rajas).

name: The Lord's descent (avatāra / prādurbhāva)

definitions.definition: Though unborn, the Lord comes into being by his own māyā whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); knowing his divine birth frees one (4.9).
Nārāyaṇa's successive manifestations: Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi, the appearance at Mathurā; earlier the Swan and Hayaśiras (MBh 12.326.72–94).

Dvaita: the avatāras are Viṣṇu himself manifesting his eternal body of consciousness and bliss, flawless and without internal difference; apparent human weakness is displayed to delude the unfit. One must also know which beings are merely indwelt (āveśa).

The Lord's descents are real, taken by his will in bodies of pure sattva, not from karma, for protecting the good, destroying evil and above all for being accessible; knowing their divinity liberates. Principal (mukhya) descents are the Lord himself; secondary (gauṇa) are empowered souls.

notes: No fixed list of ten appears in the critical text of the Nārāyaṇīya; Kalki is not named there.

definitions.definition: The Lord (or his Puruṣa form) descends age after age in innumerable forms to protect the world; all are portions and parts except Kṛṣṇa, Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3); in the Śaiva and Śākta Purāṇas Śiva and the Goddess likewise appear repeatedly ('whenever trouble arises I will descend', DM 11).
Rūpa's classification: svayaṃ-rūpa, tad-ekātma-rūpa (vilāsa, svāṃśa), āveśa; puruṣa, guṇa, līlā, manvantara, yuga and śaktyāveśa avatāras; Kṛṣṇa is their source.

name: The lists of avatāras

definitions.definition: BhP 1.3 lists twenty-two by ordinal; BhP 2.7 adds others (Hayagrīva, Haṃsa, Hari who saved Gajendra, the Manvantara-avatāras); the Agni (2-16, 49) and Garuḍa (1.142) teach ten (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki); a count of twenty-four is common in later tradition (its membership varies and no single Bhāgavata verse gives it).

members: ten: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa/Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki

twenty-two (BhP 1.3): Kumāras, Varāha, Nārada, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Kapila, Dattātreya, Yajña, Ṛṣabha, Pṛthu, Matsya, Kūrma, Dhanvantari, Mohinī, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Rāma, Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki

name: The whole (avayavin) as a real new substance

definitions.definition: The whole is a substance over and above its parts, perceived as one, inhering in its parts (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17); the notion of the whole is also named as the cause of passion, countered by the notion of parts (NS 4.2.3; NBh).

notes: The same tradition affirms the whole's reality and prescribes attending to parts against lust — different contexts (ontology vs. practice) within Nyāya.

name: Avidyā (ignorance) in Advaita

relations.note: in the later view avidyā is the material cause of superimposition
the second covering hides the knowledge of the Supreme

definitions.definition: For Śaṅkara, the superimposition of self and not-self, removed by discrimination; for later Advaita a positive, beginningless, indescribable power with veiling and projecting powers, the cause of saṃsāra, removed by knowledge alone.
One ignorance located in and directed to pure consciousness.
Ignorances located in the jīvas, directed to Brahman.

Dvaita: a real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold — one hiding the soul's own nature and qualities, one hiding (its knowledge of) the Supreme; only the Lord removes them and grants liberation. It does not affect God or the self-luminous in the Advaita sense; Madhva's refutations deny ignorance of a self-luminous, attributeless Brahman.
Karma, which contracts the soul's knowledge and makes it take the body for the self; not an indescribable cosmic ignorance.

members: covering of the soul's own qualities

definitions.definition: Brahman becomes the world while remaining wholly unchanged, as gold in ornaments; creation is manifestation, not change.

Avimukta (Kāśī) is where Rudra gives the dying the tāraka — the mantra that carries across — so that they are freed; it is also located in the body between brows and nose (Jābāla 1–2; Muktikā 1.19–21; Rāmottaratāpanī; Tārasāra). The tāraka is identified variously as Oṃ, the Rāma mantra or the Nārāyaṇa mantra.

name: Manifestation and concealment of sat, cit and ānanda

definitions.definition: In matter only being is manifest; in souls being and consciousness (bliss concealed); in the Lord all three; creation and dissolution are manifestation and concealment.
A cognition is sublated when a later valid cognition shows its object was never as it appeared; degrees of sublatability define the levels of reality.

name: Bandhu — the correspondences between rite, cosmos and person

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas explain every element of a rite by a hidden connection (bandhu) to a cosmic and a bodily counterpart — bricks and days, metres and classes and gods, the breaths and the seers — organized on three planes: of the gods (adhidaivata), of the self (adhyātma) and of the sacrifice (adhiyajña); knowing the connection is what makes the rite work.
Carried into the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads as upāsanā — meditations on correspondences (e.g. breath-oblations satisfying senses, gods and regions, ChU 5.19–23; the saṃhitā-upaniṣad, TU 1.3).

Eight principal powers of the Lord (aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitā, vaśitā, kāmāvasāyitā), ten from the guṇas and five lesser ones, each gained by a dhāraṇā on the Lord - and all obstacles for one seeking him.

relations.note: the powers waste the time of one seeking the Lord

name: The Bhāgavata's ten marks (daśalakṣaṇa)

definitions.definition: Two lists: (1) BhP 2.10.1 - sarga, visarga, sthāna, poṣaṇa, ūti, manvantara, īśānukathā, nirodha, mukti, āśraya, the first nine told for understanding the tenth; (2) BhP 12.7.9 - sarga, visarga, vṛtti, rakṣā, antara (manvantara), vaṃśa, vaṃśānucarita, saṃsthā, hetu, apāśraya.

members: list 2.10.1: sarga, visarga, sthāna, poṣaṇa, ūti, manvantara, īśānukathā, nirodha, mukti, āśraya
list 12.7.9: sarga, visarga, vṛtti, rakṣā, antara, vaṃśa, vaṃśānucarita, saṃsthā, hetu, apāśraya

relations.note: ten marks of the 'great' vs five of the 'small' Purāṇas (BhP 12.7.10)

name: Bhairava's severing of Brahmā's head and the skull-penance

definitions.definition: Śiva as Bhairava cuts off Brahmā's fifth head, wanders as the skull-bearer to expiate brahmin-murder, and is freed at the holy tīrtha; remembering his skull-bearer's guise destroys sin.

name: Devotion (bhakti)

definitions.definition: Dvaita: firm love for Viṣṇu, greater than love for anything else, preceded by knowledge of his greatness; the sole means of liberation to which gifts, pilgrimage, austerity and sacrifice are subsidiary; it continues in liberation as eternal bliss.

Devotion to the Lord: accepting a leaf or flower offered with love (BhG 9.26), bearing the devotee's welfare (9.22), making even the wicked righteous (9.30), the means by which he is seen and entered (11.54), preferred over worship of the unmanifest as easier (12.2–5), attained in its supreme form by one who has become Brahman (18.54).
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, the highest dharma, by which the ekāntins enter Vāsudeva directly (MBh 12.336.3–4, 12.332.18).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23), the earliest Upaniṣadic use of the word in this sense; prayers and refuge in ŚU 3-6.

relations.note: by bhakti is liberation, not otherwise

notes: U05's contribution (the Gītā and Nārāyaṇīya); later bhakti theory is given by U16 and U25.

definitions.definition: The 'knowledge' that liberates is meditation — repeated, unbroken, loving remembrance of the Lord, vivid as seeing — practised daily till death and supported by the seven aids; it is bhakti, and the Lord, pleased, grants himself.

relations.note: the alternative means for those unable

definitions.definition: Tāmasa (with violence, pride, anger in view), rājasa (for objects, fame, power), sāttvika (to remove karma, as duty) and nirguṇa devotion that flows unbroken to the Lord (BhP 3.29.7-12).
Pure devotion is nirguṇa — beyond the three guṇas — unmotivated and uninterrupted like the Gaṅgā flowing to the sea (BhP 3.29.11–12); devotion in the modes is mixed.

Tāmasa (with violence, pride, envy), rājasa (for objects, fame, power), sāttvika (to be rid of karma or because enjoined), all seeing difference; beyond them nirguṇa devotion, motiveless and unbroken.
Tāmasī, rājasī and sāttvikī devotion to the Goddess, and supreme devotion beyond them.

Devotion to the Lord purifies and steadies the mind and is supreme among the means; defined as dwelling on one's own nature (VC 31); the knower is the highest devotee (Gītā 7.17); for Madhusūdana a rasa and supreme goal in itself.
Sthāyibhāva (love for Kṛṣṇa) + vibhāva (ālambana, uddīpana) + anubhāva + sāttvika-bhāva + vyabhicārī-bhāva = rasa.

The highest dharma is that which produces unmotivated, uninterrupted devotion to the Lord (BhP 1.2.6); devotion beginning with the name is the supreme dharma known to the mahājanas (6.3.22); neither yoga nor Sāṃkhya wins the Lord as devotion does (11.14.20).

Devotion is ninefold, outer and inner — setting the breath in the liṅga and the liṅga in the breath with a still mind — and arises from grace as grace arises from it; its presence, not birth, makes the bhakta; it is the power of the soul as śakti is of the liṅga (manual tradition).

name: Bhārata as the land of action

definitions.definition: Only in Bhārata are deeds done that bear fruit and lead to heaven or liberation; the gods envy those born there (VP 2.3.22-25).
The verbal suffix conveys bhāvanā: the injunction's prompting force (śābdī) and the agent's activity (ārthī), each with three expectancies — what, by what, how.
Ignorance is a positive though indescribable entity, known by perception ('I am ignorant'), inference and presumption.

name: Difference in practice, non-duality in union (SSM)

definitions.definition: The SSM assigns difference and non-difference to stages: at the māheśvara stage the worshipper rejects total non-duality because worship rests on the difference of Lord and servant, and non-duality comes only with realization (10.37–43); at aikya, difference and even lordship and boundness are seen to be imagined by māyā, and one who no longer thinks 'I am servant, Śiva master' stands in non-duality (14.8–9; 14.37). The text grounds this in its own principle that its teaching differs by sthala and by qualified aspirant (5.22–23).

name: Difference as the nature of things (bheda = svarūpa)

definitions.definition: Difference is not a separate property or negation but the very nature of each thing, apprehended together with the thing itself; hence the Advaita charge of mutual dependence in grasping difference fails.

relations.note: each of the five differences is the nature of its relata

name: Difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) of Brahman, souls and world

definitions.definition: Brahman is one as cause and many as effect; the souls and world are both different and non-different from it (Bhartṛprapañca: like ocean and waves; Bhāskara: difference through real adjuncts).
The relation is natural (svābhāvika), like snake and coils, sun and rays.
The relation is inconceivable (acintya).

relations.note: Advaita's unreal appearance
Viśiṣṭādvaita's inseparable body–soul relation; Rāmānuja criticised both forms of bhedābheda

name: The two purposes: experience and release

definitions.definition: Prakṛti acts for puruṣa's sake — for another as if for itself (SK 56, 60) — for experience and release; the conjunction is for seeing and for isolation (SK 21); like milk flowing for the calf (SK 57) or people acting to satisfy a longing (SK 58); once both purposes are fulfilled there is no motive for creation (SK 66; Gauḍapāda).

name: Bhū-maṇḍala: Meru, seven island-continents and seven oceans

definitions.definition: The earth-disc: Jambudvīpa with Meru at its centre, surrounded by the salt ocean; then Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka and Puṣkara dvīpas, each ringed by an ocean (of sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curd, milk and sweet water respectively), then a golden land, the Lokāloka range and darkness; Jambudvīpa has nine varṣas, of which Bhārata is the land of action.

notes: Order of the oceans from memory (VP 2.2-4; BhP 5.16-20); Phase D to check.

name: Enjoyment and liberation as the twofold goal (bhukti-mukti)

definitions.definition: Śiva's scriptures in all four pādas are means to enjoyment (powers, higher worlds) and to liberation; initiates are bubhukṣu or mumukṣu accordingly.

The culmination of Sanatkumāra's teaching: plenitude is happiness, there is none in the small; where one sees, hears, understands nothing else, that is plenitude; it is immortal and rests on its own greatness; it is all, and it is the self (ChU 7.23-25).

name: The soul as God's reflection (bimba–pratibimba, Dvaita sense)

definitions.definition: The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God, its original (bimba): dependent on him, resembling him, and eternally different; the reflecting 'adjunct' is the soul's own nature, so the relation is eternal. The worshipper contemplates: 'You are the original, I am the reflection, though there is a difference between us.' (Not the Advaita reflection theory, in which the reflection is Brahman appearing in an adjunct.)

In the Yoga Upaniṣads: (1) the seed-essence of the body, white (Śiva) and red (Śakti), whose retention and union are sought (Dhyānabindu, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā — summary-only); (2) the point of Oṃ; (3) identified with mind (Yogakuṇḍalī 3.5; Yogaśikhā 6.73).

name: The two material causes: bindu (pure māyā) and māyā

definitions.definition: Bindu (mahāmāyā, śuddhamāyā) produces the pure universe, the bodies of pure beings and sound; māyā (aśuddhamāyā) produces the impure universe; prakṛti with the three guṇas arises within the māyic range.

name: The bird's path and the ant's path

definitions.definition: Śuka's path (vihaṅgama): immediate liberation through inquiry; Vāmadeva's path (pipīlikā): gradual liberation through yoga over births (Varāha 4.34–42).

name: The Black and the White Yajurveda

definitions.definition: The Black (kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda mixes formulas and explanatory prose (Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka, Kapiṣṭhala); the White (śukla) keeps the formulas (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā) apart from the Brāhmaṇa. The tradition tells that Yājñavalkya disgorged the Yajus learned from Vaiśampāyana, which his fellows took up as partridges (Taittirīya), and received new Yajus from the Sun as a horse (Vājasaneyi).
Bliss is Brahman's nature; the bliss of deep sleep and the joys of objects are its reflections or fragments (Pañcadaśī 11–15).

name: Bodily loci of concentration and saṃyama

definitions.definition: Places for binding the mind: the navel wheel, the heart-lotus, the light in the head, the tips of nose and tongue (YBh 3.1); the throat-well, the tortoise channel in the chest (3.30–31); the heart, 'the small lotus-house in the city of Brahman' (3.34); on the navel wheel one knows the three humours and seven constituents (YBh 3.29).

name: The body as the city of the gods

definitions.definition: The body is the eight-wheeled, nine-gated unconquerable stronghold of the gods with a golden sheath covered in light, in which dwells the self-possessed wonder (yakṣa) that the knowers of Brahman know; Brahman entered it; the person (puruṣa) is so called from this stronghold (pur) of Brahman (AVŚ 10.2.28–33); the nine-gated lotus covered with three strands holds the same yakṣa (10.8.43); all the gods dwell in the person as cows in a stall (11.8.32).

relations.note: The 'three strands' (guṇa) of AVŚ 10.8.43 are later read as the Sāṃkhya qualities; the verse itself does not define them — contested.

notes: Readings of 'eight wheels' as the body's centres (cakras) are later and interpretive; not asserted.

definitions.definition: 'The body is a temple and the jīva in it is Śiva' (Maitreya 2.1; Skanda 10); the Yogaśikhā calls it Śiva's or Viṣṇu's temple; the Bhāvanā makes the body the Śrīcakra.

name: The body in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: The substrate of movement, senses and experience (NS 1.1.11), earthy (NS 3.1.27), produced by past karma (NS 3.2.60).

Bodies of earth (ours), water (Varuṇa's world), fire (Āditya's world) and air (Vāyu's world); some beings are not womb-born (VS 4.2.9 C; Tarkasaṅgraha); breath is air moving in the body, one but named prāṇa, apāna etc. by adjuncts.

notes: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika has no subtle-body (liṅga-śarīra) or cakra anatomy in its root texts; the transmigrating mind is atomic.

definitions.definition: One who thinks himself free is free, one who thinks himself bound is bound (Aṣṭāvakra); bondage and liberation are said of the Lord only through the guṇas (Uddhava Gītā); bondage is bondage to vāsanā (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha).

name: Brahman's real transformation into the world (pariṇāma)

definitions.definition: The world is a real transformation of Brahman through its power; effect is both different and non-different from cause.
The world is a real transformation of the Lord's power.
Transformation without change (avikṛta).
Transformation of the external power only (śakti-pariṇāma).

In dissolution Brahman has souls and matter as a subtle body without name and form; in creation, as a gross body with name and form; Brahman is thus the material and efficient cause, and the transformation is real, yet belongs to the body, leaving Brahman untouched.

relations.note: Advaita's apparent transformation
the effect is a real state of the existent cause

definitions.definition: The student, initiated by the teacher who bears him as an embryo, fills the worlds with fuel, girdle, toil and tapas; by brahmacarya and tapas the king guards the realm, a maiden wins a husband and the gods struck down death (AVŚ 11.5).

In the Upaniṣads brahman is that from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they return (TU 3.1.1); being, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1); truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1); understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); plenitude (ChU 7.23-24); the imperishable (BAU 3.8.8; MuU 1.1.5). It has two forms, formed and formless (BAU 2.3.1), and is also given only by negation — 'not so, not so' (BAU 2.3.6).
The cause of the world's origin, sustenance and dissolution, known from scripture, the purport of all the Upaniṣads.
The one non-dual reality, existence–consciousness–bliss, identical with the inner self; nirguṇa in itself, saguṇa (Īśvara) through māyā.

relations.note: the texts first speak of each separately and then declare them one

definitions.definition: In the Ṛgveda brahman is the potent formulation and prayer (its lord is Bṛhaspati); in the Atharvaveda and White Yajurveda it becomes the name of the highest: 'homage to the highest Brahman' (AVŚ 10.8.1), 'those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme' (10.7.17), Brahman entered the golden city of the body (10.2.33), 'that is brahman' (VS 32.1), 'Oṃ, the void is brahman' (VS 40.17).

Brahman is the sacred formulation and Veda, and also the first principle: 'in the beginning this was Brahman', which descended into the worlds by name and form (ŚB 11.2.3); 'Brahman the self-existent' heads the teacher-lineages (ŚB 10.6.5.9), offers itself into all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1), and as a 'great wonder' creates a second god from itself (GB 1.1.1).

relations.note: The Skambha hymn identifies the frame of the world with the highest Brahman.

definitions.definition: The one non-dual reality called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11); Bhagavān possesses the six excellences and is properly Vāsudeva (VP 6.5.74-79); Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).
One non-dual reality realised in three ways: as Brahman (effulgence, incomplete), Paramātman (indwelling partial expansion) and Bhagavān (full, with all powers); Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself.

relations.note: the one Lord seen by function

name: Creation accounts of the Brāhmaṇas

definitions.definition: Several coexisting accounts: the waters and the golden egg with Prajāpati's first words (ŚB 11.1.6); non-being as the breath-seers (ŚB 6.1.1); neither being nor non-being but mind (ŚB 10.5.3); Prajāpati as boar raising the earth (TB 1.1.3), as tortoise (ŚB 7.5.1.5); the dwarf Viṣṇu (ŚB 1.2.5); the fish and the flood (ŚB 1.8.1); worlds, lights, Vedas, utterances and Oṃ (AB 5.32).

notes: The boar, tortoise, fish and dwarf appear here before their later Purāṇic form as avatāras (U07).

definitions.definition: The Lord's command to Vallabha at Gokul: by dedicating oneself to Kṛṣṇa in initiation, the five kinds of faults of body and soul are removed, and one becomes fit for service.

Women are recorded as seers of Ṛgveda hymns and verses — Lopāmudrā, Ghoṣā, Apālā, Viśvavārā, Vāc Āmbhṛṇī, Śraddhā, Sūryā, Yamī, Indrāṇī, Śacī, Romaśā, Śaśvatī, Sārparājñī, Godhā, Agastya's sister and others — and listed together by the Bṛhaddevatā; the Atharvaveda says a maiden wins a husband by brahmacarya (AVŚ 11.5.18).
Formal question-and-answer contests on the hidden meaning of rite and cosmos, with a wager and sometimes deadly stakes (ŚB 11.6.3; 11.4.1).

The first evolute (= mahat), whose nature is determination; bearer of the eight dispositions (SK 23); it accomplishes all experience for puruṣa and discriminates puruṣa from pradhāna (SK 37); unconscious, it appears conscious by taking on the shade of consciousness (Vācaspati on SK 5).

name: Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa combined

definitions.definition: Caitanya is Kṛṣṇa who took Rādhā's mood and complexion to taste her love; also the yuga-avatāra of Kali inaugurating the chanting of the name.

Six centres (mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddhi, ājñā) in most Yoga Upaniṣads, with the thousand-petalled lotus above; the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa counts nine cakras, sixteen ādhāras; the Yogaśikhā adds four pīṭhas (Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Uḍyāna); counts and attributes differ between texts.

name: The candidate causes of the Śvetāśvatara

definitions.definition: ŚU 1.2 lists time, inherent nature, fixed order (niyati), chance, the elements, the womb and the person as causes to be considered, and rejects them singly and in combination; ŚU 1.3 and 6.1 answer that the cause is God's own power and greatness.

name: Categories (padārtha) in Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: Substance, quality, action, universal and absence (the later Bhāṭṭa manuals), with darkness and sound among substances.
Eight: substance, quality, action, universal, dependence (paratantratā), power (śakti), similarity (sādṛśya) and number (saṅkhyā).

notes: From memory (Mānameyodaya; Prakaraṇapañcikā's Tattvāloka); not checked here.

name: The fourfold scheme of the śāstra (heya, heya-hetu, hāna, hānopāya)

definitions.definition: As medicine has four parts — disease, its cause, health, remedy — so the śāstra has four: saṃsāra (what is to be avoided, future suffering), its cause (the conjunction of seer and seen), liberation (avoidance, the absence of conjunction) and its means (right seeing, unwavering discernment) (YBh 2.15; YS 2.16–26).

The self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins, the senses the horses and their objects the roads; with understanding and a yoked mind the senses are like good horses and one reaches Viṣṇu's highest step; without it one goes on in saṃsāra (KU 1.3.3-9).

The mind is a product of the guṇas (YBh 1.2), seen and not self-luminous (4.19), variegated by countless latent tendencies yet existing for another (4.24); it is one, has many objects and endures (YBh 1.32); it has seen properties (cognitions) and seven unseen ones — stilling, merit, impressions, transformation, life, movement, capacity (YBh 3.15); coloured by seer and seen it apprehends all (4.23). Commentators equate it with the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

name: The five levels of the mind (citta-bhūmi)

definitions.definition: Scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed and stilled (YBh 1.1); samādhi in the distracted mind is not yoga; samprajñāta occurs in the one-pointed, asamprajñāta in the stilled mind.

The mind is not self-illuminating because it is seen (4.19); it cannot know itself and its object at one time (4.20); if seen by another mind there would be infinite regress and confusion of memories (4.21); awareness of one's own cognition arises when unmoving consciousness takes its form (4.22).
Bound (baddha), freed (mukta) and eternal (nitya); bound souls seek enjoyment or release, and seekers of release seek kaivalya or the Lord, by bhakti or prapatti.
Five kinds: eternal, freed, bound, isolated (kevala, those in kaivalya) and seekers of release (mumukṣu).

name: Obligatory, occasional, desire-prompted and prohibited acts

definitions.definition: Nitya acts (lifelong) and naimittika acts (on occasions) are to be performed — they destroy past sin and avert the demerit of omission; kāmya acts bring their fruits and more births; niṣiddha acts bring demerit. The seeker of release does the first two and avoids the last two.
The seeker of release abstains from prohibited and desire-prompted acts, exhausts past karma by experience, and destroys it by self-knowledge with calm, restraint and celibacy.
Pots are only clay, names being a matter of speech; so the world is non-different from Brahman (ChU 6.1.4; BS 2.1.14).

name: Cognition as an adventitious quality of the self

definitions.definition: Cognition (buddhi = jñāna = upalabdhi) is a non-eternal quality of the self produced by the contact of self, mind, sense and object; it is not the self's nature and is absent in liberation (NS 1.1.15, 3.2.1–9; NBh 1.1.22).
The individual self's cognition, desire and effort are non-eternal; the Lord's are eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Vedānta's self-luminous consciousness as the self's nature.

definitions.definition: Non-injury, truth, not stealing, purity and sense-restraint for all four classes (MDh 10.63), with giving, self-control, compassion and patience (YS 1.122); the Arthaśāstra's list for all (1.3.13).

relations.note: both are class-independent lists of virtues (MDh 6.92; 10.63)

name: The conjunction of puruṣa and prakṛti (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: Their conjunction, like that of the lame and the blind, produces creation (SK 21), makes the unconscious seem conscious and the indifferent seem an agent (SK 20); it is due to non-discrimination (SS 1.55) and its cause is variously given as karma, non-discrimination (Pañcaśikha) or the subtle body (Sanandana) (SS 6.67–69).

A recurring story: the vital powers (speech, sight, hearing, mind and others) dispute which is best; each leaves the body in turn and it survives; when breath begins to leave, all are uprooted, and they acknowledge breath as best (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1; PrU 2.3-4; KauU 2.14; cf. BAU 1.3 and 1.5.21).

name: Correspondences (bandhu) between body, ritual and cosmos

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads pair items of the body (adhyātma) with items of the cosmos (adhidaivata) and of the ritual: the horse and the cosmos (BAU 1.1), the senses and deities (AU 1.1-2), mind and space (ChU 3.18), wind and breath as 'gatherers' (ChU 4.3), the fivefold (TU 1.7), combinations (TU 1.3), the person as sacrifice (ChU 3.16-17).

name: Cosmology: space, time and the worlds

definitions.definition: The path of space (deśādhvan): the worlds from Kālāgni to the highest, measured and ordered within the tattvas (TĀ 8); the path of time (kālādhvan): the cycles of time mirrored in the movement of the breath (TĀ 6); the world as the Lord's play and as phases of cognition.

notes: Chapter-level; no worlds enumerated here.

name: Courting dishonour and the exchange of merit and sin

definitions.definition: The second-stage ascetic hides his sign and provokes contempt; those who revile him receive his demerit and he receives their merit; dishonour is the highest restraint and makes his austerity complete. Kauṇḍinya: undertaken only after gaining knowledge, with impurity reduced and the teacher's leave, without breaking the restraints.

From Brahman associated with māyā arise space, air, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1) as subtle elements, then by quintuplication the gross; creation is sport, a superimposition taught to lead to the uncreated; Brahman is both material and efficient cause.

name: Creation and dissolution of the world

definitions.definition: There is no proof of a first creation or of a dissolution destroying everything; beings arise and perish continually, 'as today' (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 66–68, 113).
Things arise and perish gradually; people were always born of parents (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).

notes: Kumārila's Tantravārttika (on MS 1.3.6) nevertheless speaks of fourteen Manus in every kalpa; how this sits with ŚV 113 is not discussed in the passages checked.

name: Cosmic creation and dissolution by Maheśvara's will

definitions.definition: At the end of a Brahmā's lifespan Maheśvara wills dissolution and all products are resolved into atoms; then He wills creation for the selves' experience: through adṛṣṭa motion arises in atoms, dyads and the elements arise in order, Brahmā is born in a cosmic egg and appointed to create beings (Praśastapāda).

name: Creation accounts of the principal Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The self alone in the beginning says 'I am', divides into man and woman and emits all pairs (BAU 1.4.1-4); death/hunger at the beginning (BAU 1.2); the self creates worlds and a cosmic person whose organs become deities (AU 1); being thinks 'may I be many' and emits heat, water and food (ChU 6.2-3); non-being becomes being and an egg (ChU 3.19); from the self space, wind, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1); Prajāpati's pair of matter and breath (PrU 1.4); like sparks from fire (BAU 2.1.20; MuU 2.1.1); by tapas (TU 2.6; MuU 1.1.8).

name: Vedic ritual and scripture in Vīraśaiva teaching

definitions.definition: Basava will put the Veda to the touchstone and fetter the śāstras; worship of the moving replaces sacrifice and temple.

The SSM upholds the Veda and Āgama as one in meaning but declares sacrifices, the Agnihotra and austerities not worth a fraction of liṅga-worship or the five-syllable mantra, and useless without devotion.
A clear crystal appears red near a red flower; so the self appears with the qualities of its adjuncts.

The four ages and dharma's decline through them (MBh 3.148; Vyāsa to Śuka 12.224); the Lord's coming age after age (BhG 4.8); Mārkaṇḍeya's vision of the dissolution (3.186); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Nārada ties austerity by each varṇa to the ages (7.74).

name: Śiva as the small space in the heart

definitions.definition: The dahara of Chāndogya 8.1 is Śiva, the supreme ether that is his cit-śakti.

Giving to worthy recipients at due times and places; the sixteen great gifts (tulāpuruṣa, hiraṇyagarbha, etc.); gifts made in life or at death ease the road of the dead (Vaitaraṇī cow, umbrellas, sandals, food).
The giver's wealth does not waste away; who eats alone has only sin (RV 10.117); givers of gifts stand high in heaven and partake of immortality (10.107.2).

name: The dance of Naṭarāja and the Chidambaram tradition

definitions.definition: Śiva dances the ānanda-tāṇḍava in the hall of Chidambaram (the 'space of consciousness'), witnessed by Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda; the dance is the five acts, the raised foot being grace; Chidambaram is also the heart within the body.
Śiva as dancer in the cremation ground (Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār) and in the golden hall of Tillai (Tēvāram, Tiruvicaippā, Tirumantiram's ninth tantra).

name: Darkness as mere absence of light

definitions.definition: Darkness is not a substance but the absence of light (VS 5.2.21 C).
The devotee's stance 'I am your servant' rather than 'I am He', and the giving of the fruits of work to the jaṅgamas and the community; in modern maṭhas, free feeding and schooling.

name: The day and night of Brahmā

definitions.definition: Brahmā's day and night each last a thousand ages; at day beings emerge from the unmanifest and at night dissolve into it, again and again (BhG 8.17–19); at the end of a kalpa beings enter the Lord's prakṛti (9.7).

At death the body burns with the sacrificial implements, but the self, its owner, goes to the heavenly world; the fruits of rites are enjoyed in another world, which is why knowing the self as distinct from the body matters for ritual.

For the knower the place and manner of death do not matter - even without memory, in a holy place or an outcaste's house, he is liberated at the moment of knowledge (Paramārthasāra 83); the last moment only assists the deluded (90); funerary rites and a rite of immediate departure exist for initiates (TĀ 19, 24-25).

At death the body born of mother and father perishes, while the constant subtle body, perfumed by the dispositions, transmigrates to divine, animal or human birth according to virtue and non-virtue (SK 39–40, 44, 53); suffering from old age and death lasts until the subtle body ceases (SK 55). The knower's body falls when impressions are exhausted, and isolation follows (SK 67–68). The teachers disagreed on the subtle body at death and birth (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).

name: Death in Yoga: clinging, omens, departure

definitions.definition: Clinging to life (abhiniveśa), a fear of death found even in the newborn worm, shows past births (2.9, YBh 2.9); karma ripening as life-span is fast or slow, and saṃyama on it or omens give knowledge of death — omens personal, from other beings and from the gods (3.22, YBh 3.22); mastery of udāna gives departure at will at death (3.39); the mass of karma manifested at death forms the next birth (YBh 2.13).
At death speech merges in mind etc.; the knower of the attributeless Brahman does not depart (his prāṇas merge here); the meditator departs by the crown channel and the path of light.
Triśikhi 119–127: the cessation of throbbing at particular points of the limbs and failure to see the tip of one's tongue foretell the time of death.

name: The debts (ṛṇa) and the possibility of liberation

definitions.definition: The objection that lifelong Vedic debts, afflictions and duties leave no room for liberation is answered: 'debt' is figurative; the renunciant places the fires within the self; the stages of life allow for liberation (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).

For Yoga, sleep is itself an activity of the mind, whose support is the cognition of absence (YS 1.10) — a cognition because it is recollected on waking ('I slept happily', 'I slept heavily') — and it must be stilled in samādhi like other cognitions (YBh 1.10); the knowledge of dream or sleep may serve as a support for steadying the mind (1.38).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): in deep sleep one has merged with being, 'gone to one's own' (ChU 6.8.1); one desires no desire and sees no dream, embraced by the intelligent self, beyond sorrow (BAU 4.3.19-22); one lies in the hitā channels (BAU 2.1.19); the mind overcome by light (PrU 4.6); Indra objects that there one does not know oneself (ChU 8.11).
In deep sleep the self rests in the Lord within the heart, its knowledge contracted; it persists as 'I', as the memory 'I slept happily' shows.
In deep sleep the soul, covered by tamas, rests in Hari as Prājña, neither desiring nor seeing; yet the witness still perceives time (and the self), so deep sleep is not the absence of all awareness.

name: Deep sleep in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: In dreamless sleep there is no affliction — the analogy for liberation's possibility (NS 4.1.63).
No cognition arises in deep sleep because the mind rests in the channel purītat and lacks contact with the skin-sense, which every cognition requires (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).

notes: The purītat account is confirmed in a local commentary e-text (Subodhinī) but not traced to a root text here.

definitions.definition: The deity is that to which the offering is directed, as named in injunction or mantra; the sacrificial act, not the deity, is principal and produces the fruit; the deity's embodiment and eating are not established — mantra and arthavāda statements implying them are not meant that way (MS 9.1.6–9, Śabara).
The Brahma Sūtra reports Jaimini as denying gods eligibility for certain meditations.

name: Destiny according to the measure of Oṃ at death

definitions.definition: Nādabindu 12–16: one who dies while dwelling on each of the twelve measures attains a corresponding birth or world, the last giving the eternal Brahman.

Both born of Prajāpati, they contend over the worlds; the Asuras offer into their own mouths in pride, the gods into one another's, and so win the sacrifice (ŚB 5.1.1.1–2); the Asuras lose by barbarous speech (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24) and receive darkness and illusion from Prajāpati (ŚB 2.4.2.5).

name: The two paths after death: of the gods and of the fathers

definitions.definition: Those who know (the five fires) and who venerate faith and austerity in the forest go by the flame, the day, the waxing fortnight, the northern course, the year/gods' world, the sun, the moon and lightning to brahman and do not return; those who venerate sacrifice, works and gifts go by smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern course, the fathers' world and the moon, and return; those who know neither become small creatures (ChU 5.10; BAU 6.2.15-16; PrU 1.9-10; KauU 1.2-3; ChU 4.15.5).
The path of the gods (beginning with light) for meditators, without return; the path of the fathers (smoke, the moon) for ritualists, with return and residual karma.
The Śākta Upaniṣads declare the Goddess — Devī, Tripurā, Sītā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī — to be Brahman, the primordial nature and the inner self; the great sayings are her (Bahvṛca).

name: The Goddess as Mahāmāyā and the supreme

definitions.definition: The Goddess is eternal, the world is her form; she deludes even the wise and, pleased, liberates; she is the cause of all worlds, the primordial Prakṛti beyond Hari and Hara; all knowledges and women are her forms; she alone exists and her powers return into her.

name: The three episodes of the Devī Māhātmya

definitions.definition: First carita (ch. 1): Yoganidrā leaves Viṣṇu to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha; middle carita (chs. 2-4): the Goddess from the gods' radiance slays Mahiṣa; last carita (chs. 5-13): Ambikā with Kālī-Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers slays Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa-Muṇḍa, Raktabīja, Niśumbha and Śumbha.

name: The devotee's indifference to powers and liberation

definitions.definition: Those who desire enjoyment, liberation or powers are restless; the devotee is desireless and so at peace.
The 'supernatural capacity' given by grace is capacity to relish the Lord, not yogic power.

Dharma is the beneficial object (artha) marked by injunction: the enjoined act that joins a person with the highest good; perception cannot know it, and what the Veda states only as a means for harm (the Śyena) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose made known by the Veda — the sacrifice and the like (Arthasaṅgraha).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): created by brahman as the power of the ruling power; nothing higher; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); the three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); one's own dharma lifts the elemental self (MaiU 4.3); the self is beyond dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14).

relations.note: dharma lies outside the reach of perception and the means based on it
the declared fruit of the paradigm rites

definitions.definition: The property-bearer conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14); since everything has the nature of everything, without an enduring continuant there could be no experience or memory (YBh 3.14).

Virtue is a disposition of buddhi that leads upward but not to release (SK 23, 44); Gauḍapāda defines it through compassion, giving and the Pātañjala restraints and observances. Vedic means are impure through animal killing (SK 2; Vācaspati with Pañcaśikha). The knower of the principles is liberated in any stage of life (verse quoted by Gauḍapāda); outward signs of renunciation without knowledge are a false contentment (Gauḍapāda on SK 50); gifts given with conceit bind (Kramadīpikā); one's own duty supports meditation (SS 3.35).

name: Transformation of property, time-mark and state

definitions.definition: What holds for the mind holds for the elements and senses: transformation of property (dharma), of time-mark (lakṣaṇa: future, present, past) and of state (avasthā) (3.13, YBh 3.13); difference of sequence explains difference of transformation (3.15).

name: Dharma as the source of prosperity and the highest good

definitions.definition: That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); the Veda's authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3); merit produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); common and particular duties (Praśastapāda).

Consciousness as an attribute of the self, distinct from the self-luminous self that has it: eternal, it contracts through karma in bondage and expands to omniscience in release; it reveals objects to its owner and is manifest only to him.

For one without self-interest even in the highest reflection, complete discernment brings the samādhi called cloud of dharma (4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30), knowledge becomes infinite (4.31) and the guṇas complete their sequence (4.32). Vyāsa also names the pure mind's meditation 'dharmamegha' (YBh 1.2).

Dharman is what upholds: the first sacrifices were 'the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16); the dead go to heaven and earth 'according to dharman' (10.16.3); men break the gods' dharmas through thoughtlessness (7.89.5); the Earth bears peoples of various dharmas (AVŚ 12.1.45).
Dhī is the visionary thought the poets 'yoke' and fashion into hymns, which Savitṛ is asked to impel (RV 3.62.10, 5.81.1); with manīṣā in the heart the seers found the bond of being (10.129.4).
The liberated soul remains different from Brahman and from other souls; the five differences and gradation 'are not lost even for the liberated'.

relations.note: the five differences hold 'even for the liberated'

definitions.definition: The consecrated sacrificer is made an embryo again, the hut his womb, his garments the membranes; he is born at the final bath (AB 1.3); by consecration he makes his future world (ŚB 6.2.2.27).
Consecration for sacrifice is the twice-born's third birth, after the mother and initiation (MDh 2.169).

relations.note: both rites are conceived as births

name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: Two kinds of beings: the divine endowment (fearlessness, purity, non-harm, truth, compassion and the rest) leads to liberation; the demonic (hypocrisy, pride, anger, harshness, ignorance) to bondage; the demonic deny a Lord and live for desire (BhG ch. 16).
A sight granted by the Lord or a seer: Kṛṣṇa gives Arjuna a divine eye to see the universal form (BhG 11.8); Vyāsa gives Sañjaya sight of the whole war (MBh 6.2; BhG 18.75).

By the Lord's grace the devotee attains the eternal abode even while acting (BhG 18.56, 18.62), crosses all obstacles (18.58), sees the universal form (11.47), and is lifted from the ocean of saṃsāra (12.7); the Lord dwelling in the heart destroys the darkness of ignorance (10.11).
The temples sung by the Āḻvārs, where the Lord abides as the image; visiting and praying for his welfare (maṅgaḷāśāsana) at them is a Śrīvaiṣṇava practice.

name: The Lord's relish of his devotees' faults (doṣa-bhogya)

definitions.definition: Out of motherly love the Lord relishes the faults of those who come to him, as a cow licks its newborn calf.
The Lord overlooks the faults of the surrendered (does not see them), but does not relish faults.
Six substances — prakṛti, time, pure sattva, attributive consciousness, soul, Lord — and ten non-substances — sattva, rajas, tamas, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, conjunction and potency.
Dream objects are real while dreaming and sublated on waking; so the waking world before knowledge; the jīva sleeps in beginningless māyā.
Dream objects are created by the Lord for the dreamer's experience of the fruits of karma; they are real for their duration and for the dreamer alone.
Dreams are not false: they are produced from latent impressions (vāsanā) by the Lord as Taijasa abiding in the mind.
Dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi: the world exists only while perceived, like dream (Prakāśānanda); sṛṣṭi-dṛṣṭi: Īśvara creates an empirical world that exists before and apart from individual perception (majority view).

name: Everything is suffering for the discerning

definitions.definition: Because of the sufferings of change, anguish and impressions, and the conflict of the guṇas, everything is suffering for the discerning (2.15); the yogin is sensitive to it like an eyeball (YBh 2.15); even the happiness of contentment is suffering compared with kaivalya (YBh 3.18).

Liberation, reached by the Lord's grace: impersonal (absolute cessation of suffering) and personal (the Lord's powers of knowing and acting); it is union with and proximity to Rudra, from which there is no return.
Yāmuna reports it as mere absolute cessation of pain (opponent's report).

relations.note: Kauṇḍinya sets the Pāśupata lordship beyond others' isolation

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self gathers the particles of energy into the heart, the tip of the heart lights up, and it departs by the eye, the head or another part, followed by breath and the functions, knowledge and action holding it (BAU 4.4.1-2); speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, heat into the highest deity (ChU 6.8.6, 6.15); the creaking cart and the fruit loosed from its stalk (BAU 4.3.35-38); the inner sound is no longer heard (BAU 5.9); the breaths do not leave the dead man; the name remains (BAU 3.2.11-12).

At the appointed time illness arises, senses and strength fail, the heat of the body stirred by wind breaks the vital points, udāna rises, speech fails and sight whirls, Yama's messengers are seen; the thumb-sized person leaves the body (through an upper or lower opening according to destiny), looking back at home; the good die easily, the wicked in terror.

name: Early (pre-classical) Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: The tradition traces Sāṃkhya to Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha and to teachers such as Janaka, Vasiṣṭha and Dvaipāyana (Yuktidīpikā on SK 72). Earlier formulations are preserved in the Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma (Pañcaśikha's teaching to Janaka; Vasiṣṭha–Karāla and Yājñavalkya–Janaka dialogues with 24/25/26 principles), in the Bhagavad Gītā's 'sāṃkhya' (knowledge) and field-knower teaching (ch. 13–14, 18.13), in Caraka's account of twenty-four principles (Śārīrasthāna 1), and in Aśvaghoṣa's report of Arāḍa's teaching (Buddhacarita 12, a Buddhist report). Upaniṣadic hierarchies (Kaṭha 3.10–11) and the word 'sāṃkhya' (Śvetāśvatara 6.13) are claimed by Sāṃkhya as its scriptural basis.

relations.note: early enumerations precede the classical 25 (scholarly view)
