notes: Refers to U05 (Mahābhārata, Gītā), U30 (Caraka), U03 (Upaniṣads); chapter refs recalled, not checked.

definitions.definition: Buddhi's sāttvika form is virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power; its tāmasa form their opposites (SK 23). They are innate, natural or acquired (SK 43); they perfume the subtle body (SK 40). Virtue leads upward, non-virtue downward, knowledge to liberation, error to bondage; dispassion to absorption in prakṛti, passion to saṃsāra, power to non-obstruction (SK 44–45). By seven of them prakṛti binds herself, by one (knowledge) she releases herself (SK 63).

Existing things go unperceived through excessive distance, excessive nearness, impaired senses, inattention, subtlety, obstruction, being overpowered and mixture with the similar (SK 7); prakṛti is unperceived through subtlety (SK 8).
Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, Paiśāca (MDh 3.21).

name: The nine groups: eight pentads and one triad

definitions.definition: The Gaṇakārikā sums the system as gains, impurities, means, places, stages, purifications, factors of initiation and strengths (five each) plus three livelihoods; the teacher is the knower of these nine groups.

name: The eight qualities of the Lord (eṇkuṇam)

definitions.definition: Self-dependence, pure body, natural understanding, omniscience, natural freedom from bonds, boundless grace, infinite power, boundless bliss (from the Āgamas, used to gloss Kuṟaḷ 9).

name: The eight sāttvika signs of ecstasy

definitions.definition: Stambha, sveda, romāñca, svara-bheda, vepathu, vaivarṇya, aśru, pralaya — with degrees from smouldering to blazing.

The lists agree on eighteen but differ: VP 3.6.21-23 and BhP 12.7.23-24 name the Śiva (Śaiva); Matsya 53 and the Nārada's index name the Vāyu; KūP 1.1.13-15 names both, taking the 'Vāyavīya' as the Brahmāṇḍa. Traditional extents total four lakh verses (BhP 12.13.4-9).

Eight chief siddhis residing in the Lord (aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitā, vaśitā, fulfilment of desire) and ten from the guṇas (freedom from hunger and thirst, far hearing and seeing, speed of mind, taking any form, entering another body, dying at will, sporting with the gods, accomplishing one's resolve, unobstructed command), with lesser ones such as knowing the three times and others' minds; all are obstacles for one seeking the Lord.
There is one jīva whose ignorance projects all others, as in dream; associated with dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda (Prakāśānanda; surveyed by Madhusūdana).

name: The dharma of the one-pointed (ekāntika / sātvata dharma)

definitions.definition: Exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa, practised by the ekāntins — non-violent, knowing the self, delighting in the welfare of beings — the best dharma, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga, taught to Arjuna before the battle, handed down from the beginning of the Kṛta age (MBh 12.336).

name: The 101 sthalas of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi

definitions.definition: The SSM's full map: 44 sub-sthalas on the side of the soul (bhakta 15, māheśvara 9, prasādi 7, prāṇaliṅgi 5, śaraṇa 4, aikya 4) followed by 57 on the side of the liṅga (9, 9, 9, 9, 12, 9), from piṇḍa to jñānaśūnya.

notes: Full ordered list in pth:siddhantasikhamani-101-sthalas.

definitions.definition: Five sense capacities (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose), five action capacities (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) and manas, all from ahaṃkāra (SK 24–28); not made of the elements (SS 2.20, 5.84).
Five of knowledge, five of action and mind as the eleventh, of both natures (MDh 2.89–92).

In the womb the jīva, from the seventh month conscious, remembers its past births and prays to the Lord, resolving to lift itself out; at birth it loses that knowledge. Death is the body's ceasing to function, birth the taking of 'I am this' toward a body.

name: The formation of the body in the womb

definitions.definition: The Garbha Upaniṣad's account of the body's elements and constituents, the embryo's monthly growth, and its memory and vow in the ninth month, forgotten at birth — the tradition's own account.

name: Absorption through any emotion fixed on the Lord

definitions.definition: Desire, anger, fear, affection, oneness or friendship constantly directed at Hari bring absorption in him: the gopīs by desire, Kaṃsa by fear, Śiśupāla by hatred (BhP 7.1.30; 10.29.15; VP 4.15.2).

Evenness in success and failure is yoga (BhG 2.48); the wise see the same in all (5.18) and 'even here' conquer creation (5.19); the yogin sees the self in all (6.29) and others' pleasure and pain as his own (6.32); Jaigīṣavya is unmoved by praise and blame (MBh 12.222).

Words, i.e. the letters, are eternal and manifested by utterance: utterance is for conveying to another; the same word is recognized everywhere; utterances are counted as repetitions; there is no cause of destruction (MS 1.1.18–23, against the view of 1.1.6–11).

relations.note: the eternal word is the letters, not a sphoṭa

definitions.definition: Rules and prohibitions are equal for the knower; purity as prescribed by the half-knowing is impurity in Śiva's view (VBT 123); rules based on difference are not direct means (TĀ 4); the Mata rejects the samaya rules (TĀ 4.262); equanimity toward friend and foe (VBT 125).

Prosperity from pure food taken with restraint and recitation; taint lies in injury (VS 6.1.8–12, 6.2.6–10 C); the life-stages yield merit according to purity of intention (6.2.3–5); ablution, fasting, celibacy, residence with the teacher, forest-dwelling, sacrifice, giving and observances for the unseen (6.2.2); common duties such as non-injury, truthfulness and non-stealing (Praśastapāda).

name: Past and future exist in their own form

definitions.definition: Past and future exist in their own form because properties differ in their time-paths (4.12); otherwise knowledge of them would be objectless and action for future fruit pointless (YBh 4.12); manifest or subtle, they are guṇas (4.13).

name: Fate and human effort (daiva and puruṣakāra)

definitions.definition: Several causes are debated: nature (svabhāva, Prahlāda 12.215), time (Bali 12.217), fate (daiva), human effort (Draupadī 3.28–33) and karma (Gautamī 13.1); the Gītā counts daiva as the fifth of five causes of action (18.14), and Bhīṣma teaches that fate does not bear fruit without effort (13.6.7).

name: The fate of the one fallen from yoga

definitions.definition: One who falls from yoga is not lost: he dwells in the worlds of the meritorious, is reborn among the pure and prosperous or in a family of yogins, recovers his former understanding and, perfected through many births, reaches the highest goal (BhG 6.37–45).

name: Fitness of the student and the secrecy of knowledge

definitions.definition: Etymology is not to be taught to one ignorant of grammar, not a pupil, or incapable (Nirukta 2.3–4).
Knowledge asks to be guarded as a treasure, not given to the scornful or crooked; better to die with it than sow it in barren soil (MDh 2.113–115; VDh 2.8–9).
Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace — performed by Śiva through his power, all for the souls' release; concealment ripens mala, withdrawal gives rest.
Aintoḻil, enacted in Naṭarāja's dance: drum, fearless hand, fire, planted foot, raised foot.

Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment and grace; the bound individual performs them too - as manifesting, relishing, reflecting, planting the seed and dissolving (PH 10-11); bondage and liberation are Śiva's play (Paramārthasāra 33).

name: The five acts in the Pāñcarātra

relations.note: same five functions, differently ordered; the Śaiva list is recorded by U18/U19

definitions.definition: Concealment, creation, maintenance, dissolution and grace, performed by Śrī as Nārāyaṇa's power.

name: The five states (avasthā) in the Siddhānta

definitions.definition: Waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond-the-fourth, through which the embodied soul passes; the Tamil commentators place them at the brow, throat, heart, navel and root with decreasing numbers of instruments (35, 25, 3, 2, 1 — low confidence).
Śānta, dāsya (prīta), sakhya (preyas), vātsalya and madhura (ujjvala), in ascending intensity; each richer mood includes the qualities of the lower.

relations.note: the classical aesthetic rasas are worldly; Rūpa's are directed to Kṛṣṇa

definitions.definition: Space, air, fire, water and earth, arising from the five subtle elements; specific, and calm, turbulent or dull (SK 22, 38).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): from the self arose space, from space wind, from wind fire, from fire water, from water earth (TU 2.1); earth, wind, space, water and light as the five great elements (AU 3.1.3); the fivefold quality of yoga — earth, water, fire, wind, space (ŚU 2.12); ChU 6 has a threefold scheme (heat, water, food).

name: The five forms of God (para, vyūha, vibhava, antaryāmin, arcā)

definitions.definition: The one Lord is present as the supreme (para) in Vaikuṇṭha, the four vyūhas, the descents (vibhava), the inner controller (antaryāmin) and the consecrated image (arcā), in ascending order of accessibility; the arcā is the most accessible.
Bhagavān exists as the supreme (para), the emanations (vyūha), the descents (vibhava), the inner controller (antaryāmin) and the consecrated image (arcā).

notes: The fivefold list is standard in Pāñcarātra and Śrīvaiṣṇava writing; a single verse stating all five is not anchored here. U14 records the Viśiṣṭādvaita version.

definitions.definition: To beings (bali), men (hospitality), ancestors (svadhā), gods (svāhā) and Brahman (self-study) (ŚB 11.5.6.1–3; TA 2.10).
The householder's daily expiation of the five slaughter-places: teaching/study, water-offering, fire-offering, bali, honouring guests (MDh 3.68–70).
Nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti and śāntyatīta, the five enclosing divisions of the principles, purified in initiation.

Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla and niyati, which with māyā limit universal agency, knowledge, fullness, eternity and pervasion into the individual's 'only a little, only this, only now, only here' (Paramārthasāra 16-17).
Mādhūkara, prākpraṇīta, ayācita, tātkālika and upapanna (Sannyāsa 2.65–70).
Sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya and oneness (ekatva), which pure devotees do not accept without service to the Lord.

Ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion and clinging to life (2.3) — the five errors (YBh 2.3), called tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra and andhatāmisra (YBh 1.8); ignorance is their field (2.4); they are the root of the karmic residue (2.12); gross forms are removed by meditation, subtle ones by involution (2.10–11); they cease through the cloud of dharma (4.30).

name: The five liberations and their refusal

definitions.definition: Sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya/ekatva; pure devotees do not accept them without service (BhP 3.29.13) and desire neither powers nor freedom from rebirth (11.14.14).
Aintu malam: āṇavam, kaṉmam, māyai, māyēyam (the products of māyā) and tirōtāyi (Śiva's concealing power, called a mala by figure).
Sanskrit lists give four or five bonds: mala, karma, māyā, rodha-śakti, and for souls of the pure worlds bindu (vaindava) — enumeration varies.

name: The five means (upāya) of the Nimbārka school

definitions.definition: Karma (duty), vidyā (knowledge), upāsanā or dhyāna (meditation), prapatti (surrender to the Lord) and gurūpasatti (surrender to the guru); grace for the humble crowns them.

notes: Listed in the school's manuals (e.g. Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā); exact locus to verify.

definitions.definition: Proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32–39): e.g. 'the mountain has fire; because it has smoke; whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen; so is this; therefore so'. The members embody all four means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); a ten-member view is rejected (NBh 1.1.32).
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, going (VS 1.1.6).

Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna and samāna are all breath (BAU 1.5.3); PrU 3.5-7 assigns them places: apāna in the organs of excretion and generation, prāṇa in eye, ear, mouth and nose, samāna in the middle distributing food, vyāna in the channels, udāna leading upward at death; ChU 3.13 links them with the five openings of the heart and ChU 5.19-23 with the five first offerings of food.

relations.note: the later yoga lists of vital currents include these five

name: The five vital breaths in the Kashmirian scheme

definitions.definition: Prāṇa and apāna (waking and dream), samāna (deep sleep), udāna (the fourth, fiery, rising in the centre), vyāna (beyond, all-pervading) (ĪPK 3.2.19-20); in the āṇava practice they carry the seven blisses (TĀ 5.43-52).
Before worship: purification of oneself, of the place, of the substances, of the mantras and of the liṅga.
Protection of knowledge, austerity, absence of conflict, cessation of suffering, manifestation of bliss (Jīvanmuktiviveka ch. 4).

name: The five powers: consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, action

definitions.definition: Cit, ānanda, icchā, jñāna, kriyā - the powers of Śiva that appear as the five pure tattvas (Paramārthasāra 14).

name: The five sheaths (pañca-kośa)

definitions.definition: TU 2.1-5 teaches five selves, each within and filling the one before and each person-shaped: made of the essence of food, of breath, of mind, of understanding and of bliss, with brahman as the tail and foundation of the last; TU 3 reaches the same five as successive understandings of brahman. The TU calls them selves 'made of' (-maya); the name 'sheath' (kośa) for them is later Vedānta usage.
Food, vital air, mind, intellect and bliss sheaths, which seem to cover the self; taught progressively so that the self is known as distinct from each; the bliss-sheath is not Brahman (Śaṅkara).

notes: Correction to the task list: TU 2.1-5 is right; the word kośa is absent from TU 2 (checked locally).

definitions.definition: Bliss, leaping up, trembling, sleep and whirling (MVT 11.35; TĀ 5.107).
Powers arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1, YBh 4.1); only the mind born of meditation is without residue (4.6).
Worldly, Vedic, spiritual (Sāṃkhya-Yoga), Atimārga and Mantra, in ascending order.

name: The five streams (srotas) of Śaiva revelation

definitions.definition: The Mantra-tantras issue from Sadāśiva's five faces: Siddhānta from the upper (Īśāna), Gāruḍa from the east, Vāma from the north, Bhūta from the west (Sadyojāta) and Bhairava from the south.

name: The five systems of knowledge (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, Veda, Pāśupata)

definitions.definition: Five systems holding different views, proclaimed by Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord himself, Apāntaratamas and Śiva respectively, in all of which Nārāyaṇa is the culmination (MBh 12.337.59–67).
The non-specific elements of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, from ahaṃkāra as bhūtādi, from which the gross elements arise (SK 22, 25, 38).

Prāṇa and the others are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29; SS 2.31); the Kramadīpikā places prāṇa at mouth and nose, apāna at the navel, samāna at the heart, udāna at the throat, vyāna at the joints.

name: The five activities of the mind (pañca vṛttayaḥ)

definitions.definition: The mind's activities are five — valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep and memory — each afflicted or unafflicted (YS 1.5–11); activities and impressions produce one another in a ceaseless wheel (YBh 1.5); all have the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion and are to be stilled (YBh 1.11).

name: The five-year cycle of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: A cycle of five years (saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara, idvatsara) under Prajāpati, beginning with sun and moon together at Śraviṣṭhā in Māgha, with intercalary months to reconcile lunar and solar time.

notes: Names of the five years from memory (moderate).

name: The fivefold hierarchy of religion (laukika, vaidika, ādhyātmika, atimārga, mantra)

definitions.definition: Religious teaching is graded as worldly, Vedic, spiritual (Sāṃkhya-Yoga), Atimārga and Mantra; in the Kāmika each is spoken by one of Sadāśiva's five faces, each fivefold, making twenty-five streams.

name: Gautama's forty sacraments and eight virtues

definitions.definition: Forty sacraments (8 bodily rites, 4 Vedic vows, final bath, marriage, 5 great sacrifices, 7 cooked-food, 7 oblation and 7 Soma sacrifices) and eight virtues of the self (compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed); the virtues, not the sacraments, decide union with Brahman (GDh 8.14–25).
Prior absence, destruction, absolute absence, mutual absence (Tarkasaṅgraha), foreshadowed in VS 9.1–12.

name: Dharma and the aims of life (trivarga, puruṣārtha)

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, all treated in the epic (MBh 1.56.33); dharma is the source of artha and kāma (18.5.49); Rāma asks Bharata whether he pursues each at its time (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).

notes: U05's contribution; the Dharmaśāstra account is given by U02.

name: The four āmnāya maṭhas (the tradition's account)

definitions.definition: Śaṅkara founded four cardinal monasteries, each with a Veda, a mahāvākya, a first ācārya and Daśanāmī names: Śṛṅgeri (south; Yajur; ahaṃ brahmāsmi; Sureśvara; Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, Purī), Govardhana, Purī (east; Ṛg; prajñānaṃ brahma; Padmapāda; Vana, Araṇya), Śāradā, Dvārakā (west; Sāma; tat tvam asi; Hastāmalaka; Tīrtha, Āśrama), Jyotirmaṭh (north; Atharva; ayam ātmā brahma; Toṭaka; Giri, Parvata, Sāgara). The Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi pīṭha claims foundation by Śaṅkara too, which the others dispute. See lin:dasanami (U57) for the living order.

name: The four topics: what is to be abandoned, its cause, abandonment, the means

definitions.definition: Having understood what is to be abandoned, what produces it, its absolute abandonment and the means to that, one attains the highest good (NBh 1.1.1).

relations.note: Structural parallel with the four noble truths and with the Yoga Bhāṣya's fourfold (YBh 2.15); a parallel of form, not of doctrine.

definitions.definition: Student, householder, forest-hermit and renouncer (MDh 6.87); in sequence they lead to the highest state (MDh 6.88) with the householder as their support and best (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90); some allow free choice after studentship (GDh 3.1; VDh 7.3), 'the teachers' recognize only the householder (GDh 3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27), and Āpastamba lists them with his own order (householder first) while criticizing liberation by knowledge alone (ĀpDh 2.9.21).

name: The four attitudes (maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā)

definitions.definition: Friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the non-virtuous clarify the mind (1.33); cultivating them produces white dharma and steadiness (YBh 1.33); saṃyama on the first three yields strengths, but equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation (3.23, YBh 3.23); YBh 4.10 calls friendliness and the rest 'the abodes (vihāra) of meditators'.

relations.standpoint: as cultivations (bhāvanā) of four attitudes toward beings
relations.note: Same four names and 'vihāra' vocabulary as the Buddhist brahmavihāras (and the Jain four bhāvanās); but YS 1.33 assigns each to a class of object and aims at clarity of mind, and Vyāsa denies that upekṣā is a cultivation — the lists are not simply identical.

name: The four stages of yoga (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti)

definitions.definition: Beginning, the 'pot' stage in which breaths, mind and selves unite, familiarity (kuṇḍalinī in the suṣumnā), and completion (natural yoga, liberation while living) — Yogatattva 20ff.; Varāha 5.71–75.

name: The Siddhānta doxography of rival schools

definitions.definition: Rival doctrines are ranked in circles — outermost (Lokāyata, Buddhists, Jains…), outer (Vedic darśanas, Māyāvāda, Pāñcarātra…), inner-outer (Pāśupata, Kāpālika and other Śaiva sects), and inner (Śaiva views close to the Siddhānta) — each refuted in turn.

notes: Four groups of six are traditionally counted; membership lists low confidence.

definitions.definition: Noun, verb, preverb and particle (Nirukta 1.1); the verb signifies becoming, the noun being.
The same four read into the 'four horns' of RV 4.58.3 (Mahābhāṣya).
Pradhāna, puruṣa, the manifest (vyakta) and time (kāla) are forms of the one Viṣṇu, the supreme Brahman.
Peace, inquiry, contentment and holy company guard the door of liberation; cultivate all, or even one with all one's might, for when one is mastered the others follow.
The afflicted, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth and the knower worship the Lord; the knower is the best and is the Lord's very self (BhG 7.16–18).

Black (of the wicked), white-and-black (through external means that help and harm others), white (of those given to austerity, self-study and meditation), and neither white nor black — the yogin's, of renunciants whose afflictions are exhausted (4.7, YBh 4.7).

name: Four kinds of liberation (sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya, sāyujya)

definitions.definition: Residence in the Lord's world, likeness of form, nearness and union — reached by devotion and meditation; the Muktikā counts them as lesser than kaivalya, which comes by knowledge alone; the Kalisantaraṇa promises all four to the reciter of the names.
Dwelling in Śiva's world, nearness, sameness of form, and union — the first three 'station-liberations' (patamutti), only the fourth final.

relations.note: Vaiṣṇava lists add sārṣṭi and some reject sāyujya

definitions.definition: Renunciation from dispassion, from knowledge, from knowledge-and-dispassion, and ritual renunciation (Nāradaparivrājaka 5); the Śāṭyāyanīya's four kinds of renouncer all keep Viṣṇu's marks.

name: The four mārgas of the samayācāryas

definitions.definition: Dāsa-mārga (Appar, caryā), satputra-mārga (Campantar, kriyā), sakhā-mārga (Cuntarar, yoga), san-mārga (Māṇikkavācakar, jñāna).

name: The four pādas: caryā, kriyā, yoga, jñāna

definitions.definition: Every Āgama has four sections (vidyā/jñāna, kriyā, yoga, caryā); as a path, the initiate's conduct, ritual, yoga and knowledge.
Four successive stages, each containing all four in miniature (caryā-in-caryā etc.), with fruits sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya; the four paths of servant, son, friend and the true path.

relations.note: the textual quarters of an Āgama and the four stages share names

name: The four pādas of an Āgama

relations.note: the Tamil Siddhānta reads caryā-kriyā-yoga-jñāna as ascending stages (U18/U51)

notes: Scholarly note: the neat fourfold arrangement is an ideal that many surviving texts do not follow.

definitions.definition: Knowledge (vidyā/jñāna), ritual (kriyā), yoga and conduct (caryā); all of Śiva's scriptures are said to have them and to serve enjoyment and liberation.
The Pādma Saṃhitā is arranged in the four pādas jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā.

Constant (nitya) - the continual perishing of beings; occasional (naimittika) - of the three worlds at the end of Brahmā's day; elemental (prākṛtika) - of the whole egg into Prakṛti at the end of his life; final (ātyantika) - liberation by knowledge.
Daily (deep sleep), occasional, elemental and final (liberation).

Perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3); tradition, presumption, inclusion and non-apprehension are reduced to them (NS 2.2.1–2). Bhāsarvajña accepts only three (no separate comparison).
The four means organize the Tattvacintāmaṇi's four books.

name: The aims of human life (puruṣārtha)

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha and kāma, whose combination is the good (MDh 2.224), with mokṣa sought after the debts are paid (MDh 6.35–37); dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra in conflict (YS 2.21).
Artha is foremost, dharma and kāma being rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three pursued over a hundred-year life without mutual harm; dharma, artha, kāma in descending weight; mokṣa in old age (Kāmasūtra 1.2).

notes: The early texts speak of three aims (trivarga); mokṣa as a fourth aim (caturvarga) is systematized later.

definitions.definition: Speech is measured in four quarters; the wise brahmins know them; three are hidden and do not stir; men speak the fourth (RV 1.164.45). The verse does not name them; the Nirukta records several readings (Oṃ and the three vyāhṛtis; noun, verb, preposition, particle; mantra, ritual text, brāhmaṇa and ordinary speech; ṛc, yajus, sāman and ordinary speech; speech of creatures; speech in the self), and later schools read the levels of speech.

relations.note: Grammarians and Kashmir Śaivas later read the four quarters as the levels of speech (vaikharī, madhyamā, paśyantī, parā) — an interpretive correspondence.

name: The four kinds of established tenet (siddhānta)

definitions.definition: Common to all systems, peculiar to one system, implied (adhikaraṇa), provisionally accepted (abhyupagama) (NS 1.1.26–31).

name: The four siddhāntas of the Pāñcarātra

definitions.definition: Mantra-siddhānta (one form predominant), Āgama-siddhānta (four forms), Tantra-siddhānta (nine forms) and Tantrāntara (a four- or three-faced deity).

name: Waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): BAU 4.3 analyses this world, the other world, the junction (dream) and the state without desire or dream; ChU 8.7-12 leads Indra through the body, the dream-self and the sleeper to the self; MāU 3-7 names four quarters of the self — vaiśvānara (waking), taijasa (dream), prājña (deep sleep) and the fourth; KU 2.1.4 and AU 1.3.12 (three dwellings, three dreams); MaiU 7.11.

Waking is cognition, dream thought-construct, deep sleep non-discrimination (Śiva Sūtra 1.8-10); the fourth is enjoyed amid them and to be poured into them like oil (1.7, 3.20); spanda never departs in any state (SK 1.3).
Correlated with the breaths: prāṇa/apāna in waking and dream, samāna in sleep, udāna in the fourth, vyāna beyond (ĪPK 3.2.19-20).

relations.note: the Māṇḍūkya's scheme; the Śaivas add turyātīta

name: Waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth as forms of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: Dvaita reads the Māṇḍūkya's four quarters as four forms of the Supreme Self in all beings: Viśva presiding over waking, Taijasa creating dreams in the mind, Prājña lord of deep sleep, and Turīya at the dvādaśānta, attained by the liberated. The soul experiences the states; God governs them.

relations.note: Prājña is the form presiding over deep sleep

definitions.definition: The afflictions may be dormant, thinned, interrupted or active (2.4); Vyāsa adds a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state, found only in one whose afflictions are exhausted, 'skilled' and in his last body (YBh 2.4).

name: The four means (upāya)

definitions.definition: Anupāya (no means: realization by the teacher's word), śāmbhava (thought-free immersion), śākta (contemplation with the mind alone), āṇava (breath, seals, visualization, letters, places); graded by the intensity of grace; liberation is the same whatever the means (MVT 2.21-23; TĀ 1.165-170, chs. 2-5).

notes: The path map itself is pth:kashmir-four-upayas (owned by U51).

name: The three Vedas (trayī) and the fourth

definitions.definition: From the Puruṣa sacrifice came the verses, chants, metres and formulas (RV 10.90.9); the ṛc is speech, the yajus mind, the sāman breath (VS 36.1); the older reckoning is the threefold Veda of the śrauta rite, to which the Atharvaveda is added as the fourth in the Purāṇic account of Vyāsa's division.
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa (knowledge and strength), Pradyumna (lordship and virility) and Aniruddha (power and splendour), each nonetheless possessing all six qualities.
As reported by Śaṅkara: Vāsudeva the highest Self, Saṅkarṣaṇa the soul, Pradyumna mind, Aniruddha ego-sense — a doctrine of the soul's origination he rejects.

Vāsudeva (all six qualities), Saṅkarṣaṇa (knowledge and strength), Pradyumna (lordship and virility), Aniruddha (power and splendour), with functions in creation, maintenance, dissolution and teaching, and as objects of meditation.

name: The four yogas (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja)

definitions.definition: One yoga divided in practice into four (Yogatattva 19); for practitioners of dull, middling and superior capacity (Varāha 5.10); in the Yogaśikhā four inner stages of one great yoga, each reinterpreted (mantra as reversed haṃsa, haṭha as union of sun and moon, laya as union of knower and supreme, rāja as union of rajas and retas).

name: The paths of the Gītā: action, knowledge, meditation and devotion

definitions.definition: The Gītā names two ancient paths, knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas and action for the yogins (3.3), holds them one in result (5.4–5), adds meditation (ch. 6) and devotion (chs. 7–12), and states that some see the self by meditation, some by Sāṃkhya, some by action, and some by worship after hearing (13.24–25). Commentators rank them differently (see dsp:gita-primary-teaching).

relations.note: devotion is one of the Gītā's paths and, for the Vaiṣṇava readers, their culmination

definitions.definition: The beginner (prāthamakalpika), the honey-stage yogin (madhubhūmika) with truth-bearing insight, the one whose insight is light (prajñājyotis) who has mastered elements and senses, and the one beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrāntabhāvanīya) whose aim is the mind's dissolution (YBh 3.51).

Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years plus junctions (4,800, 3,600, 2,400, 1,200), dharma declining through them; the means of each age differ (meditation, sacrifice, worship, singing the name).
Bhīṣma's fourfold dhyāna-yoga; in the first meditation reflection, reasoning and discrimination arise (MBh 12.188.1, 12.188.15), and the persevering sage reaches the happiness of nirvāṇa.
The four Vedas, six Vedāṅgas, Purāṇa, nyāya, mīmāṃsā and dharmaśāstra (YS 1.3).
Kauṭilya's fourfold division of sciences — investigation (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Lokāyata), the triple Veda, economics, governance (Arthaśāstra 1.2).

Seven upper worlds - Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Mahar, Janas, Tapas, Satya - and seven lower worlds (the pātālas) within the cosmic egg; the first three (trailokya) are dissolved every night of Brahmā; the yogin rises through them (BhP 2.2.22-31).

name: The creation of beings and the worlds by guṇa

definitions.definition: Creation of beings is fourteenfold: eight divine, five animal, one human (SK 53); the upper worlds abound in sattva, the root in tamas, the middle in rajas, from Brahmā to a blade of grass (SK 54); even there suffering from old age and death is common (SK 55; SS 3.53). The Kramadīpikā names the eight divine classes (daiva, paiśāca, rākṣasa, yākṣa, gāndharva, aindra, prājāpatya, brāhma) and five animal (domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, plants).

name: A full life of a hundred autumns

definitions.definition: The ideal of a full human life: 'may we see, live, hear and speak a hundred autumns' (RV 7.66.16; VS 36.24); the living set a boundary against death and ask for long life (RV 10.18.4); rites for long life (AVŚ 8.1).
The āhitāgni is burned with his own fires and implements (ŚB 12.5.2); a funeral mound is later built (ŚB 13.8); the funeral mantras are collected in TA 6.
Cremation with the Yama hymn, burial of infants, water-offerings, bone-collection, ten days' impurity, the first-year offerings and the uniting with the ancestors (ĀśGS 4.1–6; YS 3.1–2; MDh 5.59–68).

relations.note: the two communities disagree on whether branding is required

definitions.definition: Through the prenatal viṣṇubali the Vaikhānasa is a Vaiṣṇava before birth and does not take the branding initiation.
The five sacraments, beginning with branding, make one a Vaiṣṇava.

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: The yoga was handed down from Vivasvat to Manu to Ikṣvāku and the royal sages, then lost and taught again (BhG 4.1–3); Arjuna becomes a disciple (2.7); knowledge is learned from seers of truth by prostration, inquiry and service (4.34); it is not to be told to one without austerity or devotion (18.67); Sañjaya heard it by Vyāsa's grace (18.75); after instruction the disciple decides (18.63); Kṛṣṇa cannot repeat it (Anugītā 14.16.11); knowledge may be received even from a śūdra (MBh 12.306.85), yet Vidura, of śūdra birth, defers to Sanatsujāta (5.41.5).

name: The Lord as the real agent (hari-kartṛtva)

definitions.definition: The soul's acts are done by Hari's impulsion within it; one performs prescribed duties without desire, remembering Hari as doer and goal, so that all activity of mind, speech and body is his worship — this is 'yoga'.

name: The gods as names of the One

definitions.definition: Several hymns hold that the many gods are names or forms of one: 'they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni … the One Being the inspired speak of in many ways' (RV 1.164.46); the poets shape the one bird into many with words (10.114.5); 'great is the one asura-ship of the gods' (3.55); the one name-giver of the gods (10.82.3); 'that is Agni, that the Sun … that brahman' (VS 32.1). Yāska: the one Self of the deity is praised in many ways, the other gods are its limbs (Nirukta 7.4). The liturgy nonetheless addresses each god as a distinct recipient.

relations.note: The names-of-the-One teaching is one aspect of the Saṃhitās' teaching on the One.

notes: The modern labels 'henotheism/kathenotheism' are scholarly metadata and not used here.

definitions.definition: Dvaita: liberation comes only by Viṣṇu's grace (his 'choosing'); knowledge and devotion win it; it is graded, and it reaches lower beings through the higher (Vāyu and the gods).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self is attained by the one whom it chooses (KU 1.2.23; MuU 3.2.3); 'by the grace of the creator' one sees the Lord (ŚU 3.20; KU 1.2.20 reads 'serenity of the constituents'); favoured by him the goose gains immortality (ŚU 1.6); Śvetāśvatara knew brahman by God's grace (ŚU 6.21); refuge in God (ŚU 6.18).

relations.note: without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation

name: Grace (anugraha) as the Lord's fifth act
notes: U18/U19 record Śiva's five acts; this is the Pāñcarātra contribution.

definitions.definition: Grace is the last of Lakṣmī's (the Lord's) five acts — concealment, creation, maintenance, dissolution, grace.
Aruḷ is Śiva's own power, always with the soul like light with the eye, embodied as the guru; liberation is by grace alone, the soul's effort being itself grace-enabled.
The Lord's grace protects in every danger and 'took me as his own' — the devotee's whole hope.

name: Grace through the hierarchy of souls

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu gives liberation, Vāyu by his permission; liberation, knowledge and their fruits come to the lower by the grace of the higher, not otherwise.

name: Gradation of the manifest self (plant, animal, man)

definitions.definition: The self is increasingly manifest from plants (sap) to animals (thought) to man, who has the most intelligence, knows tomorrow and seeks the immortal through the mortal (AA 2.3.2).

name: The grades of Śaiva initiates
notes: Standard in Siddhānta paddhatis (e.g. Somaśambhu); no verse-level teaching recorded in this pass.

definitions.definition: Samayin (after samaya-dīkṣā), putraka (after nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, seeking liberation), sādhaka (consecrated to master a mantra for powers) and ācārya/deśika (consecrated teacher who may initiate and install).
Samayin, putraka, sādhaka (seeker of powers, bubhukṣu) and ācārya; the mumukṣu is liberated at death.

Yogins are of nine kinds — mild, middling or intense in means, each with mild, middling or intense ardor; for the intensely ardent samādhi is near, and nearest for the intense in means and ardor (1.21–22, YBh 1.20–22).

name: The classification of Purāṇas by the guṇas

definitions.definition: Matsya 53.68-69: sāttvika Purāṇas glorify Hari, rājasa Brahmā, tāmasa Agni and Śiva, mixed ones Sarasvatī and the ancestors. The Padma (as cited) assigns six Purāṇas to each guṇa; the Garuḍa's Brahmakāṇḍa gives a different, graded list. Śaiva texts counter with lists in which most Purāṇas glorify Śiva (not checked here).

name: The four levels of the guṇas (guṇa-parvan)

definitions.definition: The guṇas exist at four levels: the particularized (sixteen: five elements, ten senses and mind), the unparticularized (five tanmātras and I-am-ness), the mere mark (mahat) and the unmarked (pradhāna) (2.19, YBh 2.19); subtlety of objects ends in the unmarked (1.45).

name: The guṇa-classification of knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness

definitions.definition: Knowledge, action, agent, intellect (buddhi), steadfastness (dhṛti) and happiness are each sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (BhG 18.19–39) — sāttvic knowledge seeing one imperishable being in all, sāttvic happiness 'poison at first, nectar at the end'.

name: The guru in the minor Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The guru removes darkness ('gu' darkness, 'ru' its remover) and is the supreme Brahman (Advayatāraka); he is Hari (Brahmavidyā), Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Sadāśiva (Yogaśikhā 5); his word breaks the pot that hides the lamp; without his grace the natural state is hard to reach (Varāha 2.76).
The teacher is the means (Śiva Sūtra 2.6); the revelation of the Śiva Sūtra and its lineage (Kṣemarāja; Bhāskara, Vārttika 1.3-9).
Secrecy and qualification: the teaching is for those devoted to the teacher, heroic and thought-free (VBT 157-160); the lineage from Śrīkaṇṭha and Durvāsas (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-122).
To souls who know only human forms Śiva appears in human form as the guru (as a hunter uses a decoy deer), or teaches from within to the more advanced; the guru is to be served as Śiva.
In initiation the ācārya becomes Śiva by ritual identification; Śiva's power acts through him.

relations.note: shared idea of the guru as the divine

name: Teacher, lineage and initiation in Dvaita

definitions.definition: Knowledge descends from Nārāyaṇa (as Vyāsa, author of the Brahmasūtras) through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge from the teacher's grace, hears the commentaries and reflects on them with companions; the ācārya initiates the prepared devotee into Hari's worship; renunciants receive the praṇava and new names; debate (vāda) between teacher and disciple serves the truth.

One initiating guru and many instructing gurus; the Lord within (caitya-guru); the guru is to be honoured as Kṛṣṇa's representative; qualification is knowledge of Kṛṣṇa, not birth; guru and disciple should examine each other.
Initiation is given by the ācārya's descendants (the Gosvāmī houses); the disciple's relation is to the Lord through the guru's family.

Three forms of the one Śiva met by the devotee: the guru who initiates (Śiva himself present, 11.19–21), the liṅga he gives, and the jaṅgama — the moving Śivayogin whose sight, touch and worship sanctify (11.37–43); the first three of the eight shields.

The guru is Brahman, not other than the Self; 'gu' darkness, 'ru' its remover; the roots of meditation, worship, mantra and liberation are the guru's form, feet, word and grace; the teaching is secret, for the devoted only.
The avadhūta's many teachers; the self as its own teacher.

name: Haṃsa — the swan / the self as breath-mantra

definitions.definition: The inner self as the 'swan' that moves with the breath (haṃ-sa), reversed as so'ham 'I am He'; meditated as a bird with fire and moon as wings; its knowledge (haṃsa-vidyā) is called the only means to liberation (Brahmavidyā) and the inner sacrifice (Pāśupatabrahma); also the name of the third kind of renouncer.

relations.note: Viewed as a mantra the haṃsa is the ajapā-gāyatrī.

definitions.definition: The sixteen names 'hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare, hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare' taught by Brahmā to Nārada as the means of crossing Kali, bound by no rule (Kalisantaraṇa).

Viṣṇu is supreme over all — full of qualities, free of defects, beyond the perishable and the imperishable; this is the great purport of all scripture, and 'Brahman' and all names primarily denote him.

name: The identity of Hari and Hara

definitions.definition: Passages that make Viṣṇu and Śiva one: the Kūrma's Īśvara Gītā, Hari as all the gods in Gajendra's rescue, Śambhu as the foremost Vaiṣṇava (BhP 12.13.16); set against sectarian passages that subordinate one to the other.

relations.note: unity vs Śiva's superiority to Brahmā and Viṣṇu

name: The heart as seat of inner seeing

definitions.definition: The seers searched in the heart (RV 10.129.4); a fixed light is set in the heart (6.9.5–6); the wise see with heart and mind (10.177.1); Vena saw the highest hidden in secret (VS 32.8); the mind is heart-seated (34.6).

name: The petals of the heart lotus and the moods

definitions.definition: The mind's dispositions follow the petal of the eight-petalled heart lotus on which the jīva rests — virtue, sleep, cruelty, sin, play, movement, love, charity — with the centre as dispassion or all-knowing (Haṃsa; Dhyānabindu).

name: The pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa)

definitions.definition: Five in the sūtra: inconclusive, contradictory, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, kālātīta (NS 1.2.4–9).
Five in the Navya list: inconclusive (three kinds), contradictory, counterbalanced, unestablished (three kinds), sublated; the adjunct (upādhi) makes a reason unestablished as to pervasion.

notes: The correspondence of the old and new lists (arrows) is the usual later reading, not stated in the sūtra.

definitions.definition: Objects are higher than the senses, mind higher than objects, intellect higher than mind, the great self higher than intellect, the unmanifest higher than the great, the person higher than the unmanifest; there is nothing higher (KU 1.3.10-11; restated at 2.3.7-8 with sattva).

relations.note: the top of the ladder is the puruṣa

definitions.definition: The Golden Germ who arose in the beginning as the one lord of what exists, giver of self and strength, whose shadow is immortality and death; born from the great waters; named Prajāpati (RV 10.121); Prajāpati moves unborn in the womb and is born in many ways (VS 31.19).

relations.note: One of the Saṃhitās' creation accounts.

name: The three aspects of the internal power: hlādinī, sandhinī, saṃvit

definitions.definition: Pleasure, existence and knowledge aspects of the Lord's own power (VP 1.12.69); the essence of hlādinī is love, whose summit is Rādhā.

name: How the one appears as many (the three theories)

definitions.definition: Three explanatory theories of the jīva and Īśvara: limitation (avaccheda, Bhāmatī), reflection (pratibimba, Vivaraṇa) and semblance (ābhāsa, Sureśvara); the tradition treats them as alternative methods (prakriyā) converging on identity.

name: The heart and the space within it

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self dwells in the heart, smaller than a grain and greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3); the small space in the lotus of the heart contains heaven and earth (ChU 8.1.1-3); the heart has five openings (ChU 3.13); from it spread the channels (KU 2.3.16; PrU 3.6); the person made of mind in the heart (BAU 5.6; TU 1.6).
The Heart of Bhairava, seed of the universe (Parātrīśikā 24); the heart-space of meditation (VBT 49).
Consciousness as vibrancy is 'the Heart of the Supreme' (ĪPK 1.5.14).

Forms of the formless are imagined for the sake of worshippers (Rāmapūrvatāpanī 1.7); yogins see Śiva in the Self, images are for the ignorant (Darśana 4.59); for the renouncer image-worship leads to rebirth (Maitreya 2.26).
Perception begins as a bare, non-conceptual awareness like an infant's, followed by determinate cognition of the thing with its universal etc.; both are perception.
Indra, strengthened by soma, slays the serpent Vṛtra who enclosed the waters, releasing them and becoming king of what moves and rests (RV 1.32).

Rites internalized: the haṃsa as fire and praṇava as thread (Pāśupatabrahma), eating as oblation to the prāṇas (Prāṇāgnihotra), the world offered into the fire of knowledge (Sannyāsa 2.100), the renouncer's five inner sacrifices (Śāṭyāyanīya 12–17).

name: The inner topknot and sacred thread

definitions.definition: Knowledge is the topknot and the Self, Brahman or praṇava the sacred thread of the renouncer, replacing the outer ones (Jābāla 5; Brahma; Paramahaṃsa; Parabrahma; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.77–85).
'One thinks he has drunk soma when they crush the plant; the soma the brahmins know, of that no one eats' (RV 10.85.3); only the 'cooked' by tapas attain Soma's filter (9.83.1).

relations.note: An instance of the ritual substance understood beyond its outer form.

definitions.definition: Solstices, equinoxes, new moon and eclipses are the movements of breath between iḍā and piṅgalā and between the base and the head (Darśana 4.39–47; Śāṇḍilya 1.15).

The sacred places are located within: Vārāṇasī between brows and nose, Prayāga in the heart, etc. (Darśana 4.48–59; Jābāla 2); the suṣumnā is the supreme tīrtha (Yogaśikhā 6); wandering to outer tīrthas is 'lowest of the low' (Maitreya 2.21).

name: The internalization of ritual (in its Saṃhitā beginnings)

definitions.definition: Already in the Saṃhitās the rite is referred beyond its outward form: the gods sacrificed the sacrifice (RV 10.90.16); the soma the brahmins know none eats (10.85.3); the first act of the fire-altar is the yoking of mind (VS 11.1); honouring a guest is itself the sacrifice (AVŚ 9.6); mind is the one in which the seven-hotṛ sacrifice is spread (VS 34.4).

notes: The fuller internalized rites (e.g. the prāṇāgnihotra of the Āraṇyakas) are U02's.

definitions.definition: Already in the Brāhmaṇas the rite is carried into the person: the self-sacrificer knows each rite builds his own self (ŚB 11.2.6.13); fires are built of mind and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3); the Agnihotra is 'truth offered in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1.4); feeding brāhmaṇas is 'offering into Brahman' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).
In the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads: the inner Agnihotra of speech and breath (KU 2.5), the breath-oblations at meals (ChU 5.19–24), the sacrifice in the body (Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
The renouncer deposits the sacred fires in himself (MDh 6.38) and the true self-sacrificer sees the self in all beings (MDh 12.91).

relations.note: outer rite and inner rite are two poles of one doctrine

definitions.definition: All cognitions are valid of themselves; a capacity not present in a thing cannot be given by another; validity is set aside only by a cognition of the object's being otherwise or knowledge of a defect in the cause — neither of which can arise for the authorless Veda.
Validity is known by inferring the cognition from the knownness it produces.
Validity is known with the self-luminous cognition itself.
Validity is known by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the cognition (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).

relations.note: intrinsic validity plus the absence of an author makes the Veda unassailable

name: The balance of the two deeds (iruviṉaiyoppu)

definitions.definition: When good and bad karma come to balance and the soul regards both alike, and āṇava is ripe, grace descends and the guru appears.

name: The personal liṅga worn on the body (iṣṭaliṅga)

definitions.definition: Śiva himself, given by the guru at initiation as a small liṅga worn on the body for life and worshipped on the palm; Śiva abides in it from the moment of initiation, so it needs no invocation; the outer liṅga is to be worn 'knowing it is of that same form' as the inner.
The body bearing the liṅga is itself the temple: the moving (jaṅgama) against the fixed (sthāvara) shrine.

name: Iṣṭāpūrta, merit of sacrifice and gift

definitions.definition: The merit of what one has sacrificed and given, with which the dead are reunited in the highest heaven (RV 10.14.8).

relations.note: Merit rejoins the dead in Yama's heaven.

definitions.definition: Classical Sāṃkhya posits no established Īśvara: the SK does not mention one; Gauḍapāda argues that the attributeless Īśvara could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds that Īśvara is not established (1.92–99), that karma, not a Lord, yields fruit (5.2–12), and that effects depend on ahaṃkāra, not Īśvara (6.64) — yet it admits emergent lords: the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Vijñānabhikṣu salutes the Lord (Sāṃkhyasāra 1.1.1).

Īśvara is a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), the teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27). He is ever free and ever Lord, his pre-eminence resting on excellent sattva, without equal or superior; his purpose is compassion for beings (YBh 1.24–25). Devotion to him brings samādhi near (1.23, 2.45); he favours the devotee by mere intention (YBh 1.23). He is not the material of the world. Vijñānabhikṣu makes knowledge of the Supreme Lord the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord' (Īśa 1); the lord of all, controller of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6); the one God, Rudra-Śiva, the māyin, lord of lords, whose power is innate, who gives grace and frees from fetters (ŚU 1.10, 3.2, 4.10, 6.7-9); Indra/prāṇa as lord of the world who makes one do good or bad (KauU 3.9).

Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati: no means of knowledge reaches him, a bodiless being cannot will creation, compassion would create only happiness, and purposeless action is unintelligible; later Bhāṭṭas dedicate dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
No Īśvara directs dharma and adharma or moves atoms; fruits arise from dharma and adharma with their circumstances.
The Brahma Sūtra reports Jaimini's view that dharma itself gives the fruit.

relations.note: differs from liberated puruṣas in never having been bound

definitions.definition: Brahman associated with (or reflected in) māyā: omniscient, omnipotent creator and ruler, giver of fruits of action, object of devotion; his lordship depends on adjuncts and is real at the empirical level.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness whose reflection is the jīva.

name: Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha and the transmission of Yoga

definitions.definition: Īśvara is the teacher even of the ancients (1.26); the first knower out of compassion taught the doctrine to Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25). Commentators read 'anuśāsana' (1.1) as Patañjali's re-teaching of yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and give the lineage Pitāmaha — Śeṣa (Patañjali) — Vyāsa — Vācaspati and Vijñānabhikṣu. In the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).
The Lord produces the effect as he wills, all at once or in sequence, depending neither on karma nor on the soul; karma bears fruit only when favoured by his will.
Rejected: a Lord who distributes unequal lots independently would be partial; the Lord's creation depends on beings' karma (BS 2.1.34), and a merely efficient Lord is inconsistent (BS 2.2.37).

name: The Lord's play as the ground of creation

definitions.definition: The Lord's activity is play: in play he produces, favours and conceals the effect; the teacher's activity is for grace.

A distinct self with qualities — free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness; with merit, knowledge and concentration; with eightfold lordship — who assists human effort and makes it fruitful, sets karma and the elements in motion, is like a reliable person and a father to beings (NS 4.1.19–21; NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker proved by inference (NK 5.1; Gaṅgeśa); worshipped by all schools under different names (NK stabaka 1).
Maheśvara, by whose will creation and dissolution occur; saluted as the cause at the start of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha. The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra itself does not name Īśvara.
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort, author of the Veda, whose will fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Yoga's Īśvara is a special puruṣa who is not the maker of the world; Nyāya's Īśvara is the efficient cause.

definitions.definition: The world is real, established by perception, scripture ('viśvaṃ satyam') and above all the witness, whose deliverances are never sublated; the Advaita definitions of falsity and inferences to it fail.
Since 'that' (omniscient Lord) and 'thou' (limited self) conflict in their direct meanings, the contradictory elements are dropped and pure consciousness retained, as in 'this is that Devadatta'.

Offspring of unions across classes form further birth-groups (jāti) — 'with the grain' (anuloma) or 'against the grain' (pratiloma) — each with its occupation; lineages may rise or fall in status over seven generations of marriage (MDh 10.5–65).

name: The six impediments to a universal (jātibādhaka)

definitions.definition: Uniqueness of the individual, equivalence of extension, cross-division, infinite regress, loss of nature, lack of relation (Udayana).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): being enters the elements 'with this living self' (ChU 6.3.2); life does not die (ChU 6.11.3); the bird that eats the fruit and grieves beside the Lord (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7); the jīva as a hair-tip part, fit for infinity (ŚU 5.9); the elemental self bound by karma (MaiU 3.1-2).

Eternal, atomic, self-luminous as 'I', a knower with attributive consciousness, an agent dependent on the Lord, an enjoyer, essentially his servant (śeṣa), a mode of Brahman; countless, and remaining distinct in liberation.

Dvaita: each soul is eternal, sentient, atomic, dependent, a reflection of God, different from God, from matter and from every other soul, with an innate and unalterable fitness; its identity with Brahman is denied as contrary to experience and scripture.

The individual self is consciousness conditioned by the inner organ (and ignorance): agent, enjoyer and transmigrant through adjuncts, in truth Brahman; explained by limitation, reflection or semblance.

name: The soul as a part (aṃśa) of Brahman

definitions.definition: A part delimited by real adjuncts.
A naturally distinct part and power, dependent on the Lord.
A spark-like part of Brahman with bliss concealed.
A separated part (vibhinnāṃśa) of the marginal power.

name: The soul as the Lord's marginal power, his eternal servant

definitions.definition: The soul is Kṛṣṇa's marginal (taṭasthā) power, eternally his servant, able to turn toward the internal power (devotion) or the external (māyā).

By nature souls are of three classes: fit for liberation (gods, sages, ancestors, rulers, the best humans), ever-transmigrating (middling humans), and fit for blinding darkness (daityas, rākṣasas, piśācas, the lowest humans). The texts state this plainly; souls of the third class reach darkness especially through hatred of Hari.

relations.note: the three classes are the broadest division of the gradation

definitions.definition: Steady wisdom apprehending identity; virtues arising without effort; no licence for misconduct; living for others' good; unbroken realization in activity and absorption.

After perfect knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to cause, but the knower remains embodied through the momentum of impressions, like a potter's wheel (SK 67); knowledge burns future karma like burnt seeds (Gauḍapāda). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the one liberated while living and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers — otherwise the blind would lead the blind (3.78–84).

Vyāsa: with the cloud of dharma the afflictions are uprooted and karmic residues destroyed; 'when afflictions and karma cease, the wise one is liberated while living', since error is the cause of becoming (YBh 4.30); one whose afflictions are exhausted has no karma for a future birth (YBh 2.12) and is 'in his last body' (YBh 2.4).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the word is later, but the texts say the mortal 'attains brahman here' when all desires in the heart are released (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14), that the knots are cut 'here' (KU 2.3.15; MuU 2.2.8), that the best knower of brahman delights in the self yet is active (MuU 3.1.4), and 'if one has known it here, there is truth' (Kena 2.5).

In the minor Upaniṣads: the state of one who, knowing the Self, is freed while the body continues on the momentum of prārabdha; marked by freedom from 'I' and 'mine', from vāsanā and from the mind's properties (Muktikā 2; Varāha 4; Tejobindu 4); the dissolution of mind 'with form'.

In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha: the seventh stage; outwardly engaged, inwardly cool; mind 'dead' (manonāśa); one acts as custom requires, like one half-asleep. In the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā: the liberated is neither distracted nor absorbed, the same wherever he is. In the Rāma Gītā: living out prārabdha free of ego until merging.
The perfected one does not notice the body, which lives on while its karma lasts; though in the body he is not in it.
The destruction of ignorance, completion of human aims, is the state of liberation while living.
On knowledge, past karma is destroyed and future karma does not cling, but the body continues till prārabdha is exhausted; the knower is free while living.
Rejected: while the body remains, karma remains; the knower or surrendered is assured of release but released only at death.
Denied by Bhāskara.
Redefined as the state of one who serves Hari in all conditions.
After grace and knowledge the body continues by prārabdha; the jīvanmukta acts as Śiva's servant among devotees, untouched by deeds.
The initiate liberated by nirvāṇa-dīkṣā is released at death; the body continues until prārabdha is exhausted.

name: Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in Kashmir Śaivism

definitions.definition: Firm realization of oneness with consciousness while the body is experienced (PH 16); the liberated sees all as his own glory and regards the knowable as not different from himself (ĪPK 4.12-13).
The liberated acts without taint, his conduct free of rule, his worship inner (Paramārthasāra 61, 69-80).

relations.note: shared name; the Kashmir Śaivas add that the world is known as one's own real manifestation

definitions.definition: The perfected one does not notice whether the body stands or sits, as a drunk his cloth; the body lives on until its karma is spent, but he does not re-enter the dream (BhP 3.28.37-38); Keśidhvaja acts without attachment and is freed.

name: Combination of knowledge and works (jñāna-karma-samuccaya)

definitions.definition: Liberation is attained by knowledge of Brahman combined with the lifelong performance of one's prescribed duties; works are not abandoned upon knowledge.

notes: Opposed by Śaṅkara and Sureśvara, for whom knowledge alone liberates (see dsp:jnana-karma-samuccaya).

name: Limbs of yoga redefined as knowledge

definitions.definition: In the Tejobindu, Triśikhi, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa and Darśana each limb is given an inner Vedāntic meaning — e.g. prāṇāyāma as seeing all as Brahman, āsana as indifference, dhyāna as 'so'ham' — alongside or instead of the bodily practice.

name: Knownness (jñātatā) and the inference of cognition

definitions.definition: Cognition is not perceived; it produces a property of manifestness in the object, from which it is inferred.
The soul's fulfilment is service to the Lord with Śrī, done for his pleasure alone, here and eternally in Vaikuṇṭha; its highest form is service to his devotees.

The goal: when discrimination arises, prakṛti — her purpose served — ceases for that puruṣa like a dancer who has shown herself (SK 59, 65–66); the knower remains embodied for a time (SK 67), and at the body's end attains isolation that is certain and final (SK 68). It is not the manifestation of bliss, nor going anywhere, nor annihilation (SS 5.74–83), but the destruction of obstacles (SS 6.20) and the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1, 3.85). Strictly, bondage and release belong to prakṛti (SK 62).

The absence of the conjunction of seer and seen (2.25); arising when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55) and from dispassion even toward the highest power (3.50); the return of the guṇas, their purpose fulfilled, to their source, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34). Vyāsa: then the puruṣa is the light of its own form alone, stainless, alone (YBh 2.27, 3.55).
Enjoyment of one's own self apart from the Lord; a lesser goal.
Not permanent.
Permanent, with no return.

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's account of liberation

definitions.definition: Dvaita: time is eternal (as a flow) and non-eternal (in its divisions), directly perceived by the witness even in deep sleep; everything seen or remembered is set in it.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): time is one of the candidate causes rejected by the Śvetāśvatara (1.2, 6.1); God is the maker of time (6.2, 6.16); brahman has two forms, time and the timeless; 'time cooks all beings in the great self' (MaiU 6.14-16).
An eternal insentient substance without guṇas, part of the Lord's body, ruling change in the realm of play and present but not ruling in the eternal realm.

Time is the seven-reined horse whose wheels are all beings; in Time are tapas, the eldest and brahman; Time is lord of all and father of Prajāpati; from Time arose the waters, brahman, tapas, the quarters and the Vedas (AVŚ 19.53–54).

name: Kālāmukha monasteries, assemblies and royal preceptors

definitions.definition: Temple-based maṭhas (chief among them the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāve) grouped in the Śakti- and Siṃha-pariṣads, their pontiffs learned in many systems and serving as rājagurus; the maṭhas fed, taught and healed.

name: The dharma of the Kali age

definitions.definition: Kali is full of faults, and gambling, drink, illicit women, slaughter and gold are its dwellings; yet in Kali merit comes quickly: singing the name gives what earlier ages won by meditation, sacrifice and worship, and śūdras and women gain merit easily by service.
Congregational chanting of the name is the dharma of Kali, inaugurated by Caitanya; in Kali there is no other way.
In Kali all paths are ruined; Kṛṣṇa alone is the refuge.

name: Kalpa, the day of Brahmā and his lifetime

definitions.definition: A thousand cycles of four ages (mahāyugas) with fourteen Manus make a day of Brahmā (kalpa), followed by a night of equal length; Brahmā lives a hundred years of such days, in two halves (parārdha); the present is the first day of his second half (Śveta-Vārāha kalpa, seventh manvantara, Kali age - tradition's reckoning).

Countless unsurpassed qualities: the six (knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour) and those that make him approachable — compassion, motherly love, gracious condescension, accessibility, lordship; they belong to him in every form.

relations.note: the Pāñcarātra's six are the core set

name: Desire as the first seed of mind

definitions.definition: Desire (kāma) arose in the beginning as the first seed of mind (RV 10.129.4; AVŚ 19.52.1).
Ear-ornament/necklace, rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash and sacred thread, with skull and khaṭvāṅga as sub-insignia; knowing and wearing them is claimed to prevent rebirth (opponents' report).

name: Death and the hells in the Kapila Gītā

definitions.definition: The attached householder dies in torment, is led by Yama's messengers, suffers in hells the fruit of his deeds and returns to birth.

name: The principles in the Kapila Gītā

definitions.definition: Twenty-four principles — five gross elements, five subtle elements, ten senses, and the fourfold inner instrument (mind, intellect, ego, citta) — with time as the twenty-fifth, identified with the Lord.

relations.note: one of the counts the Uddhava Gītā treats as valid by intention

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): first taught in secret — 'one becomes good by good action, bad by bad' (BAU 3.2.13); 'as one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes'; desire → resolve → action → result (BAU 4.4.5); rebirth 'according to action and knowledge' (KU 2.2.7; KauU 1.2); conduct determines the womb (ChU 5.10.7); action does not cling to the knower (ChU 4.14.3; Īśa 2); the knots cut, actions are exhausted (MuU 2.2.8).

In Sāṃkhya virtue and non-virtue are dispositions of buddhi, not of puruṣa (SK 23; SS 5.25); they carry the subtle body upward or downward (SK 44) and ripen as experience; the fruit of action comes from karma, not from a governing Lord (SS 5.2); with knowledge they cease to act as causes — future karma burnt like seeds, present karma exhausted (SK 67; Gauḍapāda).
Karma is primarily the enjoined act; its fruit comes through the apūrva; dharma and adharma produce bodies and experiences until exhausted.
The way of action is deep: one must know action, wrong action and inaction, and see inaction in action and action in inaction (BhG 4.16–18); actions burnt in the fire of knowledge (4.19, 4.37).

name: Karma and rebirth in Kashmir Śaivism

definitions.definition: Karma bound by false knowledge perishes in the fire of knowledge like a roasted seed; the knower is untouched by merit and demerit; the one who dies midway on the path enjoys higher worlds and completes the path in another birth (Paramārthasāra 55-62, 96-102).

name: Classes of action for the seeker

definitions.definition: Desire-prompted (kāmya) and forbidden (niṣiddha) acts to be avoided; daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika) and expiatory (prāyaścitta) rites and meditations (upāsana) to be performed for purity.
Sin not yet fructifying, latent, as seed and about to fructify are destroyed in sequence by devotion; even prārabdha yields.

Karma cannot be exhausted by experiencing it, for new karma is always made; ritual works win only the lowest grace (heaven); release needs grace won by knowledge; prārabdha karma still runs its course.

relations.note: purified by duties the student acquires the four means

definitions.definition: Works cannot remove ignorance, being not opposed to it; performed without desire they purify the mind and generate the desire to know (or knowledge); knowledge excludes the sense of agency, so works and knowledge are not combined.

name: Karma of mind, speech and body

definitions.definition: Ten wrongs — three mental, four verbal, three bodily — with mind as instigator; bodily faults lead to plant-births, verbal to bird and beast births, mental to low human births (MDh 12.3–9); the residue of deeds shapes birth, form and fortune (ĀpDh 2.1.2.3); one's own conduct raises or lowers class in the next birth (ĀpDh 2.5.11.10–11).

name: The six means of distinguishing rites

definitions.definition: A different word, repetition, number, quality, context and name (Śabara's list at MS 2.1.1; treated in adhyāya 2).

Rooted in the afflictions, the karmic residue ripens in this or a future birth (2.12); while the root remains it ripens as birth, life-span and experience (2.13); the mass accumulated in a life, manifested at death, produces one birth (YBh 2.13); merit only removes obstruction, like a farmer opening a dyke (4.3).

name: No fruit without deed, no deed without fruit

definitions.definition: Body and experience arise from the fruits of one's own past acts (NS 3.2.60); accounts that would make one reap what one did not do (akṛtābhyāgama) are rejected (NS 3.2.38, 3.2.72 DCS); even the Lord brings about fruits without annulling what each has done (NBh 4.1.21).

name: The Kula ritual as interpreted by Abhinavagupta (summary)

definitions.definition: Tantrāloka 29 treats the secret Kula worship with a consort and Kaula substances as the outward form of the union of Śiva and Śakti in consciousness, for qualified initiates; one born of such a union is 'yoginībhū', a vessel of knowledge (29.162-163). Summary only.

notes: Restricted subject: summary only.

definitions.definition: Honest labour in one's own occupation is worship — 'work is Kailāsa' — and must not be interrupted even for guru, liṅga or jaṅgama, nor gather beyond the day's need.

relations.note: the fruit of kāyaka is shared as dāsōha

name: Knowledge-itself and the means of knowledge (kevala / anupramāṇa)

definitions.definition: Valid knowledge is what accords with its object; it is knowledge itself (of God, Lakṣmī, yogins, others) and its three means (perception, inference, authoritative word); memory is valid; presumption and comparison are inference.
Prior absence, absence by destruction, mutual absence and absolute absence; if absence were not real, curd would be in milk and consciousness in earth.

Knowledge: perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge; non-knowledge: doubt, error, indefinite cognition, dream (Praśastapāda); non-knowledge arises from defects of senses and impressions (VS 9.25–27 C).

name: Kinds of initiation (dīkṣā) in the Āgamas

definitions.definition: Initiation acts on the soul, not caste or body; it is the cause of the other means and, as nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, destroys past and future karma through mantra-power, the present body continuing like a potter's wheel. It is samaya- (or viśeṣa-) and nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, followed by consecrations (abhiṣeka) of sādhaka and ācārya; for the incapable the observances are purified away ('seedless', nirbīja), for the capable they remain ('with seed').
Initiation (dīkṣā) into Bhagavān's mantras and worship; in Śrīvaiṣṇava usage the five sacraments.
Samaya, viśeṣa and nirvāṇa dīkṣā, then consecrations (ācāryābhiṣeka, sādhakābhiṣeka); nirvāṇa-dīkṣā with or without 'seed'.
Seven modes: by look, touch, word, thought, scripture, yoga and the fire rite.
Self-manifest (svayambhu), divine (daiva), bāṇa, sages' (ārṣa) and man-installed liṅgas are the supports of temple worship; the liṅga given by the guru is the support of one's own worship.

name: The grades of the descent of power (śaktipāta)

definitions.definition: Grace depends on the Lord's freedom alone; intense, middling and mild, each in three degrees (nine grades); its signs are devotion to Rudra, mantra-success, control of beings, completion of undertakings and poetic power with sudden knowledge of scripture (MVT 2.14-16; TĀ 13); graded by scripture (TĀ 13.300-301).

notes: Nine-grade scheme recalled from TĀ 13 / Tantrasāra 11 (chapter level).

definitions.definition: Originative (utpatti), applicatory (viniyoga), performative (prayoga) and eligibility (adhikāra) injunctions.
Meditators on the qualified Brahman go by the path of light to the Brahma-world and are liberated with its ruler at the end of the cycle.

name: Liberation together with Brahmā at the dissolution

definitions.definition: Knowers who go by the path of light to Brahmā's world reach the Supreme together with Brahmā at the great dissolution; some others are liberated without departing.

Every cognition unfolds as emission (sṛṣṭi), persistence (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhāra) and the nameless (anākhya), in the object, the means of knowledge and the subject - twelve Kālīs in all (TĀ 4.145, 4.148-172).

name: The six means of fixing sequence

definitions.definition: Direct statement, purpose, textual order, position, the order of principals, and the order once begun.

name: For the rite or for the person

definitions.definition: An element is either for the sake of the rite or for the sake of the person; what is for the person is what gives him delight (MS 4.1.1–2). Self-knowledge is argued by Bhāṭṭas to be both (Śāstradīpikā).
Austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.1), for cultivating samādhi and thinning the afflictions (2.2); taught for the unconcentrated mind; austerity must not disturb the mind (YBh 2.1).

name: Kṛṣṇa as the Lord himself (svayaṃ bhagavān)

definitions.definition: Kṛṣṇa is the source of all avatāras, not an avatāra of Viṣṇu (BhP 1.3.28 as governing statement).
Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa is the highest form of Brahman.
Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Brahman with Rādhā.

The moment is time at its utmost minuteness and alone real; sequence is the flow of moments; hours and days are constructions of the buddhi (YBh 3.52); sequence is apprehended at the end of a transformation (4.33); saṃyama on moment and sequence gives discriminative knowledge (3.52). Permanence is twofold: unchanging (puruṣa) and changing (guṇas) (YBh 4.33).

name: Perishable, imperishable and the Supreme Person

definitions.definition: Following Gītā 15.16–18: the perishable are all souls whose bodies perish (Brahmā, Śiva and the gods included); the imperishable is Lakṣmī; the Supreme Person beyond both is Hari.

Several teachings are placed in the mouths of kṣatriyas who teach brahmins: Ajātaśatru teaches Gārgya Bālāki, noting that this reverses the natural order (BAU 2.1); Pravāhaṇa Jaivali says the five-fires knowledge had never before gone to brahmins (ChU 5.3.7; BAU 6.2.8); Aśvapati teaches the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11); Citra teaches Āruṇi (KauU 1.1); Janaka is taught by and rewards Yājñavalkya (BAU 4).

name: The field and the knower of the field (kṣetra–kṣetrajña)

definitions.definition: The body and all of prakṛti with its modifications is the field; the one who knows it is its knower; the Lord is the knower in all fields; knowledge of both is true knowledge (BhG 13.1–6, 13.33–34).
Vāsudeva is the knower of the field (MBh 12.326.38).

relations.note: the knower of the field corresponds to the Mokṣadharma's twenty-fifth ('the knower is the twenty-fifth', 12.294.38)

definitions.definition: Kula is the totality of powers (Śakti), Akula Śiva beyond it; consciousness finally dissolves into the Akula abode (TĀ 4.170); the Kaula rule dwells in Bhairava's heart (Parātrīśikā 4).

The coiled power lying at the base of the suṣumnā, blocking the door to Brahman; awakened by fire, breath and mind she rises through the centres and knots to unite with Śiva in the crown; 'bondage for the ignorant, liberation for yogins'; in the Varāha the supreme power from which breath, fire, bindu, nāda and mind arise.

relations.note: Rising kuṇḍalinī pierces the three knots (the knots obstruct her path).

definitions.definition: Śrī is Nārāyaṇa's eternal, independent power whose body is the six qualities, who performs his five acts, and in whom one takes refuge.

name: Lakṣmī as eternally free and dependent

definitions.definition: Lakṣmī is the highest dependent being: eternally untouched by sorrow, never bound, 'imperishable' (akṣara) in body, superior to all souls in every quality, yet infinitely below and wholly dependent on Viṣṇu; as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā she is the higher prakṛti.

name: The incarnation of Śiva as Lakulīśa

definitions.definition: The tradition's accounts: Śiva enters an abandoned corpse in a cremation ground and becomes the brahmacārin Lakulī at Kāyāvatāra, with four disciples (Liṅga P.); the Lord in a brahmin's body descends at Kāyāvataraṇa and teaches Kuśika at Ujjayinī (Kauṇḍinya); Śiva is born to Viśvarūpa and Sudarśanā, enters the body of the dead infant, and at last merges into the Brahmeśvara liṅga at Kāyāvarohaṇa (Kāravaṇa-māhātmya).

notes: Scholarly dating (c. 2nd c. CE) is kept on tch:lakulisa as labelled metadata.

definitions.definition: Bhaṇḍāsura, born from the ashes of Kāma burnt by Śiva, conquers the worlds; Lalitā arises from the gods' sacrificial fire, weds Kāmeśvara, defeats Bhaṇḍa with her śaktis and revives Kāma.

name: The last thought and resolve at death

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'as his resolve is in this world, so he becomes on departing' (ChU 3.14.1); 'with whatever thought one has, one enters breath' (PrU 3.10); 'mind, remember what was done' (Īśa 17); meditation on Om until death determines one's world (PrU 5); the refuge in three sayings at death (ChU 3.17.6).

What one remembers at death shapes what follows: Bharata dying absorbed in a fawn became a deer; Ajāmila calling 'Nārāyaṇa' was rescued; remembrance of Nārāyaṇa at the end is the highest gain of life (BhP 2.1.6); the dying should meditate on the Lord (12.3.50); the yogin whose karma remains should recall yoga at departure (MkP 42.16-17); Kāśī tradition speaks of Śiva's instruction at death.
What one thinks at death determines what one becomes (Yogaśikhā 1.31; Nāradaparivrājaka 5).
Remembering or uttering the name at death saves even a sinner (Ajāmila); Haridāsa died with the name and Caitanya's form before him.
Tradition's account: Vallabha took renunciation at the end of life, left a final instruction (Śikṣāślokī) and entered the Ganges at Kāśī.
Liberation after death: the devotee attains the Lord's nature by his grace (Daśaślokī 2, 9).

relations.note: absorption at death vs absorption through a lifelong emotion

definitions.definition: Whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes, having been absorbed in it; so one should remember the Lord at all times (BhG 8.5–7); the guṇa prevailing at death determines the next birth (14.14–15).

name: The levels of speech (parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī)

definitions.definition: Speech sprouts in parā, leafs in paśyantī, buds in madhyamā and blossoms in vaikharī; reversed, sound dissolves (Yogakuṇḍalī 3.18–19); from the power at the base arise all letters, mantras, scriptures and the seven notes (Yogaśikhā 3).

Parā (supreme speech = reflexive awareness itself, ĪPK 1.5.13), paśyantī, madhyamā and vaikharī; the Kashmir Śaivas add parā above the grammarians' three and deny that paśyantī is ultimate (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1).

Release comes by the exhaustion of karma: avoiding desire-prompted and prohibited acts, performing obligatory and occasional ones, knowing the self, and exhausting past karma by experience, so that no new body arises; release is an absence, hence permanent, not an enjoyment of pleasure (Kumārila); the absolute dissolution of the threefold bond, without bliss (Pārthasārathi); some Bhāṭṭas held that innate bliss manifests.
The absolute end of embodiment through complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma, reached by abstention, experience and self-knowledge with calm and restraint; the self remains in mere being.
The sūtra and Śabara speak of heaven as the fruit of rites; release as a goal is added by the later teachers; later Bhāṭṭas teach dharma offered to Īśvara as the cause of the highest good.

In the Gītā: brahmanirvāṇa (2.72, 5.24–26), non-return (8.15–16), entering the Lord after knowing him by devotion (18.55), freedom from birth, death and old age beyond the guṇas (14.20); in the Mokṣadharma: the twenty-fifth becoming alone (kevala) on awakening and attaining the state of the twenty-sixth (12.294, 12.296).
Entry through the sun and the vyūhas into Vāsudeva, the ekāntins entering him directly (MBh 12.332.13–18).

relations.note: release, being an absence, is permanent; heaven, being produced, perishes

definitions.definition: Not produced but eternal: the bodiless nature of the self, the attainment of bliss and cessation of sorrow, revealed by knowledge; one in all (BS 3.4.52); no return.

name: Liberation while living

definitions.definition: The Gītā speaks of creation conquered 'even here' by those established in sameness (5.19), of brahmanirvāṇa near on every side for self-knowers (5.26), and of the one of steady wisdom and the one beyond the guṇas; Janaka claims freedom while ruling (MBh 12.17.18) and Sulabhā tests the claim (12.308).

notes: The word 'jīvanmukta' is later; see U13 for the Advaita concept.

name: The stages of life (āśrama)

definitions.definition: Bhṛgu teaches the four āśramas (MBh 12.184); Yudhiṣṭhira's wish to renounce is answered with arguments for the householder's and king's stage (12.7–36); Janaka teaches Śuka that the āśramas are to be passed in order, though one already free may renounce (12.312–313); the son urges seeking the self without delay (12.169).

notes: U05's contribution; the Dharmaśāstra account is given by U02.

name: The limbs of yoga in the Yoga Upaniṣads
