definitions.definition: The Yoga Upaniṣads give six-limbed (Amṛtanāda — with tarka; Dhyānabindu; Yogacūḍāmaṇi), eight-limbed (Darśana, Śāṇḍilya, Triśikhi, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa, Varāha, Yogatattva) and fifteen-limbed (Tejobindu) schemes, often with a second, knowledge-based definition of each limb.
The whole path is framed as the relation of the soul (aṅga, 'limb') to Śiva (liṅga): knowledge is the aṅga and the eternal knowable the liṅga; the aṅgaliṅgī has each mounted in the other.

name: Liṅga-initiation

definitions.definition: The guru bathes the disciple with consecrated water, whispers the five-syllable mantra secretly into his right ear, installs a liṅga in the disciple's breath and places it in his hand, to be worn for life; dīkṣā gives knowledge and destroys the fetters and removes the duality of guru and disciple.
Initiation is open to all — women, children and every occupation; Allama received the liṅga from the yogi Animiṣa.

notes: Secrecy: the mantra is given 'secretly' (nigūḍham, SSM 6.21).

name: Śiva as niṣkala and sakala; the liṅga

definitions.definition: Śiva alone is both partless Brahman and with form, so he alone is worshipped both in the formless liṅga and in the image; the unmarked (aliṅga) Śiva is the root of the mark (liṅga).

The subtle body, produced first, unattached, constant, made of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, the ten capacities and the five subtle elements), transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions, without enjoying (SK 40); it needs a support like a picture or shadow (SK 41) and plays its parts like an actor (SK 42). The subtle bodies are constant; the bodies born of mother and father perish (SK 39). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra calls it 'seventeen, one' (3.9) and admits a conveying (ātivāhika) body (5.103). Vindhyavāsin denied the subtle body (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).

relations.note: corresponds to the subtle body of Vedānta's three bodies, though composed differently (interpretive)

name: Death as union with the liṅga

definitions.definition: The death of a devotee is liṅgaikya; the dead are buried seated, holding the liṅga, rather than cremated, and no ancestral rites or death-pollution follow; the saints' deaths are narrated as union at sacred places.
One who at death drinks water in which a rudrākṣa has been pressed, thinking of Rudra, goes to Rudra's world.

notes: Burial practice details are general knowledge of the community (moderate confidence), not from a cited text.

name: Union of liṅga and aṅga (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya, aikya)

definitions.definition: Liberation as the soul's immersion in the ocean of Śiva's bliss, free of longing for sense-pleasure; the self contemplated as dissolved in the sky of consciousness by the nature of sāmarasya; 'like water in water' in common exposition.
Death of the devotee is itself called liṅgaikya: Basava at Kūḍalasaṅgama, Allama and Akka at Kadaḷi.
In Śrīpati's Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita the soul (aṅga) qualified by devotion and Śiva (liṅga) qualified by Śakti attain union in equal essence; the non-duality is real, not an appearance.

name: The appearance of the liṅga of fire

definitions.definition: While Brahmā and Viṣṇu disputed supremacy a boundless column of fire appeared; neither could find its ends; Śiva appeared from it.

The wise act unattached for the welfare and cohesion of the world, as Janaka did and as the Lord himself acts though he has nothing to gain, without unsettling the understanding of the ignorant (BhG 3.20–26).

name: The Lord in the heart of all beings

definitions.definition: The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); he is the self seated in the heart of all (10.20), the source of memory and knowledge (15.15), seated in the heart of all as the light of lights (13.17), and dwelling in his devotees' hearts destroys their darkness (10.11).

name: Powers, wealth and self-enjoyment as lower ends

definitions.definition: Wealth, lordly power (aiśvarya) and even kaivalya are ends the Lord can grant but lesser than him; the wise devotee seeks nothing but the Lord (ananya-prayojana); seeking other ends is an obstacle.
The central consciousness whose unfolding gives the bliss of consciousness (PH 17-18).
The gap between breaths, cognitions, pleasure and pain, where reality shines (VBT 24-26, 61-62, 103, 126).
The unmeṣa between one thought and the next (SK 3.9).

Four Upaniṣadic sentences of identity — prajñānaṃ brahma, ahaṃ brahmāsmi, tat tvam asi, ayam ātmā brahma — understood through implication as conveying a partless meaning; the means of liberating knowledge.

name: The four great sayings (mahāvākya)

definitions.definition: A later grouping (Advaita tradition) of four Upaniṣadic sentences, one from each Veda: prajñānaṃ brahma (Ṛgveda: AU 3.1.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (White Yajurveda: BAU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (Sāmaveda: ChU 6.8.7), ayam ātmā brahma (Atharvaveda: MāU 2; also BAU 2.5.19). The Upaniṣads themselves do not use the word 'mahāvākya'.

U04 contribution: the minor Upaniṣads treat the four sayings as a secret initiatory teaching (Śukarahasya), assign one to each Veda and maṭha (Maṭhāmnāya), give them to the renouncer at initiation (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka) and read them as the Goddess (Bahvṛca).

notes: Ref correction: AU 3.1.3 is also cited as AU 3.3 (two-level numbering); both refer to the same passage.

name: The great vow of the skull (mahāvrata)

definitions.definition: Living as a Kapālin with a skull-bowl and skull-staff, in imitation of Bhairava's penance for Brahmā's head; by it a man becomes an ascetic (as reported).
The Lākula observance 'beyond the world' with skull and khaṭvāṅga.

relations.note: the vow re-enacts the myth

name: The four Māheśvara schools of the doxographers

definitions.definition: Vācaspati: Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Kāruṇika-siddhāntins, Kāpālikas.
Yāmuna and Rāmānuja: Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas, Śaivas.
Guṇaratna: Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Mahāvratadharas, Kālamukhas.
Āṇava mala, one with many powers, ripens through embodied experience and Śiva's concealing power until it is ready to be removed; then śaktipāta.
Malaparipākam, with iruviṉaiyoppu, is the condition for the descent of grace.
The eleventh organ, partaking of both sense and action capacities, whose function is construction (saṅkalpa) (SK 27).

name: The mind (manas) as one and atomic

definitions.definition: One per body, atomic; its mark is the non-simultaneity of cognitions; apparent simultaneity is like the firebrand circle, due to its swift movement (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56–59); cognition belongs to the self, not the mind (NS 3.2.19).
An eternal atomic substance, one in each body because efforts and cognitions are not simultaneous (VS 3.2.1–3, 7.1.30 C); its first motion at creation is caused by adṛṣṭa (VS 5.2.14).

Mind is swiftest of flying things (RV 6.9.5), it wanders far and can be called back from Yama (10.58), it is yoked by the inspired (5.81.1; VS 11.1); the Śivasaṅkalpa verses call it the divine far-goer of waking and sleep, the one light of lights, knowing, thought and steadfastness, the immortal light within, holder of past, present and future, in which the Vedas are set and all thought woven, the heart-seated charioteer (VS 34.1–6); desire was its first seed (RV 10.129.4).
The Goddess's supreme abode - the jewel island with enclosures of metals and gems and the Cintāmaṇi palace (Devī Bhāgavata), and Lalitā's city Śrīnagara with its enclosures (Lalitopākhyāna).

name: The maidservant's mood (mañjarī-bhāva)

definitions.definition: Summary: the aspiration to serve Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa as one of Rādhā's young maidservants, seeking no union with Kṛṣṇa, taught in Raghunātha Dāsa's Vilāpakusumāñjali and cultivated through the inner perfected identity; its specifics are transmitted by the guru.

notes: Recorded at summary level; the lineages treat detailed identity instruction (siddha-praṇālī) as confidential.

definitions.definition: The part of the Veda recited as prompting the performance; meaningful like any sentence against the objection that mantras are meaningless (MS 1.2.31–40, 2.1.32).
Mantras serve by recalling items connected with the performance.

Śiva has no body of māyā; for worship and grace he is given a body of mantras — the five brahma-mantras (Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta) as his faces and the six limb-mantras — made of the pure śakti; the mantras themselves are conscious beings in office.

relations.note: scripture as Sadāśiva's body (U08)

definitions.definition: 'Veda is the name for mantra and brāhmaṇa'; Brāhmaṇas are injunctions, the rest explanatory statement (ĀpŚS 24.1.30–33).

name: The division of Śaivism into Atimārga and Mantramārga
members: Atimārga (Pāśupata, Lākula; later also Kālāmukha/Kāpālika in scholarly schemes)
Mantramārga (Siddhānta; Bhairava tantras — Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha; Vāma; Gāruḍa; Bhūta)

relations.note: the Mantramārga's dual goal marks it off from the Atimārga

notes: U17 owns the Atimārga's own account (lin:atimarga). The 'householder vs ascetic' contrast follows scholarly synthesis (Sanderson) of the texts and is to be checked against the Niśvāsamukha in Phase D.

definitions.definition: The Mantramārga's scriptures rank the Atimārga (the ascetic Pāśupata and Lākula paths, for liberation alone) below the Mantramārga, whose initiates may seek powers and enjoyments as well as liberation, and which is open to householders.

name: Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha
notes: The Kāmika says only that the Bhairava tantra is 'twofold'; the names Mantrapīṭha/Vidyāpīṭha are from other scriptures (e.g. Jayadrathayāmala) and scholarly synthesis.

definitions.definition: The twofold Bhairava tantra of the southern face (Kāmika: 'twofold'): the Mantrapīṭha centred on male Bhairava forms such as Svacchanda, and the Vidyāpīṭha centred on goddesses and feminine mantras, subdivided into Yāmala and Śakti tantras.

name: The manvantaras and the fourteen Manus

definitions.definition: Each day of Brahmā has fourteen Manus: Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama (Auttama), Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata (the present), then the Sāvarṇis beginning with Sūrya-Sāvarṇi (the Devī Māhātmya's Suratha); each interval has its Indra, gods, seven sages and avatāra; names of the later Manus vary between Purāṇas.

notes: MkP 50-100 (chapter colophons checked) narrates the manvantaras.

definitions.definition: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, cognition (NS 1.1.10).
Inhalation and exhalation, closing and opening of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, modifications of the other senses, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort (VS 3.2.4 C).

Known through the Trika: Mata scriptures reject the samaya rules and lineage-based exclusions in favour of realizing one's own unbounded awareness, and rank between Dakṣiṇa and Kula (or between Kula and Trika) in the hierarchy of revelations.

The fifty letters in natural order (mātṛkā, A to KṢA) as the emanation of the tattvas (Parātrīśikā 5-9), and in the scrambled order mālinī uniting vowels and consonants (Śiva and Śakti); the ground of limited knowledge when unrecognized (Śiva Sūtra 1.4) and of liberation when awakened by the teacher (2.7).

name: Fifty letters, fifty forms of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: The fifty letters designate fifty forms of Viṣṇu — Aja, Ānanda, Indra, Īśa, Ugra, Ūrja, Ṛtambhara and so on — used in nyāsa and worship.

The word appears as Indra's many-formed powers (BAU 2.5.19, quoting RV 6.47.18), as deceit (PrU 1.16), and in the Śvetāśvatara as the Lord's power: 'know prakṛti to be māyā and the great Lord the māyin' (4.10), from which the māyin projects the world and in which the other is confined (4.9); knowing him there is 'the cessation of all māyā' (1.10). Whether māyā here means the world's unreality is not stated by the texts (see dsp:world-real-or-appearance).
The Lord's beginningless indescribable power of three guṇas, inferred from its effects, by which Brahman appears as the world; neither being nor non-being; removable by knowledge.

relations.note: One entity viewed cosmically (māyā) and individually (avidyā) in the Vivaraṇa/Saṃkṣepaśārīraka usage; distinguished by Vidyāraṇya.

definitions.definition: Māyā is the wondrous, creative or cunning power of a god: by it Varuṇa measured out the earth (RV 5.85.5), Indra goes in many forms (6.47.18); the wise see the bird anointed with the asura's māyā with heart and mind (10.177.1).

name: Māyāmoha: the Purāṇic account of Buddhist and Jain teaching

definitions.definition: The Purāṇas report that Viṣṇu emitted a deluding form (Māyāmoha), or became the Buddha, to lead the demons away from the Veda by teaching Jain and Buddhist doctrine (VP 3.17-18; Agni 16; BhP 1.3.24; cf. BhP 5.6.9 on the Arhat king) - an opponent's report.

Dvaita's case against Advaita: ignorance cannot belong to a self-luminous attributeless self or to the all-knower; the indeterminable is unproven; the world's falsity is unproven; 'māyā' in scripture means God's will; and an attributeless Brahman is indistinguishable from the Mādhyamika void.

In the texts 'upaniṣad' means a secret teaching or hidden name/correspondence: its upaniṣad is 'the real behind the real' (BAU 2.1.20); the upaniṣad of the asuras (ChU 8.8.4); 'we have told you the upaniṣad' (Kena 4.7); the rule 'do not beg' is the upaniṣad of the breath-brahman (KauU 2.1). The gods love the cryptic (AU 1.3.14).

Against Kautsa's claim that mantras are meaningless, Yāska holds they are meaningful because their words are those of ordinary speech; the one who recites without understanding is a load-bearing post (Nirukta 1.15–18).

Six: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation and non-apprehension; a means of knowledge apprehends the previously unapprehended and is free from causal defect and from any sublating cognition.
Five: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison and postulation; every experience other than memory is a means of knowledge.

relations.note: dharma is known only by verbal testimony (the Veda)

definitions.definition: The inner sense by which the self grasps its relation to objects and by which the self is known in saṃsāra; some Bhāṭṭas held it persists in release as the organ of the self's bliss.
The conjunction of self and mind, located in the body, is the non-inherent cause of the self's qualities; hence the self's qualities appear only where the body is.

name: Mind and speech — the two tracks of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: Mind and speech are a yoked pair carrying the sacrifice, mind the greater (ŚB 1.4.4.7); the sacrifice has two tracks, mind (the silent brahman priest) and speech (the other priests) (ChU 4.16.1–2; AB 5.33); in the inner Agnihotra speech and breath are offered into each other (KU 2.5).

name: The mind as the cause of bondage and liberation

definitions.definition: Not people, gods, the body, planets, karma or time but the mind turns the wheel of saṃsāra; all disciplines culminate in its mastery (Bhikṣu Gītā); the mind attached to the guṇas binds, devoted to the Person frees (Kapila).

relations.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha extends the mind's causality to the world itself

name: Mind as the cause of bondage and liberation

definitions.definition: Mind attached to objects binds, mind free of objects liberates (Amṛtabindu 2; Śāṭyāyanīya 1–3); mind alone is saṃsāra (Maitreya 1.5).

The editorial division of the non-principal Muktikā Upaniṣads into Sāmānya-Vedānta, Yoga, Sannyāsa, Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava groups, used by the Adyar Library series and later catalogues; it is not found in the Muktikā.

The world is false (mithyā): not unreal like a hare's horn, not real like Brahman, but indescribable and sublatable; defended by the inference 'because it is seen, insentient, limited' and by five definitions.

Release from saṃsāra by Viṣṇu's grace into the unobstructed enjoyment of one's own bliss, in eternal difference from and dependence on him, in forms such as sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya, graded by fitness, with bhakti continuing and the liberated desiring only in accord with the Lord's will; not the mere cessation of ignorance.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the goal is named 'immortality' — the desireless knower's breaths do not depart; being brahman he goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.6); the serene one reaches the highest light and appears in his own form (ChU 8.12.3); the knower becomes brahman (MuU 3.2.9); freed from name and form like rivers in the ocean (MuU 3.2.8); knowing God one is freed from all fetters (ŚU 1.8, 6.13); ŚU 6.16 names saṃsāra and mokṣa.

After the body falls, the soul goes by the path of light to Vaikuṇṭha, manifests its own nature, keeps its individuality, experiences the whole Brahman as his mode, shares his bliss and powers except cosmic functions, never returns, and serves him eternally.
Non-difference with Brahman after death, once the adjuncts have fallen.
Attainment of the Lord's nature in non-separation, with the soul's distinctness preserved; by grace.
Maryādā souls attain union (sāyujya) or Akṣara; puṣṭi souls receive service in the Lord's play, valued above liberation.
Freedom from māyā is a by-product; the goal is prema-service in Kṛṣṇa's abode; sāyujya is rejected.
Equality with Śiva.

When adṛṣṭa is absent there is no contact with a body and no new appearance (VS 5.2.20 C); knowledge of the categories arising from dharma brings detachment, no new merit and demerit accrue, and when the old are exhausted the self, without seed, takes no body — a quiescence like fire whose fuel is burnt (Praśastapāda).

name: The monkey's way and the crow's way

definitions.definition: Yogaśikhā 1.140–144: gradual completion within one body (monkey), or rebirth and swift fruition through a siddha guru (crow).

Death has its own path (RV 10.18.1) and fetters (AVŚ 8.1.4); the mind can go to Yama and be called back (RV 10.58); 'let me not go to the house of clay' (7.89.1); one prays to be freed from death 'like a cucumber from its stalk, not from immortality' (7.59.12); the immortal and mortal are of one origin (1.164.30).

The list of 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān in the Muktikā, one for each surviving Vedic branch, with their Vedas and peace-chants, taught as a graded curriculum for liberation (Māṇḍūkya → 10 → 32 → 108).

name: The muni and the long-haired one

definitions.definition: The wind-girdled munis in soiled brown, entered by the gods, ecstatic with munihood, ride the winds while mortals see only their bodies; the long-haired one bears fire, poison-drink and heaven and earth, flies through the air seeing all forms, knows the minds of beings and drank with Rudra (RV 10.136).

The unstruck sound heard within when breath and mind are stilled; listened to in stages from loud to subtle it absorbs the mind 'like milk in water'; its end is the soundless Brahman and the state beyond mind; in the Yogaśikhā nāda is bindu and bindu is mind, and no mantra is higher than nāda.

relations.note: Listening to nāda dissolves mind into the state beyond mind.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 101 channels of the heart, one going to the crown by which one reaches immortality (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); the 72,000 hitā channels in which the sleeper rests (BAU 2.1.19); 101 × 100 × 72,000 branch channels through which vyāna moves (PrU 3.6); coloured fluids and the sun's rays in the channels (ChU 8.6.1); the suṣumṇā (MaiU 6.21).

72,000 channels spread from the kanda near the navel; ten or fourteen are principal (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, sarasvatī, gāndhārī, hastijihvā, pūṣā, yaśasvinī, alambusā, kuhū, śaṅkhinī, vāruṇī, viśvodarī, payasvinī); the suṣumnā is the path of liberation; iḍā carries the moon, piṅgalā the sun.

The heart has a hundred and one channels; the one rising to the crown (suṣumnā) is the knower's path at death; in seated worship the suṣumnā is contemplated as shining, lit above the crown by the sun's rays.
The name uttered inattentively or with another intent destroys sin and gives liberation (Ajāmila), but only pure chanting gives love; offences block its fruit.
Words in injunctions that name rites rather than enjoin qualities, recognized on four grounds.

name: Name and form (nāmarūpa)

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the unmanifest became manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7); being entered with the living self and differentiated name and form (ChU 6.3.2); space accomplishes name and form (ChU 8.14); at release name and form are left behind like rivers in the ocean (MuU 3.2.8; PrU 6.5).

notes: Buddhist nāmarūpa (mentality-materiality) is a different technical sense.

name: Non-difference of the name and the named

definitions.definition: The name is Kṛṣṇa himself, fully empowered, not an ordinary word; it reveals itself to a tongue turned to service.

Places of torment below the earth in the south within the three worlds, ruled by Yama, each matched to classes of sin (BhP 5.26: twenty-eight; VP 2.6 and MkP 12 other lists); release comes by exhaustion of the karma, by remembrance of the Lord, or by the transfer of a righteous person's merit (MkP 15); VP 2.6.46 teaches that heaven and hell are names for merit and sin.

name: Before creation: the Nāsadīya account

definitions.definition: Before creation there was neither non-being nor being, death nor immortality, night nor day; That One breathed windless by its own power; darkness hidden by darkness; That One was born by tapas; desire arose as the first seed of mind; seers found the bond of being in non-being in their hearts; the gods came later; whether even the overseer in the highest heaven knows is left open (RV 10.129).

members: the overseer who knows or does not know

definitions.definition: Hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, obeisance, servitude, friendship and self-offering (BhP 7.5.23-24); the Śiva Purāṇa's three means (hearing, singing, reflection) are a Śaiva counterpart.

name: The nine means of devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa)

definitions.definition: Holy company; talk of the Lord's stories; singing his qualities; expounding his words; guileless service of the teacher as the Lord; virtuous conduct with steady worship; worship through his mantra; honouring devotees and seeing him in all with dispassion; inquiry into his nature — open to women, men and animals alike; the first leads to the rest in order.

relations.note: differs from the Bhāgavata's nine forms (hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, bowing, servitude, friendship, self-offering)

name: The nine relations of Lord and soul

definitions.definition: Father–son, protector–protected, master–servant, husband–wife, knower–known, owner–owned, support–supported, self–body, enjoyer–enjoyed.

name: The Navya-Nyāya analysis of cognition and its contents

definitions.definition: Every qualified cognition has a qualificand (viśeṣya), a qualifier (prakāra) and a relation (saṃsarga), with corresponding properties (viśeṣyatā, prakāratā, saṃsargatā) that determine one another (nirūpaka / nirūpita); properties and absences are specified by their delimitors, counterpositives and relations; valid cognition is apprehending in X the property X has as qualifier.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the instruction (ādeśa) about brahman — 'not so, not so', for there is nothing beyond this 'not so' (BAU 2.3.6) — and the description of the self as ungraspable, indestructible, unattached, unbound (BAU 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15); akin to the negations of the imperishable (BAU 3.8.8), of the fourth (MāU 7) and 'from which words turn back' (TU 2.4).

In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra the practice of the principles proceeds by giving up each with 'not this, not this', whence discrimination (3.76) — the renunciation of identification with each principle, as in the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64).
Brahman is taught by negating every specification; negation terminates in Brahman, the 'reality of the real', which is not negated.

name: The nine creations of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa

definitions.definition: Three primary (of mahat, the elements, the senses), five secondary (immobile, animals, gods, humans, anugraha) and the Kaumāra creation of the Kumāras, both primary and secondary.
Earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa, time, space, self, mind (VS 1.1.4 C); substance is what has motion and qualities and is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C).
Four formless (Śiva, Śakti, Nāda, Bindu), one form-formless (Sadāśiva, the liṅga), and four with form (Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā) — the one Śiva appearing for worship.

Varāha 1's enumeration of 96 tattvas: the 24 Sāṃkhya principles plus elements, bodies, states, six modifications, six waves, six sheaths, six enemies, three jīvas, guṇas, karmas, actions, inner functions, four sublime attitudes and fourteen deities; the Pāśupatabrahma makes the 96 the haṃsa's sacred thread.

relations.note: saguṇa Brahman is Īśvara

definitions.definition: Brahman in itself is without attributes; the same Brahman with the adjunct of māyā is the Lord with attributes, object of worship, real at the empirical level. Texts teaching form serve meditation (BS 3.2.15).
The Lord's grace needs no cause in the soul ('the kitten carried by the cat').
The Lord's grace is free, but he takes the soul's surrender as its occasion (vyāja) so as not to be partial ('the baby monkey clinging').

Minds created from I-am-ness alone (4.4), all directed by one mind (4.5); of the five kinds (by the five sources), only the meditation-born is without residue (4.6, YBh 4.6); the first knower taught Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25).
The drawing of the soul's attachment from the world into Kṛṣṇa through his play, culminating in forgetfulness of the world and love in separation.
Read by Vācaspati into NS 1.1.4 ('non-verbalizable' and 'determinate').
Indeterminate perception ('this is something') is inferred, not perceived; determinate perception has a qualifier (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A prohibition turns one away from harmful acts; where the negation cannot attach to the injunctive, it is an exclusion forming a positive vow of not-doing.

relations.note: both link degrees of the divine form to kinds of worship; neither tradition equates the schemes

definitions.definition: The supreme Brahman Nārāyaṇa has a subtle, imperishable, partless form, stood for by the fixed image, and a gross form with parts, cause of all, stood for by the movable image that receives full worship.

name: Action without attachment to its fruit (niṣkāma karma)

definitions.definition: Acting as duty, with evenness, abandoning attachment and the fruit, offering the act to the Lord; action so done does not bind (BhG 2.47–48, 3.19, 4.20, 9.27–28, 18.6).
Yudhiṣṭhira's dharma practised 'not for the fruit of dharma' (MBh 3.32.4).
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.32, YBh 2.32).

name: Niyoga / kārya (the command, what is to be done)

definitions.definition: The content of injunctions and the primary meaning of Vedic sentences: the act as to be done, identical with the apūrva, prompting the eligible person by itself.

relations.note: the rival Bhāṭṭa account of what the injunction conveys

definitions.definition: Called the highest dharma (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116; 3.297.55); taught by Tulādhāra (12.253–256), Vicakhnu (12.257) and Vidura (5.33.48); the meat-seller notes that no one lives without harm (3.199); the kṣatriya's righteous war is his own dharma (BhG 2.31).
The ekāntins are non-violent; the Lord is worshipped by sacrifice without slaughter (MBh 12.336; 12.323–324).
Śākaṭāyana and the Nairuktas hold that all nouns derive from verbs; Gārgya and some grammarians deny it; Yāska defends derivation, always attending to meaning (Nirukta 1.12; 2.1).

name: The chain from false knowledge to liberation (NS 1.1.2)

definitions.definition: False knowledge → faults (attachment, aversion, delusion) → activity (good and bad acts of body, speech and mind, producing merit and demerit) → birth → pain; this unbroken series is saṃsāra. When knowledge of truth removes false knowledge, each successive link falls away and absolute liberation results (NS 1.1.2; NBh 1.1.2).

name: The yogic means to knowledge of truth in Nyāya

definitions.definition: Knowledge of truth arises from repeated practice of a particular samādhi (NS 4.2.38), which is possible through prior practice despite intruding objects and hunger (4.2.39–41); yoga is to be practised in forests, caves and sandbanks (4.2.42); for liberation one purifies the self by yama and niyama and by yoga and the method of the inner self — austerity, breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, fixation, and repeated contemplation of objects (4.2.46; NBh); with study, reflection and discussion (4.2.47–49).

name: The object does not depend on one mind

definitions.definition: A thing is common to many minds and stands on its own (4.14–16): the same thing produces pleasure, pain, delusion or indifference in different minds (YBh 4.15); if it depended on one mind, what would it be when that mind was distracted? (4.16); it is known or unknown as it colours the mind (4.17). Vyāsa rejects those who say the object is only a construction of cognition, like a dream (YBh 4.14), and those who say 'all is mind only' (YBh 4.23).

name: Oṃ

definitions.definition: The one-syllabled Brahman to be uttered at death (BhG 8.13), the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8), the first word of 'oṃ tat sat' with which rites begin (17.23–24), 'among words the one syllable' (10.25).

notes: U05's contribution; the Upaniṣadic and mantra-śāstra accounts are given by U03 and U31.

definitions.definition: Oṃ analysed into three measures plus the half-measure (with Vedas, fires, worlds, deities, guṇas and colours), into twelve measures with destinies at death (Nādabindu), and sixteen measures ending in parā (Nāradaparivrājaka 8; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).

An omniscient knower of dharma is not seen now, cannot be proved to have existed, cannot be established by his own scripture without circularity, and could not be recognized by the non-omniscient; an omniscience by all six means of knowledge would not be denied, but not a perception of dharma.

In Īśvara the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25); for one with only discernment of sattva and puruṣa there is knowledge of all (3.49); discriminative knowledge is all-embracing and without sequence (3.54); when coverings are gone knowledge is infinite and what remains to be known is little (4.31).

name: One ultimate, many names

definitions.definition: Brahman, one without a second, is sung in many ways by the seers, so knowledge from a single teacher is not firm; the Veda's interpretations differ with natures.

The one from which words turn back is the Person of the Sāṃkhyas, the Brahman of the Vedāntins, the pure consciousness of the Vijñānavādins and the void of the Śūnyavādins; for the one established in the supreme it may be described with the terms no-self and emptiness; the external-object and consciousness doctrines are one for us.
The undivided understanding regarding Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakti, the Sun and Gaṇeśa is right yoga; the one lord became fivefold.

notes: Text-layer statements that bear directly on ult:the-one (ṚV 1.164.46). Traditions that deny such equivalence (e.g. Buddhist schools on 'śūnya' as a name of a substantial ultimate) are not represented in these verses.

name: How speech arises in the body

definitions.definition: The self grasps meanings with the intellect and joins the mind to the wish to speak; the mind strikes the body's fire, which drives the wind up from the chest to the head and mouth, where the phonemes are formed (PŚ 6–9).

relations.note: the Śikṣā's physiology of breath serves pronunciation, not meditation

definitions.definition: Absence of certainty not accompanied by a desire to infer.
Kṛṣṇa as devotee in five aspects: Caitanya, Nityānanda, Advaita, Śrīvāsa, Gadādhara.
Fixed (dhruva), worship (kautuka), festival (utsava), bathing (snapana) and offering (bali) images; the dhruva receives flowers only, the kautuka full worship.

Five real and eternal differences — God and soul, God and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, matter and matter — holding in every state including liberation; knowing them is a condition of liberation.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, closing the five adhyāyas, muttered daily as the five purifiers.

Five codes of conduct: liṅgācāra (exclusive worship of the liṅga), sadācāra (honest livelihood and moral life), śivācāra (equality of all devotees), bhṛtyācāra (servant-humility) and gaṇācāra (defence of the community and faith).
The SSM's exclusivity (no other gods), its duty to protect liṅgas and devotees at the cost of life and its rule on revilers of Śiva are the textual background of liṅgācāra and gaṇācāra.

name: The Pañcācārya lineage and the transmission of the SSM

definitions.definition: Śiva taught the doctrine to the Goddess and Nandin; the gaṇa Reṇuka, emerging from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki, taught Agastya; five ācāryas appear from liṅgas in every age and found the five pīṭhas; the SSM's compiler stands in the ācārya line of Muddadeva and Siddhanātha.

name: The doctrine of the five fires

definitions.definition: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali's teaching: yonder world, the rain-god, this world, man and woman are five sacrificial fires; the offerings are faith, Soma, rain, food and semen, so that at the fifth offering water becomes 'person'; the knower of it goes by the path of the gods (ChU 5.3-10; BAU 6.2).

name: The five periods of the day (pañcakāla)

definitions.definition: The Pāñcarātrin's day is ordered as approach, gathering, worship, study and yoga.
Na-ma-śi-vā-ya, read as concealment, mala, Śiva, grace, soul; the order of the letters maps the soul's path from bondage to Śiva; meditated as the means of purification (Civañāṉa Pōtam 9).
Namaccivāya as the devotee's refuge and the essence of the Vedas (Tēvāram, Tiruvācakam).

name: Mantra: the five syllables and the praṇava

definitions.definition: 'Namaḥ śivāya' is the designation of Śiva and root of all mantras; the name 'Śiva' reveals brahman in its primary sense; the five syllables comprise all that exists in fives; with Oṃ it is six-syllabled; Oṃ arises from 'so'ham'; mental repetition is best.

name: The five marks of a Purāṇa (pañcalakṣaṇa)

definitions.definition: A Purāṇa treats creation (sarga), secondary creation (pratisarga), dynasties (vaṃśa), the Manu-intervals (manvantara) and the deeds of the dynasties (vaṃśānucarita) (VP 3.6.24; KūP 1.1.12; Matsya 53.65); the Bhāgavata calls the five-mark Purāṇas the 'small' ones (12.7.10).

name: The 108 Pāñcarātra saṃhitās
notes: Scholarly metadata: F. O. Schrader (1916) combined several saṃhitās' lists into over 200 titles; many titles are lost. Members are the src entries with lineage lin:pancaratra.

definitions.definition: Tradition speaks of 108 saṃhitās spoken by the Lord; lists of titles in different saṃhitās disagree.

name: The five categories of the Pāśupatas (pañcārtha)

definitions.definition: The whole teaching is summed up as effect (kārya), cause (kāraṇa), union (yoga), rule (vidhi) and the end of suffering (duḥkhānta), all implied in the first sūtra.
Śaṅkara reports the same five as taught by Paśupati for release from the paśus' bond, and rejects the accompanying view of the Lord as merely efficient cause.
Liṅga-wearers are not subject to the pollutions of birth, death, menstruation, leftovers or caste.
The teacher who has become Śiva is not tainted by birth- and death-pollution (14.16).

name: The five flows (pañcavāha) of goddesses

definitions.definition: Vyomavāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Dikcarī, Gocarī and Bhūcarī - the goddess-groups of consciousness, subject, inner organ, outer senses and objects - which delude the ignorant and liberate the knower (Kṣemarāja on PH 12, citing the Krama).

notes: The correlation of each group with a level is recalled from Kṣemarāja's commentary; low confidence.

definitions.definition: The gross elements are formed by combining half of each subtle element with an eighth of each of the other four.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): MuU 1.1.4-5 is the root text — the lower knowledge is the four Vedas and six ancillary sciences, the higher that by which the imperishable is grasped; Nārada knows only mantras, not the self (ChU 7.1.3).

Knowledge is twofold by eligibility: Śiva's knowledge, revealing the Lord, is higher; the Veda and the rest, revealing the bound soul and its bonds, are lower — different as the night-vision of a man and a cat.

relations.note: Pāñcarātrins and Vaikhānasas claim Vedic roots instead

name: Supreme devotion, supreme knowledge, highest devotion

definitions.definition: Three ripening states of love for the Lord prayed for in the Śaraṇāgati Gadya: longing that cannot bear separation, direct vision, and love for which loss of the vision would be unbearable.

Rūpa: the gopīs' paramour love is the summit of amorous rasa; Jīva: they are Kṛṣṇa's own potencies, so svakīyā in truth; Viśvanātha: parakīyā eternally. Love is defined as desire for Kṛṣṇa's pleasure, not one's own.
Rādhā as Kṛṣṇa's eternal consort; the school's view is generally described as svakīyā.

name: Consideration (parāmarśa) as the instrument of inference

definitions.definition: The cognition 'this has smoke pervaded by fire' is the proximate cause of inferential cognition, not the memory of pervasion alone (Gaṅgeśa; Tarkasaṅgraha).
The validity of a cognition is produced by excellences in its causes and known extrinsically — from the success of the activity it prompts (NBh 1.1.1) or other inference (Gaṅgeśa).
Prakṛti really transforms into its products through the guṇas, by combination and transformation, like water differing in different receptacles (SK 16); the world so produced is real (SS 6.52).

relations.note: Advaita's apparent transformation (the Advaita account)

name: Parokṣa — the gods' love of the hidden

definitions.definition: 'The gods love the cryptic and dislike the obvious': ritual and cosmic realities are given indirect names (indha → Indra; svāpyaya → svapna), and the teaching of correspondences is itself 'secret' (ŚB 10.5.2.20; 14.6.11.2; AB 3.43).

name: The parts of a sāman

definitions.definition: A sāman is a verse (from the ārcika) turned into song, with stretched vowels, repetitions and stobhas, divided among the chanters as hiṅkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, upadrava and nidhana.

notes: The fivefold and sevenfold sāman are expounded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (U03).

name: The paśu (bound soul) in the Pāśupata system

definitions.definition: All conscious beings but the Lord, with or without bodies, including gods and those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga; bound by the kalās; their bondage is lack of lordship.

The jīva bound by ego is the paśu, the Lord is Paśupati; release from the bond (pāśa) through the pāśupata vow and ash (Atharvaśiras 5; Jābāli); 'bound by the husk it is paddy, without husk rice' (Skanda 6–7).

name: Death and the final stage in Pāśupata practice

definitions.definition: In the fourth stage the ascetic lives in the cremation ground until the body falls, remembering Rudra; the fifth stage is without body, its place Rudra himself; the liberated brahmin does not return.
Dying at Kāyāvarohaṇa leads to Rudra's world (Kūrma P.).
Knowledge, austerity, permanence (constant union with the god), steadiness and perfection (Gaṇakārikā); Kauṇḍinya: knowledge, austerity, constant union with the god, yoga, arising of the qualities.

False knowledge, demerit, the cause of attachment, falling away and the root of the paśu-state (Gaṇakārikā); Kauṇḍinya: ignorance, demerit, habituation to objects, non-attainment of steadiness, lack of lordship.
Residence (with the teacher, i.e. the faculties of learning), observance, muttering and meditation, constant remembrance of Rudra, and grace.
Teacher, people, cave (or empty house), cremation ground and Rudra - the places of the five stages in order.
Kauṇḍinya's list: the dwelling, the world, the empty house, the cremation ground, Rudra.
The absolute removal of each of the five impurities.

name: The five stages of Pāśupata practice (avasthā)

definitions.definition: Manifest (vyakta: the sign shown, in the temple), unmanifest (avyakta: sign hidden, courting dishonour among people), conquest (jaya: of the senses, in cave or empty house), cutting (cheda: in the cremation ground), completion (niṣṭhā: all activity ceased, in Rudra).

relations.note: each stage has its place

definitions.definition: Devotion to the teacher, clarity of mind, conquest of opposites, merit and vigilance.

Material (knowledge of disciple and teacher, the ritual items, the brahmin disciple), time (forenoon), rite, image and teacher; initiation is by ash consecrated with the five mantras before the southern image.

name: The kalās: ten effects and thirteen instruments

definitions.definition: The insentient parts that bind the soul: ten effects (earth, water, fire, air, space; sound, touch, form, taste, smell) and thirteen instruments (five knowledge-senses, five action-organs, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas).
The Lord (Pati) alone is the independent cause who emits, maintains, withdraws and favours the effect; he acts by will and play, not by dependence on karma.
Everything dependent on the Lord: the knowledge-qualities of souls (vidyā), the insentient parts (kalā) and the souls (paśu); eternal but produced, favoured and concealed by the Lord in play.

name: The powers of the Pāśupata yogin

definitions.definition: Powers arise with yoga: distant seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing and omniscience (power of knowing); swiftness of mind, taking forms at will, acting without organs (power of acting); and eight marks of perfection - subject to none, not to be entered, not to be slain, fearless, imperishable, unaging, deathless, unobstructed. They arise gradually after six months of constant yoga and make the yogin a chief of Mahādeva's troops. The texts present them as signs and as part of liberation, not as dangers.
The Skanda Purāṇa tells of Pāśupata siddhas who went to Śiva's abode in the same body.
Hostile dramas attribute flight and power over gods and heavens to Kāpālikas.

name: Teacher and disciple in the Pāśupata tradition

definitions.definition: The disciple is a tested brahmin of good family, keen senses and desire to know, who seeks the end of suffering, not dharma, wealth, pleasure or isolation; the teacher acts from grace, knows the nine groups and consecrates; one with scripture but without faith or knowledge of the groups is a pseudo-teacher.
Alms (stages 1 and 3), discarded food (stage 2), whatever is obtained (stage 4); none in stage 5.
Perception, inference and scripture (the teaching from Maheśvara through the teachers); other alleged means are included in these.
The teachers from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara saluted daily (Ratnaṭīkā); eighteen are named by Jain doxographers; the Mathurā inscription counts ten generations from Kuśika to 380 CE.

name: The rule (vidhi): observance and its aids

definitions.definition: Activity producing merit: primary - the observance (vows and the six doors) - and secondary - re-bathing and the like; it begins with ash, has censure in the middle and ends with feigned folly, and has three limbs, gift, worship and austerity.
A quality of the paśu: cognitive (discriminating - called citta - or not) or non-cognitive (merit and demerit).
Yamas: non-harming, celibacy, truthfulness, non-dealing, non-stealing; niyamas: non-anger, service of the teacher, purity, light diet, vigilance - all ten counted as yamas.

relations.note: a parallel five-and-five scheme; members differ (asaṃvyavahāra, akrodha, guruśuśrūṣā, āhāralāghava, apramāda)

name: Yoga as union of self and Lord

definitions.definition: Yoga is the conjunction of the self with the Lord through the mind; in action (muttering, meditation on Oṃ in the heart) or in the cessation of action; it arises for one of unclouded mind who practises.

name: The paths of smoke and light (Kapila Gītā)

definitions.definition: Ritualists go by smoke to the moon and return; the desireless go by light to the Person; devotion is best.

notes: Parallels the Upaniṣadic pitṛyāna and devayāna (owned by U03).

name: Pati, paśu, pāśa — the Lord, the bound soul, the bonds

definitions.definition: The three eternal, irreducible categories (padārtha): Śiva, the countless souls, and the bonds (mala, karma, māyā). None is created; souls are not parts or appearances of Śiva; bonds are real.
Mupporuḷ ('the three realities') — pati, pacu, pācam; the Civañāṉa Pōtam's twelve sūtras prove and define each, then give the means and fruit.
All selves in saṃsāra are paśus; Śiva is their lord (Paśupati), who binds them with the noose of māyā and alone frees them; he himself is bondage, binder, noose and bound (Īśvara Gītā).
The Kiraṇa teaches the knowledge of paśu, pāśa and pati; the soul is eternal, pervasive, ignorant and inactive, lodged within māyā and bound through kalā, vidyā, rāga, prakṛti and the instruments.
Śrīkaṇṭha uses the Śaiva triad within a Vedānta frame: Śiva the Lord, souls bound by the impurity, karma and māyā, freed by his grace to equality with him.

relations.note: Kashmir non-dualism derives all categories from Śiva's consciousness; the Siddhānta keeps three
the Siddhānta denies that soul and bonds are superimposed on one reality

notes: Contribution from U08; U18 owns the Siddhānta concept.

name: The dharma of the devoted wife (pativratā)

definitions.definition: The devoted wife's service of her husband as a deity gives her power over an angry ascetic (MBh 3.196–197) and over death (Sāvitrī, 3.281); Anasūyā teaches it to Sītā (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119); Umā expounds women's dharma (MBh 13.126–134).
Everything is won by rightly applied effort; fate is only one's former effort, overcome by present effort; reliance on fate is delusion.
The inner organ goes out through the sense, takes the object's form, and the consciousness delimited by knower, mode and object become one (Vedāntaparibhāṣā ch.1).
Pīlupāka: in baking, the pot breaks down to atoms, whose colour changes, and is re-formed.
Piṭharapāka: the colour of the whole pot changes without its dissolution.

name: The after-death body built by the piṇḍas

definitions.definition: Piṇḍa Upaniṣad: the departed passes days in water, fire, space and wind, and the ten rice-balls successively build its new body.
By sapiṇḍīkaraṇa the preta is joined to the three generations of ancestors and thereafter receives the pārvaṇa and annual śrāddhas; offerings at Gayā free the ancestors.

Puruṣas are many, because birth, death and instruments are allotted separately, beings do not act all at once, and the guṇas are differently proportioned (SK 18; SS 1.149, 6.45); some were liberated while others were not (SS 1.157). Scriptures of non-duality refer to sameness of kind, not number (SS 1.154).

There are many puruṣas: the seen ceases for one whose purpose is accomplished but continues for others, being common to them (2.22, YBh 2.22); the end of saṃsāra holds for the skilled, not for others (YBh 4.33).

relations.note: each puruṣa is pure consciousness; plurality is of puruṣas, not of kinds of consciousness

definitions.definition: Selves are many because their states are distinct and on the authority of scripture (VS 3.2.15–17 C).
Individual selves are distinct in each body; the Lord is one (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Advaita's one self; the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika tradition insists on real, eternal plurality.

definitions.definition: Space enclosed in pots seems many but is one space; so the self appears as many jīvas through bodies.
The wheel keeps turning after the potter's push has ceased; so the knower's body continues until prārabdha is spent.

The three accents (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.29–31) carry meaning and efficacy: Tvaṣṭṛ's mis-accented 'indraśatru' made Indra the slayer (ŚB 1.6.3.10), and a mantra faulty in accent is a thunderbolt against the sacrificer (PŚ 52).

name: The power of the divine name

definitions.definition: Uttering the Lord's name, even indirectly, destroys all sin and is the best expiation (BhP 6.2.9-14); it is the fearless way for all (2.1.11), the supreme dharma (6.3.22) and the means of the Kali age (12.3.51-52; VP 6.2.17); offences against it hinder its fruit (Padma, as cited).

name: Powers and freedom of movement from knowledge

definitions.definition: The texts promise results: whoever venerates X as brahman moves at will as far as X reaches (ChU 7); the knower of the self's real desires moves at will in all worlds and by intention alone obtains the fathers' world and the rest (ChU 8.1.6-8.2.10); whatever world the pure-minded desires he wins (MuU 3.1.10); the self-ruled moves at will (ChU 7.25.2).

name: Prajāpati's falling apart and his restoration

definitions.definition: After emitting the creatures Prajāpati, who is the year, fell apart (vyasraṃsata) — his joints being the junctions of day and night, the moon's phases and the seasons; the gods healed him by the Agnihotra, the new- and full-moon and seasonal rites (ŚB 1.6.3.35–36), and he is rebuilt as the fire-altar whose bricks are his days and nights (ŚB 10.1.1.2–3); he put himself together with the metres, whence 'saṃhitā' (AA 3.2.6).

relations.note: the altar is the means of restoration

notes: Correction to the task wording: the Brāhmaṇas speak of Prajāpati 'coming apart' through the exhaustion of creating, not of a dismemberment by others (contrast the Puruṣa Sūkta, RV 10.90).

definitions.definition: The ultimate is light (prakāśa) whose very nature is reflexive awareness (vimarśa); without vimarśa light would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11); vimarśa is supreme speech and freedom (1.5.13).
Kṛṣṇa's play is eternal in the unmanifest abode and becomes manifest on earth once in a day of Brahmā; the parakīyā appearance belongs (for Jīva) to the manifest play.

Any method that brings one to know the inner self is valid, and none is fixed (Sureśvara); the ancients, intent on the oneness of the self, were indifferent to the explanation of the empirical (Appayya).

The unconscious, productive root (mūlaprakṛti, pradhāna, the unmanifest): uncaused, one, common, of three guṇas in equilibrium (SK 3, 10–11; SS 1.61). Not perceived because subtle, it is inferred from its effects (SK 8): from the limited measure of things, their homogeneity, activity through potency, the distinction of cause and effect and the merging of the manifold (SK 15–16). It acts for puruṣa like milk for the calf (SK 57), withdraws like a dancer once seen (SK 59), and is what is truly bound and released (SK 62). Gauḍapāda lists its synonyms pradhāna, brahman, avyakta, bahudhānaka, māyā; there is only one prakṛti (Gauḍapāda on SK 66).

The seen has the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, consists of elements and senses, and exists for experience and liberation (2.18); the guṇas are called pradhāna (YBh 2.18); it is real and common to all puruṣas (2.22).
Eternal, real, insentient matter with three guṇas (mixed sattva), the Lord's body; called māyā for its wonderful effects, not because it is illusory.

Dvaita: an eternal-and-non-eternal insentient reality, the material cause of the world, dependent on and moved by Viṣṇu, presided over by Lakṣmī; its products are the principles from mahat to the elements. God is not the material cause.

relations.note: Advaita's māyā is not a second reality (the Sāṃkhya–Advaita contrast; interpretive)

definitions.definition: Dispassion leads to absorption into prakṛti (SK 45) — not liberation: those who take prakṛti or its evolutes for the self dissolve into them (Gauḍapāda on SK 48, 'darkness') and rise again like a diver (SS 3.54); the Kramadīpikā calls it 'bondage to prakṛti'. The one who rises may become an all-knowing lord in the next creation (SS 3.55–57).

Sāṃkhya accepts three: perception (determination concerning each object), inference (threefold; from general correlation for things beyond the senses) and reliable testimony (for what neither establishes) (SK 4–6); other proposed means are included in these (SK 4; Vācaspati). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra defines perception as cognition that, in contact, reflects its object (1.89).

Yoga accepts three means of valid cognition — perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7) — defined in YBh 1.7; the insight of samādhi has the particular as object, beyond testimony and inference (1.49), and the perception of nirvitarkā samāpatti is the 'highest perception' (YBh 1.42).
Six means, valid for the empirical and following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā; all within the sphere of ignorance; scripture alone reveals Brahman; perception grasps being, not difference.
Three: perception, inference, scripture; all have qualified objects; the Lord is known from scripture alone.

The same object may be known by several means (fire by testimony, inference and perception), though some objects are restricted to one (heaven to scripture); knowledge culminates in perception (NBh 1.1.3).

relations.note: Buddhist logicians restrict each means of knowledge to its own kind of object.

definitions.definition: Breath is the eldest and best of the vital powers, on whose departure the body fails (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1); the one god (BAU 3.9.9); born from the self like a shadow, dividing itself fivefold (PrU 3.3-7); brahman (KauU 2.1) and the intelligent self (KauU 3.2); the gatherer into which the senses go in sleep (ChU 4.3.3); breath is father, mother, all (ChU 7.15).

name: Prāṇa (breath) in the Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas

definitions.definition: The breaths are the primordial seers who made the one Person, Prajāpati (ŚB 6.1.1.1); breath is the consecrated (KB 7.1); the one god is the breath (ŚB 11.6.3); in sleep the breaths enter the self (ŚB 10.5.2.20); the Ṛgvedic seers are forms of the breath (AA 2.2.1); the breaths are counted as five (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna) and sometimes as seven in the head.

name: The five vital airs in Yoga

definitions.definition: Life is the joint activity of the senses, fivefold: prāṇa (mouth and nose to the heart), samāna (to the navel), apāna (down to the soles), udāna (up to the head) and vyāna (pervading); prāṇa is chief (YBh 3.39); mastery of udāna and samāna yields powers (3.39–40).

name: Prāṇa, the life-breath, in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: Wind was born from the Puruṣa's breath (RV 10.90.13); Vāta is the breath of the gods, germ of the world (10.168.4); the Atharvaveda hails Prāṇa as lord of all, clothing creatures as a father his son, death and fever, the swan that never lifts one foot, awake among sleepers, bound to oneself for life (AVŚ 11.4).

name: Prāṇāgnihotra — the fire-offering into the breaths

definitions.definition: The first morsels of every meal are offered with 'svāhā' to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna, satisfying in turn the senses, their deities and regions; one who eats knowing this offers in all worlds and all selves and his evils burn up like a reed-tuft in fire (ChU 5.19–24); the mantras 'in faith, entered into the breath, I offer the immortal' frame the meal (TA 10.69–70); the whole body becomes the sacrificial ground (Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
Prescribed in the Dharmasūtra rules for eating as the daily rite of the twice-born at meals.

The praṇava designates Īśvara by a fixed, not conventional, relation, like a lamp and its light (1.27, YBh 1.27); its repetition with contemplation of its meaning makes the mind one-pointed (1.28, YBh 1.28) and removes obstacles (1.29).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): Om is the udgītha and the essence of essences (ChU 1.1); all speech is held by Om (ChU 2.23.3); Om is brahman, all this (TU 1.8; MāU 1); the word all Vedas proclaim, the best support (KU 1.2.15-17); the bow (MuU 2.2.4); the higher and lower brahman whose measures lead to different worlds (PrU 5); A, U, M and the measureless as the four quarters (MāU 8-12); the upper fire-stick (ŚU 1.14); the word-brahman (MaiU 6.22).

name: The eightfold praṇava

definitions.definition: Om is the designator of Viṣṇu and has eight components, from 'a' to 'atiśānta', naming eight of his forms (Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya, Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman, Jñānātman); the other mantras derive from it.

members: nāda, bindu, ghoṣa, śānta (intermediate names recalled, not verified)

definitions.definition: Taking refuge in the Lord with Śrī as the sole refuge, by those with no other means and no other refuge; done once, it brings liberation at the end of the body.
An independent means (svatantra-upāya), performed once with five limbs and self-offering, equal in fruit to bhakti-yoga; the occasion of the Lord's grace.
Not a means but the soul's acceptance of the Lord, who alone is the means; it befits the soul's nature of dependence; regarding it as a means is a fault.

relations.note: the Purāṇic taking of refuge (Gajendra etc.) read as prapatti

definitions.definition: For the knower, prārabdha karma continues to move the body but has no hold, like dream-objects after waking; knowledge destroys accumulated and future karma (Nādabindu 21–29).
Purity of mind is grace; everything to be enjoyed is first offered to the liṅga and received back as prasāda, which purifies the mind; so too the prasāda of guru and jaṅgama.
Veda, Gītā, Brahma Sūtra and Bhāgavata, each later one resolving doubts about the earlier.
Upaniṣads, Bhagavad Gītā and Brahma Sūtras, on which every Vedānta ācārya comments.
The jīva is Brahman's reflection in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype; Īśvara is the prototype (or, for Sarvajñātman, the reflection in ignorance).

name: The reflection doctrine (pratibimbavāda) of the Trika

definitions.definition: The universe appears in consciousness as a city in a mirror - undivided from the mirror yet appearing distinct - but, unlike a mirror, consciousness is itself the source of the image (TĀ 3; Paramārthasāra 12-13).

When harmful thoughts oppress, cultivate their opposites (2.33): reflect that violence and the rest, done, caused or approved, from greed, anger or delusion, have endless suffering and ignorance as fruit (2.34, YBh 2.33–34).
The series of rites from ploughing the site to installation, performed with a single root āgama; by it the deity is established in liṅga or image.
The fixed and movable images are installed and linked; the fixed stands for the partless, the movable for the partite form.
Installation of the seven deities, reserved to the tantri.
Liberation as recognition: the Lord is already one's self but unnoticed through delusion; revealing his powers brings recognition, as a woman recognizes the lover beside her (ĪPK 1.1.3, 4.17).

name: The creation of cognitions (pratyaya-sarga): the fifty

definitions.definition: The intellectual creation of fifty kinds: five errors (darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom; 62 subdivisions), twenty-eight incapacities (11 injuries of the organs, 17 of buddhi), nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 46–51). Error, incapacity and contentment curb accomplishment (SK 51). With the ten fundamental topics they make the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra.

Pravṛtta action, done with desire, leads to prosperity and the gods' state; nivṛtta action, desireless and preceded by knowledge, leads beyond the elements (MDh 12.88–90); abstention bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).

Sins — omission, commission, attachment — are removed by confession, remorse, austerity, recitation and gifts (MDh 11.44, 11.227–229), by japa, tapas, offering, fasting and giving and by purifying texts (GDh 19.11–12); sins are graded from the five great sins down (MDh 11.54ff.).

name: Love of God as the fifth and highest goal

definitions.definition: Prema surpasses the four aims including liberation; devotees reject the five liberations without service.
Puṣṭi devotees seek service and nirodha, not liberation.

The condition of the dead between death and union with the ancestors; it becomes fixed for those who die badly, do great wrong or lack the rites (e.g. no bull released on the eleventh day), who then suffer hunger and thirst and trouble their kin (dreams, signs); it is ended by śrāddha, gifts, nārāyaṇa-bali and hearing sacred texts (the Bhāgavata saptāha frees Dhundhukārī).

name: From the departed (preta) to ancestor (pitṛ)

definitions.definition: The newly dead remains a preta nourished by the rites of the first days and the monthly offerings of the first year, until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa unites him with father, grandfather and great-grandfather, the most distant then passing out of the piṇḍa circle.

notes: Doctrine stated from the Gṛhya/Dharmaśāstra tradition at large; specific verse anchors to be added in Phase D (Garuḍa Purāṇa → U07).

definitions.definition: The Earth is upheld by truth, order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice; she is mother and the speaker her son; she bears peoples of many speeches and dharmas; one digging her asks not to wound her vitals or heart (AVŚ 12.1).
Those who lack the knowledge or the rite are 'born again and again as Death's food' and die again in the other world; the fire-altar and the Nāciketa fire conquer re-death (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).

relations.note: the Brāhmaṇa fear of repeated death is developed in the later doctrine of rebirth by action

name: The Purāṇa as the fifth Veda

definitions.definition: Itihāsa and purāṇa are called the fifth Veda (BhP 1.4.20; cf. ChU 7.1.2); the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas (Matsya 53.3); it was composed out of compassion for those without access to the Veda (BhP 1.4.25); the Bhāgavata is the ripe fruit of the Veda-tree (1.1.3).

relations.note: the Purāṇa's eternal origin vs its human line of reciters

definitions.definition: The Purāṇas teach the eight limbs with their own contents: the ethical lists vary (MkP 41.16-17; ŚiP 7.2.37.18-19), the support of dhāraṇā and dhyāna is the deity's form (VP 6.7; BhP 3.28, 11.14) or Śiva (ŚiP 7.2.39), and the goal is joining the mind with Brahman (VP 6.7.31) or nirvāṇa, Maheśa's state (LiP 1.8.5).

Viṣṇu is worshipped through the conduct of one's varṇa and āśrama (VP 3.8.9); the Purāṇas add vows, pilgrimage, gifts, śrāddha, image worship and temple building as dharma for all classes, and praise devotion above all rites.

name: The transmission of the Purāṇa

definitions.definition: Brahmā remembered the one Purāṇa first; Vyāsa condenses it in each Dvāpara; he gave the Purāṇa-saṃhitā to Romaharṣaṇa, whose disciples made saṃhitās, giving four root saṃhitās (VP 3.6.15-19; BhP 12.7.5-7 with a different list of six disciples); the Sūta Ugraśravas recites to Śaunaka at Naimiṣa; each Purāṇa also has its own chain of speakers (e.g. Viṣṇu - Garuḍa; Parāśara - Maitreya; Śuka - Parīkṣit).

members: VP: Sumati, Agnivarcas, Mitrāyu, Śāṃśapāyana, Akṛtavraṇa (Kāśyapa), Sāvarṇi
BhP: Trayyāruṇi, Kaśyapa, Sāvarṇi, Akṛtavraṇa, Vaiśampāyana, Hārīta

definitions.definition: Creation proceeds from the Lord's Śakti as a pure creation (the vyūhas from pairs of qualities) and an other-than-pure creation from prakṛti; the Jayākhya orders the Vaiṣṇava (pure), primordial-matter and Brahmā's creations.
Śiva creates the pure universe (śuddhādhvan) directly from bindu, and delegates the impure (from māyā) to Ananta, first of the Vidyeśvaras.
The perfect 'I' whose essence is light and bliss, the potency of the great mantra (PH 20); the 'aham' spans the letters from A to HA (PTV).

name: The seen exists for the seer (bhoga and apavarga)

definitions.definition: The seen exists for experience and liberation (2.18); its very being is for the seer's sake (2.21); the mind, acting in combination, exists for another (4.24); bondage is the buddhi's not completing the puruṣa's purpose, liberation its completion (YBh 2.18).

Protection of the Veda, adaptation of mantras, obedience to the scriptural command, brevity and removal of doubt; avoiding barbarous speech; the merit of a single well-used word (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā and on 6.1.84).

The conscious principle, neither producer nor product (SK 3), the opposite of the guṇa-made (SK 11): witness, isolated, neutral, seer, non-agent (SK 19), unattached and by nature ever free (SS 1.15–19), light itself, without consciousness as a property (SS 1.145–146). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, because something must stand opposite the guṇas, because of control, experience and the striving for isolation (SK 17). It is many (SK 18). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

The puruṣa is seeing alone, pure, yet conforming to cognitions (2.20); unchanging, it always knows the mind's activities (4.18); consciousness that does not pass over into objects (4.22); utterly unlike sattva (3.35); neither the same as the buddhi nor entirely different (YBh 2.20); pure, alone and liberated when established in itself (YBh 1.51). Knowledge of the puruṣa comes from saṃyama on what exists for itself (3.35).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self in the form of a person at the beginning (BAU 1.4.1); the cosmic person with a thousand heads (ŚU 3.14); the highest principle beyond the unmanifest (KU 1.3.11); the divine formless person (MuU 2.1.2); the person in the eye (ChU 4.15.1).

relations.note: Both name the self; Sāṃkhya insists on plurality and non-agency, which Advaita's one ātman and Nyāya's qualified ātman do not share (graded partial; interpretive)

definitions.definition: The thousand-headed Person who is all this, past and future, of whom one quarter is all beings and three quarters the immortal in heaven; sacrificed by the gods, he became the world, the Vedas, the varṇas, sun, moon and gods (RV 10.90); 'knowing him alone one goes beyond death' (VS 31.18).

relations.note: One of the Saṃhitās' creation accounts.
The four varṇas are said to come from the Person's mouth, arms, thighs and feet.

definitions.definition: Śrī intercedes between the soul and the Lord, making the soul turn to him and moving him to receive it; one approaches the Lord through her.

name: The relation of Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: The two inquiries (into dharma and into Brahman) are distinguished; Śabara drew his proof of the self from the Śārīraka and Upavarṣa deferred it there (as reported by Śaṅkara); Kumārila says the Upaniṣads make the knowledge of the self firm; later Bhāṭṭas read Upaniṣads on the agent-self as serving rites and those on the non-transmigrating self as serving meditations.

name: The path of grace (puṣṭi) and the path of rule (maryādā)

definitions.definition: In the maryādā path the Lord gives fruits according to scriptural means; in the puṣṭi path his grace alone gives devotion and service, independent of means and merit.

relations.note: partial analogy: Gauḍīya rule-devotion vs spontaneous devotion (both lineages contrast rule and love)

definitions.definition: One Brahman alone exists, but as qualified: souls and matter are its real, inseparable modes and body; hence difference and non-difference are both true, the former of the modes, the latter of the one qualified whole.

relations.note: the positive doctrine against which Advaita's avidyā is rejected

name: The qualified recipient of the tantra

definitions.definition: One who does not revile scripture, has faith and devotion to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and knows ritual, other tantras, yoga, Veda and Vedāṅga, Paśupati's doctrine, logic and all spiritual śāstras.
Those fit for ritual, knowledge or conduct are joined to Śiva accordingly; the incapable receive initiation without the observances.
Some twenty-eight qualities of the holy person (compassionate, harmless, forbearing, truthful ... friendly, merciful, wise).
The same list repeated in the Avadhūta Gītā.

name: Rādhā as Kṛṣṇa's pleasure-power and supreme devotee

definitions.definition: Rādhā is the hlādinī-śakti, the embodiment of mahābhāva, one in self with Kṛṣṇa yet in a separate body for the play.
Rādhā, daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, is worshipped on Kṛṣṇa's left as his eternal consort.
Rādhā as Svāminī (mistress), emphasised in Viṭṭhalanātha's writings.
Practice following the spontaneous love of the Vraja residents, qualified by eager longing (lobha), performed in the practitioner's body and the inner perfected body; kāmānugā or sambandhānugā.

The tirumantra (the soul's nature), the dvaya (the act of surrender and the prayer for service) and the carama-śloka (the Lord's command to surrender), received from the teacher and meditated on daily.

The king protects the people by the science of punishment first composed by Brahmā (MBh 12.59); Rāma's questions to Bharata on counsel, treasury, army and the aims of life (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100); the debate on capital punishment (MBh 12.259).
The Rāmāyaṇa's Rāma, 'dharma in bodily form' (3.37.13), keeps his father's word as dharma (2.21.40), holds truth as the lord of the world (2.109.13), and teaches the duties of kingship (2.100).
Kṛṣṇa's dance with the gopīs (BhP 10.29-33), whose hearing gives supreme devotion and removes lust; not to be imitated by those who are not lords (10.33.30-31).

name: The three gems of the Pāñcarātra and their expansions

definitions.definition: Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya issue directly from the Lord; their expansions Īśvara, Pārameśvara and Pādma govern practice at Melkote, Śrīraṅgam and Kāñcī respectively.

name: Reasoning about the Lord as worship

definitions.definition: Reasoning about the Lord, being reflection (manana) after hearing, is itself a form of worship (NK 1.3); worship of Him is the path to heaven and liberation (NK 1.2).

relations.note: Nyāya places itself at the stage of manana in the Upaniṣadic triad.

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads describe return to this world: like grain a mortal is born again (KU 1.1.6); the path of the fathers returns through rain and food (ChU 5.10.3-6; BAU 6.2.16); the self takes another body as a caterpillar or goldsmith (BAU 4.4.3-4); the third birth (AU 2.1.4); tiny creatures that are born and die (ChU 5.10.8).
Bodies arise for the experience of the fruits of karma; while dharma and adharma remain, a new body arises; when they are exhausted it does not.

name: Nyāya arguments for previous and future births

definitions.definition: A newborn's joy, fear and grief presuppose memory of earlier experience; its desire for the breast presupposes the practice of eating in a former life; no one is born free of desire; since the self is eternal, rebirth is established (NS 3.1.18–24, 4.1.10).

Kṛṣṇa redefines some thirty virtues and states inwardly (calm = intellect fixed on the Lord; strength = breath control; heaven = rise of sattva; the friend = the teacher; the home = the human body) and concludes that seeing merit and fault is the fault, being beyond both the merit.

name: Reflection of the sun in water

definitions.definition: The one sun appears as many trembling reflections; so Brahman appears as many jīvas sharing their adjuncts' changes.

Buddhi, unconscious, takes on the shade of consciousness and appears conscious, while puruṣa, reflected in it, appears to know and enjoy (Vācaspati on SK 5; cf. SK 20); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra speaks of coloring (uparāga) that is misidentification rather than real coloring, like the red flower and the crystal (1.164, 6.28). Vijñānabhikṣu is reported to teach a mutual reflection of puruṣa and buddhi (recalled, low confidence).

name: The authority of regional, caste and family custom

definitions.definition: Customs of regions, castes and families are authoritative when not contrary to the Veda (GDh 11.20); marriage follows local custom (ĀśGS 1.7.1); whether southern and northern practices that the cultured reject are valid is debated (BDh 1.1.2.1–8).

name: The renouncer's permitted modes of death

definitions.definition: The Jābāla and Kaṭharudra mention modes by which a renouncer may end life; recorded summary-only, with no guidance.

Staff (one or three), water-pot, sling, strainer, ochre or no cloth, shaven head, topknot and thread kept or abandoned; the texts differ on which marks are kept, and many say the true marks are inner (staff of knowledge, thread of the Self) and that marks do not liberate.

Pāṇini received the list of phonemes from Maheśvara (PŚ 56–57); Śiva sounded the fourteen sūtras on his drum at the end of his dance (Nandikeśvara-kāśikā); Bṛhaspati taught Indra words for a thousand divine years (Mahābhāṣya).
The Yogaśikhā's claim that the body must be 'cooked' by the fire of yoga; the unripe body of the mere knower is subject to rebirth.
The snake seen in the rope in dim light: superimposition, the substratum, and sublation when the rope is known.

name: The ṛṣi as seer of the mantras

definitions.definition: The seers 'saw' the hymns and had direct perception of dharma, handing them on by instruction (Nirukta 1.20, 2.11); speech was found entered into the seers (RV 10.71.3); Vāc makes whom she loves a seer (10.125.5); Varuṇa made Vasiṣṭha a seer (7.88.4); the hymns also speak of being 'fashioned' by the poets (5.2.11).
A ṛṣi is so called from seeing the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon the seers in their austerity; they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 2.11; 1.20).
Seers are no longer born because of transgression, yet some become 'seers by learning' through residual merit (ĀpDh 1.2.5.5).

Ṛta is the order by which the cosmos moves, the sacrifice succeeds and men act rightly; Agni is its guardian, Varuṇa and Mitra its lords; it was born with satya from tapas (RV 10.190.1); the year is its wheel (1.164.11); by it the Ādityas stand (10.85.1); with truth, consecration and tapas it upholds the earth (AVŚ 12.1.1).

relations.note: The ordinances (dharman, vrata) are the particular forms of the one order.

definitions.definition: In the lucidity of nirvicārā coalescence there is inner clarity (1.47); insight there is truth-bearing (1.48), with the particular as its object unlike testimony and inference (1.49); its impression obstructs other impressions (1.50). Vyāsa quotes: 'having climbed the clarity of insight, the wise one looks on the sorrowing as one on a mountain looks on those below' (YBh 1.47).

The Śvetāśvatara names the one God Rudra, Śiva, Hara and Maheśvara: Rudra is one, ruling the worlds, creating and withdrawing them (3.2); his auspicious (śivā) form is prayed to (3.5); he is Śiva present everywhere (3.11), hidden in all beings like the film on ghee (4.16), 'Śiva alone' when there is neither day nor night (4.18); the māyin (4.10).

names.name: Rudra, Tryambaka, Paśupati, Bhava, Śarva, Nīlagrīva, Śiva (epithet)

definitions.definition: Rudra is feared as the archer whose wrath and arrows harm men and cattle and is begged to turn them away, and loved as the best of physicians with a thousand remedies and a healing hand; he is lord of cattle (Paśupati), Bhava and Śarva, blue-necked; the Śatarudrīya pays homage to him as present in all places, beings and callings and names his auspicious, non-terrible body (śivā tanūḥ) and him as 'śiva, śivatara'; the Keśin drank with him from the cup.
Two brahmans are to be known: the word-brahman and the highest; one skilled in the word-brahman attains the highest; by sound alone the soundless is revealed (MaiU 6.22).

name: Revelation as the decisive means of knowledge, the Bhāgavata as supreme (Jīva)

definitions.definition: Of the means of knowledge, revelation alone reaches the transcendent; the Bhāgavata, natural commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, is supreme.

relations.note: both make the Bhāgavata the decisive scripture

definitions.definition: Verbal cognition requires expectancy, compatibility, proximity and knowledge of intention (Tattvacintāmaṇi; Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Samādhi with seed and seedless (sabīja, nirbīja)

definitions.definition: The four coalescences have an external thing as seed and are samādhi with seed (1.46); when even the impression of truth-bearing insight is stilled there is seedless samādhi (1.51); the three inner limbs are outer relative to it (3.8).

Brahmāvarta between the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī, the land of the brahmarṣis, Madhyadeśa and Āryāvarta between the mountains and seas; the land of the black antelope is fit for sacrifice (MDh 2.17–24; VDh 1.8–12; YS 1.2).

name: The sacrifice as the cosmic Person and the world

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas identify the sacrifice with the Person (ŚB 1.3.2.1), with Prajāpati and the year, and with Viṣṇu; the cosmos itself arose from a sacrifice — Brahman offering itself into all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1), the world-creators' thousand-year session with austerity, truth and breath as priests (TB 3.12.9.3–7) — and the gods live by offering to one another (ŚB 5.1.1.2).

relations.note: the identification is one of the bandhus
the identity of rite, cosmos and person makes an inner rite possible

name: The true teacher and the disciple

definitions.definition: A true teacher belongs to the unbroken lineage, knows the doctrine, lives it, and teaches out of compassion without gain; the disciple approaches with humility, is initiated by the five sacraments, serves, keeps the secret mantras from the unfit and hands them on; Rāmānuja's public disclosure of the mantra is remembered as the compassion that overrides secrecy.

Viṣṇu is known only through the true scriptures — the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa, consonant Purāṇas and works that follow them — not by reasoning alone or the senses; other texts are false scriptures, some produced to delude.

Discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues (calm, restraint, withdrawal, forbearance, faith, concentration) and longing for liberation — prerequisites for study of the Upaniṣads (Muktikā prose; Varāha 2).
Discrimination of the eternal and non-eternal, dispassion, the six virtues, and longing for liberation — the prerequisites of the inquiry into Brahman.
Viveka, vimoka, abhyāsa, kriyā, kalyāṇa, anavasāda and anuddharṣa — purity of food, desirelessness, practice, ritual duties, virtues, freedom from dejection and from elation.

name: The marks of purport (liṅga) in Dvaita exegesis

definitions.definition: Opening and conclusion, their agreement, repetition, novelty, result and praise — with reasoning — are the marks of a text's purport; name, sentence, context and position are further marks.
Devotion deepens through six forms matching the sthalas: śraddhā (faith), niṣṭhā (steadfastness), avadhāna (attentiveness), anubhava (experience), ānanda (bliss) and samarasa (equal flavour).

name: The six liṅgas

definitions.definition: Śiva met as six liṅgas corresponding to the six sthalas: ācāraliṅga (bhakta), guruliṅga (māheśvara), śivaliṅga (prasādi), jaṅgamaliṅga (prāṇaliṅgi), prasādaliṅga (śaraṇa), mahāliṅga (aikya); in the manual tradition each is correlated with a sense (smell, taste, sight, touch, hearing, the heart) and an element.

notes: Not set out in these terms in the SSM (whose liṅga-sthalas differ); sense and element correlations from memory of later manuals — low confidence.

name: The six śaktis on the side of the liṅga

definitions.definition: In the manual scheme the liṅga's power appears as six śaktis facing the six bhaktis of the soul: kriyā, jñāna, icchā, ādi, parā and cit, from the bhakta to the aikya stage.

notes: Reconstructed from memory of ṣaṭsthala manuals; verify.

definitions.definition: Brahman has three forms: with parts (sakala), without parts (niṣkala) and both; its most manifest form is Dattātreya (Śāṇḍilya 3; Brahmavidyā 37–40).

Dvaita: the soul's own intrinsic faculty of awareness (its essential sense), the seventh kind of perception; it apprehends the self, mind and its states, pleasure and pain, time and space, and the validity of knowledge; its deliverances are infallible and never sublated, and it is the final guarantor of knowledge, including the reality of the world.
