Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'you cannot see the seer of seeing' (BAU 3.4.2); 'by what would one know the knower?' (BAU 2.4.14); the unseen seer (BAU 3.7.23, 3.8.11); the ear of the ear (Kena 1.2); the word sākṣin itself in ŚU 6.11 (the one God, witness, knower, alone, without qualities).

Puruṣa is witness, seer and neutral (SK 19), witness through direct relation (SS 1.161) and of deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148); upon knowledge it sees prakṛti like a spectator, at ease (SK 65).
The unchanging consciousness that illumines the mind's modes, the three states and ignorance itself, never an object (DDV 1; the theatre-lamp of Pañcadaśī 10).

relations.note: the witness establishes the world's reality
the witness of the three states is the fourth

definitions.definition: Only the external power transforms into the world; the Lord remains unchanged, like the touchstone that yields gold.

Śrīpati: Śiva (liṅga) qualified by Śakti and the soul (aṅga) qualified by devotion are non-dual; liberation is their union in equal essence (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya); the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi works this out through the stations (sthala).

Śiva is one, qualified by his inseparable Śakti: the pedestal is the supreme Śakti, the liṅga Paraśiva, and the union of Śiva and Śakti — the universe — is the liṅga; the soul is qualified by devotion (bhakti) as Śiva by power (Śrīpati's formulation; philosophy owned by U16).

relations.note: Śrīkaṇṭha's body–soul model vs Śrīpati's Śakti-qualified union; Vīraśaiva authors claim both as their own

Both lineages use the one term for the Lord's grace and both link it to karmasāmya; they differ on direction (Kiraṇa: equality marks the time of descent; Ahirbudhnya: the Lord's glance brings about equality).
the Kiraṇa's śaktipāta chapter leads directly into its dīkṣā chapter

definitions.definition: Śiva's awakening of the soul by his power, spoken of figuratively as a 'fall'; it occurs at the time of the equality of karma, Śiva remaining its lord as the sun is of the lotus; its sign is a distinctive devotion.
Viṣṇu's compassion, his fifth power of grace, which āgama-knowers call śaktipāta: by his glance the soul's karmas become equal and fall silent, and it is lifted from saṃsāra.
The descent of Śiva's grace-power on a ripe soul, marked by signs such as devotion and the wish for release; it qualifies for dīkṣā.
Catti nipātam in four grades suited to caryā, kriyā, yoga and jñāna.

name: The Sāman notes and the musical scale

definitions.definition: The Sāmaveda sings with seven notes — kruṣṭa, prathama, dvitīya, tṛtīya, caturtha, mandra, atisvārya — which the Nāradīya Śikṣā sets against the flute's madhyama, gāndhāra, ṛṣabha, ṣaḍja, dhaivata, niṣāda and pañcama, places in the body from head to heart and shows on the fingers.

Savikalpa and nirvikalpa samādhi as auxiliaries of contemplation, with eight limbs and four obstacles (Vedāntasāra); six samādhis inner and outer (Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka); the state of no-mind (GK 3.32). Samādhi is a means; knowledge liberates.

name: Causal efficacy without a separate power (śakti)

definitions.definition: An effect follows from the totality of causes including the absence of counteragents; no distinct causal power need be posited (Udayana; Gaṅgeśa) — an enduring thing produces effects successively as auxiliaries join it (AtV).

Words with different grounds of application referring to one object; the key to reading identity-texts ('tat tvam asi', 'sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma') as naming one Brahman under different modes, since a word denoting a mode ultimately denotes the substance it qualifies.

In a mind whose activities have dwindled, like a flawless crystal, coalescence is resting on and taking the form of grasper, grasping or grasped (1.41); it is savitarkā (mixed with word, object and knowledge constructions), nirvitarkā (object alone), savicārā and nirvicārā (subtle objects) (1.42–44), extending to the unmarked (1.45); these four are samādhi with seed (1.46).

relations.note: Shared terms vitarka/vicāra and samāpatti with the Buddhist jhāna system; the structures differ (Yoga's pairs are defined by gross vs subtle objects and presence of constructions) — correspondence contested

definitions.definition: Each level of ignorance and body has a collective (cosmic) and individual aspect: Īśvara–prājña (causal), Hiraṇyagarbha–taijasa (subtle), Virāj–viśva (gross).

The one eternal relation between inseparables — part and whole, quality and substance, motion and substrate, universal and individual, particularity and eternal substance — known from the notion 'here' (VS 7.2.29 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).
The structure of Caitanya's teaching to Sanātana and of the Ṣaṭ Sandarbha: knowledge of Kṛṣṇa and his powers, devotion as the means, love as the goal.

name: The secret teaching of the saṃhitā (continuous recitation)

definitions.definition: Meditations that read the joining of words in recitation as the joining of earth and sky, teacher and pupil, mother and father (AA 3.1.1; TU 1.3), assign phoneme-classes to worlds, gods and senses (AA 3.2.5), and explain 'saṃhitā' as Prajāpati putting himself together with the metres (AA 3.2.6).

Reasoning, hearing, study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends and giving are the eight accomplishments conducive to knowledge (SK 51) — not supernormal powers (those are aiśvarya). Gauḍapāda explains each as a route to knowledge of the principles (reflection, hearing, study, approaching a teacher, a knowing friend, serving the venerable); Vācaspati is recalled as making the three destructions primary and the other five their means in sequence (low confidence).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's 'siddhi' is not power

name: Sound, word and Veda in Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: Sound is the subtle element from which space arises (SK 22 with Gauḍapāda); speech has sound as its object (SK 34). Testimony is one of three means of knowledge (SK 4–6). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds that the Vedas are neither eternal nor authored by a person, yet valid by their own manifest power (5.45–51); sound is not eternal and there is no sphoṭa (5.57–58).

name: Order of emergence and re-absorption (sañcara, pratisañcara)

definitions.definition: From prakṛti arises mahat; from mahat ahaṃkāra; from ahaṃkāra the group of sixteen — the eleven organs from its sāttvika (vaikṛta) aspect and the five subtle elements from its tāmasa (bhūtādi) aspect, both with its taijasa aspect; from the five subtle elements the five gross elements (SK 22, 24–25; SS 1.61) — sound→space, touch→air, form→fire, taste→water, smell→earth (Gauḍapāda). In re-absorption each dissolves into its cause in reverse order; the unmanifest does not dissolve (Tattvasamāsa commentaries). The Yuktidīpikā records divergent orders taught by Vindhyavāsin and others.

Kapila, the supreme sage and first knower, gave the teaching out of compassion to Āsuri, Āsuri to Pañcaśikha, who expanded it; through a succession of pupils it reached Īśvarakṛṣṇa (SK 69–71). The Māṭhara Vṛtti names Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta and Devala; the Yuktidīpikā names Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya and Mūka, adding that the full lineage cannot be told because it began with the Blessed One. Gauḍapāda places Kapila among Brahmā's seven sons with Āsuri, Voḍhu and Pañcaśikha.
Go together, speak together, let your minds know together (RV 10.191); 'I make you of one heart and mind, free from hatred' (AVŚ 3.30); may we look on all beings with the eye of a friend (VS 36.18).

Samādhi accompanied by reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness (1.17): the first has all four, the second lacks reasoning, the third lacks reflection, the fourth is I-am-ness alone; all have a support (YBh 1.17); it occurs in the one-pointed mind (YBh 1.1). Commentators differ on the objects of the bliss and I-am-ness levels (Vācaspati, Bhoja RM 1.17, Vijñānabhikṣu YV 1.17).

Activities leave impressions that produce activities again (YBh 1.5); impressions born of samādhi-insight obstruct others (1.50), and those of stilling obstruct even these (YBh 1.51); impressions of emergence and of stilling alternate in the transformation of stilling (3.9); direct perception of impressions gives knowledge of former births (3.18); memory and impressions are of one form (4.9).

relations.note: YBh 3.18: impressions that cause memory and afflictions are vāsanā; those that cause fruition are merit and demerit

name: The sacraments (saṃskāra)

definitions.definition: Rites that purify the body from conception to death and make it 'fit for Brahman' (MDh 2.26–28); Gautama's forty, including the daily great sacrifices and the solemn rites, are of no avail without the eight virtues of the self (GDh 8.14–25); later works fix a list of sixteen from conception to cremation.

notes: The sixteen-fold list is the common later one (it varies between texts); Gautama's forty are given in cpt:forty-samskaras-eight-virtues.

definitions.definition: Concentration, meditation and samādhi on one object (3.4); from its mastery the light of insight (3.5); applied by stages, 'yoga itself being the teacher' (3.6, YBh 3.6); applied to various objects it yields the powers.

name: The conjunction of seer and seen (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: The beginningless conjunction of seer and seen is the cause of what is to be avoided (2.17); it is the cause of apprehending owner and owned (2.23); its cause is ignorance (2.24); its absence is kaivalya (2.25). Vyāsa records eight views on the 'non-seeing' that causes it (YBh 2.23).

Śāṇḍilya's meditation: the person is made of resolve; meditate on the self as made of mind, with breath for body, of the form of light, like a grain of rice within yet greater than sky and earth, and resolve to attain it at death (ŚB 10.6.3).
The Chāndogya version adds 'all this is Brahman' and 'this self within the heart is Brahman' (ChU 3.14).

Knowers of the self rise above the desires for sons, wealth and worlds and live as mendicants (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22); wanderers wander forth desiring the self as their world (4.4.22); ascetics purified by the yoga of renunciation are released (MuU 3.2.6); forest-dwellers living on alms go by the door of the sun (MuU 1.2.11); Śvetāśvatara teaches those beyond the stages of life (ŚU 6.21).

Leaving the ritual world and household to wander as a mendicant; in the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads true renunciation is the union of jīva and supreme Self (Maitreya 2.17), undertaken 'the very day one becomes dispassionate' (Jābāla 4); 'by renunciation alone some reached immortality' (Kaivalya 1.3).
Renunciation of works is enjoined for the knower and for the seeker (vidvat- and vividiṣā-sannyāsa); the paramahaṃsa ideal; institutionalized in the Daśanāmī order.

Penances, śrāddhas including one's own, the virajā homa, placing the fires in oneself, the declaration renouncing the three desires, the gift of fearlessness, abandoning topknot and thread, and receiving praṇava and great saying from the guru — a ritual death to the world (Jābāla 4; Āruṇi 2–3; Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; Kaṭharudra; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).

name: The inner and outer lineages of teachers

definitions.definition: Akaccantāṉam (inner): Nandi, Sanatkumāra, Satyajñānadarśin, Parañcōti; puṟaccantāṉam (outer): Meykaṇṭār, Aruṇanti, Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar, Umāpati; the ātīṉams descend from Umāpati's disciples.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī and Aindrī - the gods' śaktis who fight with the Goddess and then dissolve into her.

name: The seven untenables of Advaita's avidyā

definitions.definition: Rāmānuja's sevenfold refutation: no locus, no power to conceal, no coherent nature, no indescribability, no proof, no remover, no possible removal.
Gajendra surrendering to the nameless supreme; the gods taking refuge in the Goddess, 'intent on saving those who come for refuge'.

Primary creation (sarga) is the emergence of mahat, the elements and senses from the unmanifest; secondary creation (visarga/pratisarga) is Brahmā's fashioning of the worlds and beings - Brahmā born on the lotus from the navel of the Lord lying on the waters.

name: The body–self relation of world and God (śarīra–śarīrin)

definitions.definition: All souls and matter are the Lord's body — wholly controlled, supported and existing for him — and he is their self; this relation, taught by the mediating texts, explains how Brahman is one and yet the world and souls are real and distinct.

members: the Lord as self (śarīrin, ādhāra, niyantṛ, śeṣin)
souls and matter as body (śarīra, ādheya, niyāmya, śeṣa)

definitions.definition: Every word, in its primary sense, names Viṣṇu — 'Brahman', 'Agni', 'Indra' and the rest — and only secondarily other beings; ritual texts too have him as purport.

name: The sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra

definitions.definition: The SK's topics are those of the whole Ṣaṣṭitantra without its tales and polemics (SK 72). The sixty are ten fundamental topics — pradhāna's existence, oneness, purposiveness; puruṣa's distinctness; being for another; plurality of puruṣas; separation; conjunction; the remaining function; non-agency — and the fifty of the creation of cognitions (Yuktidīpikā introductory verses; Māṭhara on SK 72; Kramadīpikā; Vācaspati quoting the Rājavārttika).

name: Being and non-being at the origin

definitions.definition: ChU 6.2.1-2 teaches that in the beginning there was being alone and rejects the view that being came from non-being; TU 2.7.1 and ChU 3.19.1 say that non-being was first and being arose from it; TU 2.6 says one who knows brahman as non-being becomes non-being. See dsp:being-or-non-being-first.
The nature of Brahman indicated by three words, each excluding its opposite; also the three aspects 'is, shines, dear' present in every object, as distinct from name and form.
Calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith and concentration (BS 3.4.27; BĀU 4.4.23).

name: The devotee as bride of Śiva

definitions.definition: At the śaraṇa stage the soul is wife and Śiva husband; the śaraṇa, like a faithful wife, is turned from all else; Akka Mahādēvi lives this in her vacanas to Cennamallikārjuna.

The effect exists in its material cause before production: the non-existent cannot be produced; a definite material is taken up; not everything comes from everything; the capable produces what it can; the effect has the nature of its cause (SK 9; SS 1.114–118). Production is manifestation, destruction is dissolution into the cause (SS 1.121). It grounds the inference of prakṛti from its effects (SK 14–16).
The effect is the cause in another state: the world is Brahman-with-body in gross state, pre-existing as Brahman-with-body in subtle state; transformation is real (pariṇāma), not apparent (vivarta).

relations.note: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika's new-effect view, rejected in SK 9
the pre-existent effect points to an unmanifest cause

name: Apprehension of the real (satkhyāti) — the Viśiṣṭādvaita theory of error

definitions.definition: Every cognition is of something real; error is incomplete apprehension, not the appearance of the unreal or indescribable; explained by the triplication of elements and, in dreams, by the Lord's creation.

relations.note: Nyāya's misplaced apprehension

definitions.definition: Six stations of the soul's progress to union with Śiva — bhakta (devotion has arisen), māheśvara (steadfastness through dispassion), prasādi (serenity of mind through grace), prāṇaliṅgi (the liṅga known within as consciousness whose power is breath), śaraṇa (bridal union with Śiva) and aikya (immersion in Śiva's bliss). The first three are marked by predominance of action, the last three by the yoga of knowledge.
The vacanas, above all Cennabasava's, arrange the whole of devotional life under the six sthalas, each paired with a liṅga, a kind of devotion and a mode of the soul.

relations.note: the SSM's 101 sthalas are subdivisions of the six

name: Pure reasoning and the purification of thought

definitions.definition: In the śākta means thought is purified by pure reasoning, the teacher and scripture until the pure thought 'I am Śiva' becomes thought-free (TĀ 4).

name: The distinction of sattva (intellect) and the knower of the field

definitions.definition: Sattva and the knower of the field are different yet joined, like fish and water, the gnat and the udumbara fruit, the reed and the muñja grass (MBh 12.187.39; 12.240.21–22).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the real behind the real (BAU 2.1.20); dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'speak the truth' (TU 1.11); truth alone conquers (MuU 3.1.6); the truthful are not burned by the heated axe (ChU 6.16); Satyakāma accepted for his truthfulness (ChU 4.4); one who speaks untruth withers to the root (PrU 6.1).

name: Truth and untruth — gods and men

definitions.definition: The world is twofold — truth and untruth; gods are truth, men untruth; by the vow one passes from untruth to truth, from men to the gods, and must then speak only truth (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5).

Truth upholds the earth (RV 10.85.1); taking a vow, one goes 'from untruth to truth' (VS 1.5); Varuṇa's fetters bind the one who speaks untruth and release the truthful (AVŚ 4.16.6); Prāṇa places the truth-speaker in the highest world (11.4.11).

Purifiers include knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, wind, rites, sun and time; purity in wealth is highest; the mind is purified by truth, the self by knowledge and austerity (MDh 5.105–109).

name: Schools of Vedic interpretation in the Nirukta

definitions.definition: Yāska reports competing readings of the same deity: the etymologists (natural phenomena), the legend-tellers (persons of old stories), the ritualists, and others (Nirukta 2.16; 12.1; 12.10).

name: The hierarchy of revelations

definitions.definition: Veda < Śaiva (Siddhānta) < Vāma < Dakṣiṇa < Mata < Kula < Kaula < Trika (verse quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 13.301; TĀ 13.300-301 grades grace in the same order); the Trika is the essence of all scripture (TĀ 1.18); all philosophies are stages of the one consciousness (PH 8).

notes: A variant quoted in the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa places Kula before Mata.

definitions.definition: The teachings are to be given only to a calm, devoted, well-tested disciple or son — never to the unbeliever, ungrateful or unqualified (Muktikā 1.40–49; Subāla 16; Nirvāṇa; Mahāvākya; Yogaśikhā 2.2–3, 'after twelve years of service').

name: Secrecy and restriction of the teaching

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads restrict their teaching: Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga discuss karma apart, not in public (BAU 3.2.13); the honey-doctrine is for the eldest son or a worthy pupil only, not for the whole earth full of wealth (ChU 3.11.5-6); the mantha rite only for son or pupil (BAU 6.3.12); not to be given to one not tranquil, not a son or pupil (ŚU 6.22; MaiU 6.29); only to those who have performed the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10).

name: The seer and the seen (draṣṭṛ and dṛśya)

definitions.definition: Reality is divided into the seer — pure seeing, the puruṣa (2.20) — and the seen — the guṇas as elements and senses, for experience and liberation (2.18); their conjunction, caused by ignorance, is the cause of suffering (2.17, 2.24), and I-am-ness is their seeming identity (2.6).
A self distinct from body and cognition exists: shown by desire, memory and recognition; known to itself; taught by 'not this, not this' (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
The eternal agent and enjoyer whose existence Śabara proved against unbelief; knowing it enables rites whose fruit lies in another world, and the Upaniṣads make that knowledge firm.
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; not self-luminous, it appears as subject in each cognition and does not appear in dreamless sleep.

relations.note: in release the self remains without body, senses and objects

name: The self as consciousness; the individual as contracted Śiva

definitions.definition: The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the individual is consciousness contracted, containing the universe in contracted form (PH 4), and the mind is consciousness descended (PH 5).
The self is its own witness and refuge; the gods and the person within see the evil-doer (MDh 8.84–86).

The self is to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), is its own witness (MDh 8.84), is distinguished as knower of the field, elemental self and jīva (MDh 12.12–13), is one in all like space in pots or the sun in waters (YS 3.144), and is the one called Agni, Manu, Prajāpati, Indra, breath and Brahman (MDh 12.123); self-knowledge is highest (MDh 12.85); nothing is higher than attaining the self (ĀpDh 1.8.22.2).

name: The self as its own light (svayaṃjyotis)

definitions.definition: The self is the light by which a person acts when sun, moon, fire and speech are gone (BAU 4.3.6); in dream 'the person becomes his own light' (4.3.9, 4.3.14); 'by his light all this is illumined' (KU 2.2.15; MuU 2.2.10; ŚU 6.14).

name: 'A man is born into the world he has made'

definitions.definition: The rites performed (and the knowledge held) here construct the sacrificer's world hereafter (ŚB 6.2.2.27); as one's resolve at death, so one becomes (ŚB 10.6.3.1).

name: The self as a substance with qualities

definitions.definition: An eternal, all-pervading substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition; the one who sees and touches the same thing, recognizes, remembers and is born with memories (NS 3.1.1–24, 3.2.40); its qualities (cognition, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain) are adventitious.

One of the nine substances, all-pervading (VS 7.1.29), known by marks such as breath, eye-movements, life and desire (VS 3.2.4 C), and by the distinctive use of 'I' (VS 3.2.9–13 C); perceived in yoga (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition, of two kinds: the Lord and the individual selves (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: The Buddhist denial of a self, which Nyāya refutes.
Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is pure consciousness; the Nyāya self has consciousness only as an adventitious quality.

name: The senses as made of the elements

definitions.definition: Smell, taste, sight, touch and hearing arise from earth, water, fire, air and ākāśa, and grasp those elements' qualities (NS 1.1.12–14).
Each sense is a product of its element with a bodily seat (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: The hierarchy of senses, mind and intellect

definitions.definition: The senses are high, the mind higher, the intellect higher still, and beyond the intellect is 'he' (BhG 3.42); the body as chariot with mind as charioteer, senses as horses, understanding as reins (MBh 11.7.13).

name: How a sentence conveys its meaning

definitions.definition: Abhihitānvaya: words convey their own meanings, which then connect into the sentence meaning.
Anvitābhidhāna: words convey their meanings as already connected with one another and with what is to be done.

name: Master and servant (śeṣī–śeṣa): the soul's belonging to the Lord

definitions.definition: The soul's essential nature is to exist for the Lord, its master (śeṣin); all its good lies in his pleasure and its fulfilment in service.
Emphasis on belonging to the Lord alone (ananyārha-śeṣatva) and on total dependence (pāratantrya), such that even one's surrender is not one's own act of means.

A subsidiary exists for another's sake (MS 3.1.2); Bādari limits subsidiaries to substances, qualities and purificatory acts, Jaimini includes acts (MS 3.1.3–4); subsidiaries help either by acting on a material or remotely toward the final apūrva.
Seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep (Mahā 5, following the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha).

name: The seven blisses of the breath

definitions.definition: Nijānanda, nirānanda, parānanda, brahmānanda, mahānanda, cidānanda, jagadānanda (TĀ 5.43-52).

Śubhecchā, vicāraṇā, tanumānasī, sattvāpatti, asaṃsakti, padārthabhāvanā, turyagā (Varāha 4; Akṣi 2; Mahā 5; cf. Yoga Vāsiṣṭha); mapped in the Varāha onto the measures of Oṃ and onto degrees of knowers of Brahman.

name: The seven deities of the Tantrasamuccaya

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa, Durgā, Subrahmaṇya, Gaṇapati and Śāstā, whose installation and worship the Tantrasamuccaya prescribes.

name: The six (later seven) categories of Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: Substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence (Praśastapāda; Upaskāra VS 1.1.4), to which absence is added as the seventh (Udayana's Lakṣaṇāvalī, Śivāditya, Śrīvallabha); absence was not listed earlier because it is determined through its counterpositive, not because unreal (Kiraṇāvalī). Candramati's treatise counts ten.
Seven categories (Tarkasaṅgraha, Bhāṣāpariccheda); capacity, similarity and number are not additional categories (argued from Udayana's principle of exclusive alternatives).
Accepted as further objects of knowledge besides the twelve (NBh 1.1.9).
BhP 5.24.7: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Pātāla; VP 2.5.2: Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, Mahākhya, Sutala, Pātāla - realms of daityas and nāgas, full of delights.

Śiva, mantramaheśvara, mantreśvara, mantra, vijñānākala, pralayākala, sakala - graded by their impurities: the vijñānākala has only āṇava, the pralayākala āṇava and kārma, the sakala all three (ĪPK 3.2.6-10; TĀ 10).
Hāsya, adbhuta, vīra, karuṇa, raudra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, occasional within devotion.
Seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep, each branching a hundredfold.

name: The seven stages of knowledge (jñāna-bhūmikā)

definitions.definition: Good desire, inquiry, thinning of mind, attainment of sattva, non-attachment, non-perception of objects and the reaching of the fourth; liberation lies beyond them; the seventh belongs to the jīvanmukta and the state beyond the fourth to the bodiless liberated.

relations.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha pairs the seven stages of ignorance (3.117) with the seven of knowledge (3.118)

notes: The path map itself is pth:yoga-vasistha-seven-bhumikas (owned by U51).

name: The seven states of the jīva (Pañcadaśī 7)

definitions.definition: Ignorance, veiling, projection, mediate knowledge, immediate knowledge, cessation of sorrow, unrestricted contentment.

name: The sevenfold final insight (saptadhā prāntabhūmi prajñā)

definitions.definition: The discerning one's insight at the final stage is sevenfold (2.27): four releases regarding what is to be done (known, exhausted, realized, cultivated) and three releases of the mind (buddhi's task done; guṇas dissolving; the puruṣa alone) (YBh 2.27).
Silver seen in mother-of-pearl: error as appearance, like memory, of a previously seen thing elsewhere; the world appears real until Brahman is known.
The spiritual identity in which the practitioner mentally serves in Vraja; distinct from the practitioner's physical body, with which external practice continues.
Compare the 'body fit for service' (sevopayogi-deha), a fruit of service.

Non-duality means non-separation (ananya), not identity: the Lord is one with souls, other than them, and together with them — as the vowel 'a' in all letters, the soul in the body, the eye's light with the sun's. In release the soul, its malas powerless, abides in Śiva enjoying his bliss, neither lost nor equal as a second agent.

relations.note: rejects identity and the unreality of the world

name: Powers (siddhi) and the sādhaka in the Mantramārga
notes: The Vidyāpīṭha's observance (vidyāvrata) is recorded in summary only (restricted).

definitions.definition: The sādhaka masters a mantra through observances to gain powers and enjoyments; for the yogin striving in the limbs of yoga, powers shine forth like the sun's rays and no being can overpower him.
Those who reach the Brahma-world by meditation fulfil desires by will alone, but have no power over the world's creation and are equal to the Lord only in enjoyment (BS 4.4.8, 4.4.17, 4.4.21).
Powers belong to the realm of māyā and to saguṇa meditation; they are not liberation; the knower does not relish even the bliss of absorption (GK 3.45).

The powers are obstacles in samādhi and powers only in emergence (3.37); kaivalya comes from dispassion even toward the highest (3.50); invited by the celestials, the yogin should form neither attachment nor pride (3.51, YBh 3.51); kaivalya does not require the powers (YBh 3.55).

Powers arise from practice and concentration (far-hearing, far-seeing, invisibility, sky-travel, entering bodies); the Yogatattva calls them obstacles to be hidden; the Yogaśikhā distinguishes contrived from spontaneous powers and treats spontaneous powers as the test of a siddha.

name: Powers and the warnings about them

definitions.definition: Powers arise from union with power and pure knowledge (Śiva Sūtra 1.19-21; SK 3.1-7), but powers under the veil of delusion are not liberation (Śiva Sūtra 3.6; 2.4; 3.23); light, sound, form and taste arising from the unmeṣa distract (SK 3.10).
The fruits listed for one established in a dhāraṇā (VBT 140-142).

name: The accomplished means and the means to be done

definitions.definition: The Lord is the already-existent means (siddhopāya); bhakti-yoga or prapatti is the means to be performed (sādhyopāya) which occasions his grace.
The Lord alone is the means; there is no sādhyopāya on the soul's side in the path of surrender.

Portents by which the yogin knows his death: not seeing Arundhatī, the pole-star, the moon's shadow or the Milky Way (death within a year), a rayless sun, certain dreams, loss of shadow and bodily changes (shorter spans).

name: Signs of the descent of power and of freedom from bonds

definitions.definition: A distinctive devotion (bhakti) marks the descent of power; in one freed from bonds by initiation the sign is steadiness of disposition and absence of wavering in the prescribed action, though signs are not always evident.

name: Signs of establishment in the restraints and observances

definitions.definition: Established in non-harming, hostility ceases nearby; in truth, actions and fruits rest on one's word; in non-stealing, jewels come; in celibacy, vigour; in non-possessiveness, knowledge of births (2.35–39); purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and devotion yield their fruits (2.40–45). Vyāsa calls these 'powers' (YBh 2.39).

name: First signs of progress in yoga

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): ŚU 2.11 lists the forms that precede brahman's manifestation (fog, smoke, sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal, moon); 2.12 the body made of the fire of yoga free from sickness, old age and death; 2.13 lightness, health, freedom from craving, clear complexion, pleasant voice and smell, scant excreta.

Lightness/freedom from greed, health, gentleness, pleasant smell, scant excreta, radiance, clarity, a pleasant voice; others praise the yogin, creatures do not fear him, he is untroubled by heat and cold (MkP 39.63-65).

Offence (āgas) and sin (enas) — one's own, done in the body, through wine, anger, dice or thoughtlessness, even in sleep, and those inherited from the fathers — bind as Varuṇa's fetters; the seer examines himself, asks the wise, confesses and asks to be loosened like a calf from its tether, to be sinless before Aditi (RV 1.24.15, 2.28.5, 5.85.7–8, 7.86–89).

The learned, free of envy, pride and greed (BDh 1.1.1.5), free of desire (VDh 1.6), whose practice is authoritative where the Veda is silent; a single Veda-knower's decision outweighs myriads of the ignorant (MDh 12.113).
The self is a dancer, the inner self the stage, the senses the spectators (Śiva Sūtra 3.9-11).

name: Śiva-, Rudra- and Bhairava-tantras as teaching difference, difference-in-identity and non-difference

relations.note: the Saiddhāntikas read their scriptures as teaching the soul's distinctness and reject this ranking (see dsp:rank-of-siddhanta-and-bhairava-tantras)

definitions.definition: Jayaratha derives the ten Śiva-tantras (difference), eighteen Rudra-tantras (difference-and-non-difference) and sixty-four Bhairava-tantras (non-duality) from the combinations of Sadāśiva's faces: knowledge itself unfolds in these three ways.
Liberation as equality with Śiva in bliss and powers except world-governance.
Śiva with inseparable cit-śakti is Brahman; souls and world are his body; he is material and efficient cause.
Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva and Śiva of Viṣṇu (Skanda 8–9); whoever honours Govinda honours Śaṅkara (Rudrahṛdaya); the one Lord is Brahmā, Śiva, Indra and Viṣṇu (Kaivalya 8).

The freed soul becomes 'a Śiva': its own omniscience and omnipotence, covered since beginningless time, are manifested; it is equal to Śiva, not identical with him, and does not perform the five cosmic acts.

relations.note: the Tamil school stresses inseparability and enjoyment rather than equal powers

name: The six paths (ṣaḍadhvan)
notes: No verse-level anchor recorded in this pass.

definitions.definition: The cosmos as six 'paths' — letters (varṇa), words (pada), mantras, kalās, principles (tattva) and worlds (bhuvana) — traversed and purified in nirvāṇa-dīkṣā.

The paths of the denoting - letters, mantras, words - and of the denoted - kalās (nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti, śāntyatītā), tattvas, worlds; purified in initiation and contemplated from gross to supreme (TĀ 6-12; VBT 56-57).

name: The six characteristics of pure devotion

definitions.definition: Destroys suffering; bestows auspiciousness; makes liberation trivial; rarely attained; intense special bliss; attracts Kṛṣṇa.
Feigned snoring, trembling, limping, amorous gestures, senseless acts and senseless speech - 'doors' through which dishonour brings merit and removes demerit.

relations.note: the six are 'aprākṛta'; the Lord is nirguṇa with respect to prakṛti's three guṇas

definitions.definition: Knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility and splendour; knowledge is Brahman's very form and the other five its aspects; the six are also Lakṣmī's body; pairs of them manifest as the vyūhas.

Four (kuṭīcaka, bahūdaka, haṃsa, paramahaṃsa — Bhikṣuka, Āśrama, Śāṭyāyanīya) or six (adding turīyātīta and avadhūta — Nāradaparivrājaka 5; Sannyāsa 2), graded by freedom from marks and rules, food, bathing, worship and the world attained.

name: The six limbs of surrender (ṣaḍaṅga śaraṇāgati)

definitions.definition: Resolve to do what pleases, avoidance of what displeases, faith that he will protect, choosing him as protector, laying down oneself, helplessness.

name: The six marks of purport (ṣaḍ-liṅga)

definitions.definition: Opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, demonstration — used in hearing to determine that the Upaniṣads' purport is the non-dual Brahman (from Mīmāṃsā).

Mīmāṃsā supplies the criteria that Vedānta manuals list as six marks: the opening and close of a passage (upakrama–upasaṃhāra; their relative strength argued in the Upakramaparākrama), repetition (abhyāsa, which marks a distinct rite, MS 2.2.2), novelty (apūrvatā: an injunction is for what is otherwise unobtained), the stated result (phala, MS 4.3), praise (arthavāda, MS 1.2.7) and reasoned demonstration (upapatti); doubtful sense is settled by the complementary passage (MS 1.4.29).

notes: The versified list 'upakramopasaṃhārāv abhyāso 'pūrvatā phalam / arthavādopapattī ca liṅgaṃ tātparyanirṇaye' is cited by Vedānta authors (e.g. Madhva at BSBh 1.1.4, who ascribes it to a 'Bṛhatsaṃhitā'); I did not find it as a list in the Mīmāṃsā texts consulted.

name: The six modifications of being (ṣaḍ bhāvavikārāḥ)

definitions.definition: According to Vārṣyāyaṇi, everything that becomes is born, exists, changes, grows, declines and perishes (Nirukta 1.2).

notes: Later Vedānta uses the list for what the unchanging self is free of.

definitions.definition: Conjunction; inherence in the conjoined; inherence in what inheres in the conjoined; inherence; inherence in what inheres; qualifier–qualified relation (Uddyotakara; Tarkasaṅgraha).
Phoneme (varṇa), accent (svara), quantity (mātrā), force (bala), evenness (sāma) and connection (santāna) (TU 1.2).

name: The six limbs of the Veda

definitions.definition: Phonetics, ritual procedure, grammar, etymology, metre and time-reckoning; the Veda's nose, hands, mouth, ear, feet and eye (PŚ 41–42), studied as a duty without motive (Mahābhāṣya); compiled by later seers for ease of learning (Nirukta 1.20); among the fourteen seats of knowledge (YS 1.3); counted as lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.5).
Āśrama Upaniṣad: four kinds each of student, householder, forest-dweller and wanderer.

name: The sixteen categories of Nyāya (ṣoḍaśa padārtha)

definitions.definition: The sixteen topics whose true knowledge yields the highest good (NS 1.1.1): the means and objects of knowledge, and the elements of inquiry and debate. The Bhāṣya explains that the latter are listed separately so that Nyāya is not merely a science of the self like the Upaniṣads.

relations.note: Nyāya's sixteen are topics of inquiry; the Vaiśeṣika categories are kinds of reals; NBh 1.1.9 admits the latter as further prameyas.

name: The sixteen parts of the person

definitions.definition: The person has sixteen parts (kalā), fifteen of which depend on food (ChU 6.7); in PrU 6 the sixteen parts arise from the person and vanish into him like rivers into the ocean, and he becomes partless and immortal; MuU 3.2.7 speaks of the fifteen parts going to their foundations.

name: The sixty-four Bhairava tantras
members: Bhairavāṣṭaka: Svacchanda, Bhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Asitāṅga, Mahocchuṣma, Kapālīśa
Yāmalāṣṭaka: Brahma-, Viṣṇu-, Svacchanda-, Ruru-, (5th unnamed), Ātharvaṇa-, Rudra-, Vetāla-yāmala
Matāṣṭaka: Rakta, Lampaṭa, Lakṣmīmata, (Mata?), Cālikā, Piṅgala, Utphullaka, Viśvādya
Maṅgalāṣṭaka: Bhairavī (Picu, twofold), (3rd unnamed), Brāhmī Kalā, Vijayā, Candrā, Maṅgalā, Sarvamaṅgalā
Cakrāṣṭaka: Mantra-, Varṇa-, Śakti-, Kalā-, Bindu-, Nāda-, Guhya-, Kha-cakra
Bahurūpāṣṭaka: Andhaka, Rurubheda, Aja, Mūla, Varṇabhaṇṭha, Viḍaṅga, Jvālin, Mātṛrodana
Vāgīśāṣṭaka: Bhairavī, Citrikā, Haṃsā, Kadambikā, Hṛllekhā, Candralekhā, Vidyullekhā, Vidyumān
Śikhāṣṭaka: Bhairavī Śikhā, Vīṇā, Vīṇāmaṇi, Sammoha, Ḍāmara, Atharvaka, Kabandha, Śiraścheda
notes: Checked against Jayaratha's quotation in the local Tantrāloka e-text; three slots are unnamed or unclear in the quoted text. Surviving texts include the Svacchanda (1), Brahmayāmala (2), Jayadrathayāmala (= Śiraścheda, 8); the Vīṇāśikha and Sammoha belong to the Vāma stream.

definitions.definition: The Śrīkaṇṭhīya's eight groups of eight (Bhairava, Yāmala, Mata, Maṅgala, Cakra, Bahurūpa, Vāgīśa, Śikhā), each group 'spoken' by one of the Bhairavas; together 'the wheel of Sadāśiva'.
The 'eight times eight' of Śiva's teaching, dominated by non-duality.

name: The sixty-four tantras of the Śākta lists

relations.note: different lists of 'sixty-four', overlapping only partly (e.g. Kāmika, Vātula, Candrajñāna and Sarvajñānottara appear here, Siddhānta titles in the Śaiva lists)

definitions.definition: The Vāmakeśvara's sixty-four tantras 'of the Mothers' (Mahāmāyā, Śambara … Viśuddheśvara), by which, the Saundaryalaharī says, Paśupati beguiled the world before revealing the Goddess's own tantra; Lakṣmīdhara judges them Kaula and non-Vedic.

name: The sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and the nine groups of devotees

definitions.definition: The canonical company of Śiva's devotees: 63 individual saints and 9 groups (tokai aṭiyār), first listed in Cuntarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai (Tēvāram 7.39), expanded by Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi and told at length in Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam; their images stand in Tamil Śiva temples and their days are kept as festivals. Their stories teach that love and service of Śiva and his devotees, not birth, learning or rite, win his grace; they include kings, brahmins, merchants, farmers, a hunter, a potter, a washerman, a fisherman, an outcaste, women and a former Buddhist.

members: (groups) Tillaivāḻ antaṇar — the brahmins of Tillai
Poyyaṭimai illāta pulavar — poets without false servitude
Pattarāyp paṇivār — those who bow as devotees
Paramaṉaiyē pāṭuvār — those who sing only of the Supreme
Cittattaic civaṉpālē vaittār — those who fixed their minds on Śiva
Tiruvārūrp piṟantār — those born in Tiruvārūr
Muppōtum tirumēṉi tīṇṭuvār — those who touch the holy image thrice daily (the priests)
Muḻuniṟu pūciya muṉivar — sages smeared wholly with ash
Appālum aṭicārntār — those beyond, who reached his feet
notes: Order follows the Periya Purāṇam as usually given (moderate confidence); the nine groups' names are given at moderate confidence.

name: Skambha, the frame of the world

definitions.definition: The pillar or frame in which tapas, ṛta, vows, faith and truth abide and on which the worlds rest; identified with the highest Brahman to which homage is paid (AVŚ 10.7–8); cf. the One that propped apart the six regions (RV 1.164.6).
Both dissolve the mind, but in sleep it dissolves into tamas and does not liberate; in samādhi the world dissolves into the witness-consciousness (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 2.3).

Soma is the plant pressed in the sacrifice, the exhilarating drink that makes the drinkers say 'we have become immortal, we have gone to the light' (RV 8.48.3), the god purifying himself through the filter (book 9), bringer of bliss (9.113.6); set in heaven by ṛta (10.85.1).

relations.note: The Ṛgveda itself distinguishes the pressed plant from the soma the brahmins know (10.85.3).

definitions.definition: The soul is neither Real (like Śiva) nor unreal (like the changing world) but between, taking the nature of what it joins; it knows only when made to know.

name: Sound as a non-eternal quality of ākāśa

definitions.definition: Sound has a beginning and is sense-perceived, hence non-eternal (NS 2.2.13ff.).

Sound is the mark of ākāśa, produced by conjunction, disjunction and sound (VS 2.1.24–27, 2.2.36–37 C); it is inarticulate or phonemic (Tarkasaṅgraha); later authors explain its travel to the ear on the model of waves or of kadamba buds.

notes: The wave / kadamba-bud models are recalled from later manuals.

definitions.definition: The Veda, the smṛti and conduct of those who know it, the practice of the good, and what satisfies oneself (MDh 2.6, 2.12); with desire born of right intention (YS 1.7); where texts are silent, the agreement of the knowers and of a learned assembly (ĀpDh 1.1.1.2; MDh 12.108–113); dharma is what the Āryas praise (ĀpDh 1.7.20.6–7); the rest may be learned from women and all classes (ĀpDh 2.11.29.15).

The ultimate as dynamic, pulsing awareness - opening and closing (unmeṣa-nimeṣa) - on which all particular movements rest, never lost in any state, and graspable in intense moments and in the gap between thoughts.

relations.note: spanda read as vimarśa

name: The special qualities of the self (ātma-viśeṣaguṇa)

definitions.definition: Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit and demerit — eight special qualities of the self alone (Tarkasaṅgraha); memory-impression also resides only in the self; liberation is their cessation (Praśastapāda, as usually summarized).
Rejected: the letters themselves (through their impressions) convey the meaning; a separate sphoṭa is unperceived and superfluous (Upavarṣa in Śabara; ŚV sphoṭavāda).

name: The Lord's eternal abode (dhāma: Goloka, Vraja)

definitions.definition: Goloka/Vraja, made of wish-fulfilling gems, is Kṛṣṇa's highest abode above Vaikuṇṭha; the earthly Vraja (Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, Rādhākuṇḍa) is non-different from it.
Vraja and Gokul as the site of the Lord's eternal play into which grace admits the soul.

name: The cycle of rites for the dead

definitions.definition: Cremation; ten days of piṇḍa and water (building the preta-body); the eleventh-day rites (vṛṣotsarga, the 'middle sixteen'); sapiṇḍīkaraṇa on the twelfth day or later; monthly śrāddhas through the first year (feeding the traveller on Yama's road); the annual śrāddha; periods of impurity for the kin.
Faith kindles the fire and makes the offering; it is invoked morning, noon and evening (RV 10.151); against doubters, 'have faith in him' (2.12.5).

name: The five means: faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight

definitions.definition: The means by which samādhi arises for yogins (1.20): faith (serenity of mind, protecting like a mother), from which energy, from which mindfulness, with which the mind is concentrated, to which discerning insight comes; from its practice and dispassion, asamprajñāta (YBh 1.20).

relations.standpoint: as a list of five qualities leading to samādhi and insight
relations.note: Same five names as the Buddhist indriya/bala (saddhā, viriya, sati, samādhi, paññā); Vyāsa gives them as a causal sequence ending in asamprajñāta samādhi.

definitions.definition: Dvaita: hearing, reflection, meditation and devotion are the principal means to knowledge; meditation, not a mere subsidiary of hearing, produces the direct realization by which the Lord is pleased; hearing and the rest must never be reduced.
The threefold discipline of the qualified seeker (BĀU 2.4.5): hearing removes doubt about the means (scripture's purport), reflection doubt about the object, contemplation contrary habitual notions.
Hearing is principal, the other two auxiliaries.
Contemplation is principal; the purified mind is the instrument.

relations.note: meditation built on hearing produces direct realization

definitions.definition: The good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person; the wise examines and chooses the good, the fool the pleasant for getting and keeping (KU 1.2.1-2); Naciketas is praised for refusing the pleasant (KU 1.1.21-29).

name: The nature and rank of Śrī

definitions.definition: Śrī is the Lord's inseparable consort, mother of the world and mediator.
All-pervading (vibhu) like Viṣṇu, of the Lord's rank (Īśvara-koṭi), with him the means and the goal; the couple is one object of refuge.
The mediator (puruṣakāra), not the means; commonly reported as atomic and of the rank of souls (jīva-koṭi), though never separate from the Lord.
Viṣṇu → Śrī → Viṣvaksena → Nammāḻvār → Nāthamuni → Uyyakkoṇḍār → Maṇakkāl Nambi → Yāmuna → Periya Nambi → Rāmānuja.
Rāmānuja → Embār → Parāśara Bhaṭṭar → Nañjīyar → Nampiḷḷai → Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai → Piḷḷai Lokācārya → Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai → Maṇavāḷa Māmuni.
Rāmānuja → Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ → Engaḷāḻvāṉ → Naḍādūr Ammāḷ → Ātreya Rāmānuja (Appuḷḷār) → Vedānta Deśika.

Before creation Nārāyaṇa alone exists, holding all souls in himself with their awareness quiescent, with Lakṣmī; he creates, as his sport, so that embodied souls may reach happiness, sorrow or the mean according to their natures; creation is the real transformation of prakṛti under his control (not of Brahman itself), unfolding into the uncompounded principles and the cosmic egg.

name: Creation and dissolution as the Lord's play

definitions.definition: Creation, maintenance and dissolution are the Lord's play (līlā) in the realm of prakṛti: he creates to give souls bodies to work out karma and seek him; Brahmā and Śiva are souls whom he empowers; the eternal realm is untouched by these cycles.

name: The stages of love from prema to mahābhāva

definitions.definition: prema → sneha → māna → praṇaya → rāga → anurāga → bhāva/mahābhāva (rūḍha, adhirūḍha: modana, mādana).

name: Waking, dream and dreamless sleep (Mīmāṃsā view)

definitions.definition: Dreams present real objects of other times and places, remembered through impressions awakened by the unseen and taken as present by a sleep-affected mind; release resembles dreamless sleep in having no cognition, but without return.
In dreamless sleep the self is not manifest, since there is no cognition.

Puruṣa witnesses deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148); in concentration (samādhi), deep sleep and liberation puruṣa has the form of Brahman — in the first two with seed, in liberation with the seed destroyed (SS 5.116–117). The SK itself does not analyse waking, dream and sleep.

name: The fixed and the moving (sthāvara and jaṅgama)

definitions.definition: Temples, images and installed liṅgas are the fixed, which perish; the devotee's body and the wandering devotee are the moving, which endures and is the true temple; worship of stone while despising the living devotee is hypocrisy.

The SSM ranks worship on the palm above worship on a pedestal, the inner liṅga above stone liṅgas and calls those who cling only to the outer liṅga deluded, yet forbids using the nirmālya of fixed liṅgas and bids their protection.

relations.note: the iṣṭaliṅga replaces the temple liṅga

definitions.definition: One who has given up the desires of the mind and is content in the self, unagitated in sorrow and pleasure, senses withdrawn, awake where beings sleep, unmoved as the ocean, in the brāhmī state (BhG 2.54–72); with close parallels in the devotee dear to the Lord (12.13–20) and the one beyond the guṇas (14.22–25).

relations.note: the description is of one liberated in this life as the Advaita commentators read it; the Gītā itself does not use 'jīvanmukti'

definitions.definition: Standard images used to teach non-duality: rope-snake, shell-silver, pot-space, the reflection of the sun, dream, clay and pots, the tenth man, the crystal and the red flower, the potter's wheel, the firebrand, the mirror-city, the theatre lamp, the painted canvas.

name: Women's dharma (strīdharma), as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: Women are to be honoured, for where they are not all rites fail (MDh 3.56); a woman is to be under the protection of father, husband and sons (MDh 5.148; 9.3); a widow chooses chastity or (in some later texts) ascending the pyre (Viṣṇusmṛti 25.14); women are qualified for Śrauta rites with their husbands (KŚS 1.1.7); dharma may be learned from women (ĀpDh 2.11.29.15); an older tradition distinguishes women who study the Veda (brahmavādinī) from those who marry directly (sadyovadhū) (Hārīta, quoted).

notes: Recorded as stated in the texts; the Hārīta quotation is known only through later digests.

name: The five auspicious āgamas and the Samaya way

definitions.definition: Lakṣmīdhara's Vedic Samaya canon — the Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra saṃhitās — opposed to the 'mixed' Candrakalā group and the Kaula sixty-four.

name: The auspicious support of the mind (śubhāśraya)

definitions.definition: The mind in yoga needs a support: Brahman in its formed and formless aspects; since the beginner cannot hold the formless, he meditates on Viṣṇu's form, the ground of all powers, which alone purifies (VP 6.7.45-78).

name: The subtle body of the Netratantra

definitions.definition: Six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Netra 7.1), pierced in subtle meditation.

Dharma is hard to know: the hunter Balāka reaches heaven, the truth-telling Kauśika hell (MBh 8.49); the golden rule is its summary (13.114.8; 5.39.57); in distress other rules apply (12.139); the vulgate Yakṣapraśna says its truth is hidden in a cave.
Brahman, pure of māyā, alone is; the world is its real form produced without change; souls are its parts; only saṃsāra is unreal.

relations.note: rejects māyā as the explanation of the world

name: The void (śūnya, bayalu) in Allama Prabhu

definitions.definition: Allama names the ultimate as the void — bayalu, open space without enclosure — in which liṅga, aṅga and every attainment cease to be two; his tests of the other śaraṇas in the Śūnyasampādane bring each attainment to this void.

notes: Needs anchoring in specific vacanas in Phase D.

definitions.definition: Taking refuge in the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); those who take refuge cross his māyā (7.14); Rāma protects anyone who comes once for refuge (Rāmāyaṇa 6.18.33).
Souls and world are by their very nature both different and non-different from the Lord: different as dependent, atomic and limited; non-different as his powers without separate existence.
Yādavaprakāśa (as reported by Rāmānuja): Brahman itself naturally transforms into Īśvara, souls and matter, and so is both one and many by nature.

The duty arising from one's own nature and station, to be done even if imperfect in preference to another's (BhG 3.35, 18.47); by it, as worship of the Lord, one reaches perfection (18.46); the meat-seller holds his inherited work as his dharma (MBh 3.198).

The duty of one's class and stage, better imperfect than another's done well (MDh 10.97); each class's work is its austerity (MDh 11.235); following it brings heaven and endlessness (Arthaśāstra 1.3.14) and a good rebirth (ĀpDh 2.1.2.2–3).
Consciousness reveals itself without being an object of another cognition; defined by Citsukha.

The fruit of rites for 'one desiring heaven', understood wherever no fruit is stated; the word denotes happiness (prīti) itself (Śabara); later described as happiness unmixed with sorrow, not followed by loss.
Each soul's innate, beginningless fitness fixes its class, office, the form of worship and vision open to it and its final destiny; it cannot be altered, and to aim beyond it leads to a fall.
Dvaita: validity is intrinsic and is grasped by the witness; reasoning only removes doubts in a defective intellect; invalidity is extrinsic.
Reality is twofold: the independent, Viṣṇu alone, and the dependent — everything else — which exists, knows and acts only under his control; knowing this frees one from saṃsāra.
The absolute freedom of consciousness, its primary sovereignty, by which it manifests, conceals and reveals (ĪPK 1.5.13; PH 1).
The liberated renouncer's freedom from rule (Nirvāṇa; Avadhūta 33), qualified in the Avadhūta by the option of acting by scripture for the world's good.
The island north of the milk ocean where the white, one-pointed devotees dwell and Nārāyaṇa reveals himself (MBh 12.323.23–26; Nārada's visit 12.321–326).

Right after creation Śiva divided the one knowledge among ten Śivas and eighteen Rudras, each text then passing through a chain of recipients (a Śiva/Rudra, then gods, sages or gaṇas) to reach humans.

name: The tantri and the śānti in Kerala temples

definitions.definition: A hereditary tantri family holds ritual authority over a temple (installation, festivals, purifications), while śānti priests perform the daily pūjās; e.g. the Cēnnās family at Guruvāyūr.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): creation proceeds by tapas (TU 2.6; PrU 1.4; MuU 1.1.8-9, whose tapas is knowledge); Bhṛgu seeks brahman by tapas, 'tapas is brahman' (TU 3.2); tapas as one branch of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); the self is found by truth and austerity (MuU 3.1.5; ŚU 1.15); sickness and cremation are the supreme tapas (BAU 5.11).

Tapas is the heat by which That One was born (RV 10.129.3) and from which ṛta and satya came (10.190.1); by tapas the ancients reached heaven (10.154.2); the unheated do not attain soma (9.83.1); the student fills the worlds with tapas (AVŚ 11.5.4); the seers first undertook tapas and dīkṣā (19.41.1); Agastya's long tapas is set beside married life (RV 1.179).

Tāraka ('what makes one cross') is the yoga of lights and targets, with and without form; its later part is amanaska, the mind-less state in which the mind becomes 'like an udder after milking' (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 1.3, 3.1–2).

relations.note: Tāraka culminates in the mind-less (amanaska/unmanī) state.

definitions.definition: Souls are graded, beginninglessly and endlessly, in knowledge, bliss and office — from humans and kings up through gandharvas, ancestors, gods, Indra, Rudra, to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Lakṣmī above and Viṣṇu infinitely above; the gradation is unalterable and continues in liberation, and knowing it is required for liberation.

name: Incidental and essential definitions of Brahman

definitions.definition: Brahman is defined incidentally (taṭastha) as the world-cause and essentially (svarūpa) as existence–consciousness–infinitude/bliss.

name: The many counts of the principles, reconciled

definitions.definition: The seers count the principles as nine, eleven, five, three, twenty-six, twenty-five, seven, six, four, seventeen, sixteen or thirteen; all are right, because the principles enter into one another and each speaker counts as he intends; the dispute itself arises from the Lord's powers and ceases with calm and self-control.
Vallabha follows the Bhāgavata's count of twenty-eight principles (nine, eleven, five and three), treating them as Brahman's own real manifestation rather than as prakṛti's alone.

relations.note: a text-internal instance of reconciling divergent teachings by the intention of the speaker

notes: U16 contribution recalled with low confidence; locate in the Tattvārthadīpanibandha.

definitions.definition: Dependent reality divides into negation (prior, posterior, constant) and positive being; positive into sentient (Lakṣmī untouched by sorrow; souls touched by sorrow) and insentient (eternal: Vedas; eternal-and-non-eternal: Purāṇas etc., time, prakṛti; non-eternal: uncompounded — mahat, ahaṃkāra, buddhi, manas, ten senses, five subtle elements, five elements — and compounded — the cosmic egg and its contents).

name: The three realities (tattvatraya: cit, acit, Īśvara)

definitions.definition: Three eternal, real and distinct entities: souls, insentient matter and the Lord, the first two being the body of the third.

name: Teacher, student and transmission in Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: The teaching is secret (SK 69), given out of compassion (SK 70), to a qualified student: Kapila tested Āsuri three times over thousand-year intervals before he renounced (Māṭhara). Acquired knowledge arises with the teacher as its occasioning cause (Gauḍapāda on SK 43); among the accomplishments are hearing, study, approaching a teacher and serving the venerable (Gauḍapāda on SK 51). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra: instruction must be repeated (4.3); take the essence from many teachers like a bee (4.13); hearing without reflection does not suffice, as with Virocana, while Indra attained after obeisance, continence and long approach (4.17–19); a defiled mind lets the seed of instruction fail (4.29–30); there must be liberated teachers, else the blind lead the blind (3.80–82); there is no fixed rule since students differ (3.77).

The teacher is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, calm, compassionate, free of pride; the student approaches with humility, service and questioning, calm, self-controlled and longing for liberation; knowledge of the truth, not birth, makes the guru (Manīṣāpañcaka).
The student brings fuel and begs daily, so Death has no claim on him (ŚB 11.3.3).

The teacher is revered above the father as giver of the Vedic birth (MDh 2.145–146); learning, not age, makes one great (2.154); the serving pupil obtains the teacher's knowledge as a digger reaches water (2.218); knowledge may be received from anyone in faith (2.238); the ācārya is the one from whom the dharmas are gathered, never to be harmed (ĀpDh 1.1.1.14–15).

name: The temple as the deity's body
notes: Stated in many texts; exact loci not verified in this pass (listed as a gap). U58 owns Vāstu/Śilpa.

definitions.definition: Āgama and śilpa texts treat the temple (prāsāda) as the body of the deity, its parts named as limbs.
Pāñcarātra saṃhitās likewise identify the temple with Bhagavān's body.
Kerala tantra treats the temple and its installed deity as a living body whose power the tantri maintains.

name: Good and bad activity of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Bad: injury, theft, forbidden sex (body); lying, harshness, slander, idle talk (speech); malice, coveting, disbelief (mind) — leading to adharma. Good: giving, protecting, serving (body); truthful, beneficial, pleasant speech and recitation; compassion, freedom from craving, faith (mind) — leading to dharma (NBh 1.1.2).

relations.note: Close parallel to the Buddhist ten courses of wholesome and unwholesome action (list of shared vocabulary; no borrowing asserted).

definitions.definition: Ciṇī, ciñciṇī, bell, conch, lute, cymbal, flute, mṛdaṅga, bherī, thunder — heard in order, each with its effect; the tenth is practised (Haṃsa 4).
Tattva-rūpa, tattva-darśana, tattva-śuddhi; ātma-rūpa, ātma-darśana, ātma-śuddhi; śiva-rūpa, śiva-darśana, śiva-yoga, śiva-bhoga.

Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna and the five minor — nāga (belching), kūrma (blinking), kṛkara (sneezing, hunger), devadatta (yawning, sleep), dhanañjaya (remains after death); each has a seat and function.

Yamas: non-injury, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, rectitude, forbearance, fortitude, moderate diet, purity; niyamas: austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, hearing doctrine, modesty, discernment, japa, vows (Śāṇḍilya, Darśana, Triśikhi, Varāha).

name: Ten yamas and ten niyamas (Devī Gītā)

definitions.definition: Yamas: non-violence, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, uprightness, forbearance, fortitude, moderate food, purity. Niyamas: austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, hearing the settled doctrine, modesty, discernment, mantra repetition, oblation.
Steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth, absence of anger (MDh 6.92).
Ten men each forget to count himself; told 'you are the tenth', each knows it at once: the mahāvākya gives immediate knowledge of what was never lost.

The Saṃhitās speak of a One behind the many: That One which breathed windless by its own power before creation (RV 10.129.2), the One Being the inspired call by many names (1.164.46), the One that has become all this (8.58.2), the one-alone god in whom the gods become one (AVŚ 13.4), the Unborn that propped apart the six regions (RV 1.164.6), of whom there is no likeness (VS 32.3).

relations.note: The One is spoken of both as beyond the gods (10.129.6: the gods are later) and as what the gods' names name (1.164.46).

definitions.definition: The embodied self (ātman, dehin) is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain, passing into new bodies as into new clothes, unmanifest and unthinkable (BhG 2.11–30); the knower of the field (13.1–2); an eternal portion of the Lord (15.7); Bhṛgu defends the existence of a living self in the elemental body (MBh 12.175–185).

name: Theistic Sāṃkhya (seśvara)

definitions.definition: Forms of Sāṃkhya that admit a Lord: the epic 'twenty-sixth principle' above the twenty-five (Mahābhārata, Mokṣadharma), Purāṇic accounts where emergence from pradhāna proceeds under the Lord and Kapila is an avatāra (Māṭhara on SK 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa), a Pāñcarātra Ṣaṣṭitantra (Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā), Yoga as 'Sāṃkhya with Īśvara' in doxographies, and Vijñānabhikṣu, who salutes mahat as the self-born Lord and treats the Sāṃkhya Sūtra's denial of Īśvara as concessive.

relations.note: classical non-theism vs theistic readings

notes: Mahābhārata and Ahirbudhnya chapter details recalled, not checked.

definitions.definition: Viparītakhyāti: only the relation appearing in error is unreal; the related items are real.
Akhyāti: error is non-apprehension of the difference between a perception and a memory.

The instrument is thirteenfold — buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas (internal) and the ten capacities (external); it seizes, holds and illuminates (SK 32–33). The internal works in three times, the external in the present; the internal is the door-keeper, the external the doors (SK 33, 35). The organs act by one another's impulse, for puruṣa's purpose alone (SK 31), and like lamps present that purpose to buddhi (SK 36).

name: The thirty-nine vibhavas
notes: Forty names result if every epithet is counted separately; the text says thirty-nine (segmentation uncertain).

definitions.definition: The Lord's descents beginning with Padmanābha and ending with Pātālaśayana, whose details the Sātvata teaches.

name: The thirty-six principles (ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva)

definitions.definition: Manifestation from Śiva to earth in thirty-six levels: five pure (Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā), the impure boundary of Māyā with its five sheaths (kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati), then the Sāṃkhya series from Puruṣa to earth. All shine in the supreme like images in a mirror (Paramārthasāra 11-13).

Siddhānta form: five pure tattvas (Śiva/nāda, Śakti/bindu, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā) evolved from bindu (pure māyā), not from Śiva; seven vidyā-tattvas (māyā, kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati, puruṣa); twenty-four ātma-tattvas (prakṛti with the guṇas, buddhi, ahaṅkāra, manas, ten organs, five subtle and five gross elements). Placement of details (e.g. a separate guṇa-tattva) varies among texts.
Tattuvam 36 (5 civa, 7 vittai, 24 āṉma), which the soul must see as not-self (tattva-rūpa, -darśana, -śuddhi); expanded to 96 in Tamil lists.

relations.note: tattvas 12-36 correspond to Sāṃkhya's twenty-five; the Śaivas add eleven above them
Sāṃkhya's 25 are the lower range of the 36
in the Siddhānta the tattvas are pāśa (products of bindu and māyā), not Śiva's self-manifestation

notes: The order of the kañcukas varies slightly between sources (e.g. kāla and niyati).

definitions.definition: The gods counted as eleven in heaven, eleven on earth and eleven in the waters (RV 1.139.11), or as 3,339 (3.9.9).
Transient emotions that surge within the permanent love for Kṛṣṇa.

name: Three kinds of teacher (codaka, bodhaka, mokṣada)

definitions.definition: The one who points out the path, the one who shows the place, the one who grants the supreme (Brahmavidyā 51–53).
Kēvalam: the soul alone with āṇava, without instruments, like darkness; cakalam: embodied with the three malas; cuttam: purified by grace.
Beings' contemplation is of Brahman (the Sanandanas), of action (gods down to plants), or of both (Hiraṇyagarbha and others with office).

name: The three births of a person

definitions.definition: The first birth is as semen in the father and its placing in the mother; the second is the child's birth; the third is rebirth after the self departs at death (AU 2.1.1-4).

relations.note: gross = food sheath; subtle = vital, mental, intellectual sheaths; causal = bliss sheath

definitions.definition: Gross (quintuplicated elements, waking), subtle (seventeen members, dream) and causal (ignorance, deep sleep) bodies; the self is none of them.
Inherent (threads), non-inherent (their conjunction), efficient (loom); the instrument is the special cause (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: The three causes of the world

definitions.definition: Śiva is the efficient cause (nimitta), māyā (and bindu) the material cause (upādāna), Śiva's power the instrumental cause (sahakārin); Śiva does not transform.
Verbal, generalizing and figurative quibbles (NS 1.2.10–17).

name: The three classes of souls (sakala, pralayākala, vijñānākala)

definitions.definition: Souls classed by their bonds: sakala (three bonds), pralayākala (mala and karma), vijñānākala (mala only); subdivided by the ripeness of mala.
Tirumantiram: souls of three kinds, with one, two or three malas.

name: The three coverings of the self

definitions.definition: The subtle covering of impurity (mala), the gross covering of the kañcukas from māyā, and the outer body: the self wrapped in three sheaths (Paramārthasāra 24).
Inner absorption (antar-daśā), half-external (ardha-bāhya) and external (bāhya) consciousness, alternating in his last years of divine madness.
A brāhmaṇa is born owing studentship to the seers, sacrifice to the gods and offspring to the ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5); ŚB adds hospitality to men (1.7.2.1–6).
The debts must be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).
There are only three deities by station — Agni, Vāyu/Indra, Sūrya (Nirukta 7.5) — and because of the deity's majesty the one self is praised in many ways, the other gods being its limbs (7.4).

relations.note: both name one self behind many names (Nirukta 7.4; MDh 12.123)

definitions.definition: Attachment, aversion and delusion; delusion is the worst (NS 4.1.3–6); they arise from false knowledge and impel activity (NS 1.1.18; NBh 1.1.2).

name: The three forms of the ultimate in Śuddhādvaita

definitions.definition: Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa (highest, goal of grace-devotion), Akṣara Brahman (his abode, goal of knowers) and Antaryāmin; the world and souls are further forms — as the Gaṅgā is water, holy river and goddess.

In the recitation tradition the presiding deities of the three caritas are Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī, derived from the primordial Mahālakṣmī (Prādhānika Rahasya); the thirteen chapters themselves do not use these three names for the caritas.

relations.note: later ancillary texts map the three forms onto the three episodes

definitions.definition: Grace won by ritual works is lowest and yields heaven; won by hearing and the like is middling and yields higher worlds; won by fullness of knowledge is highest and alone yields liberation.

relations.note: grace is graded by its means

definitions.definition: Knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra on the path of the suṣumnā, pierced by kuṇḍalinī through yoga and the grace of guru and god (Yogakuṇḍalī 1; Varāha 5; Brahmavidyā).

name: The three great attitudes taught to Bhṛṅgīśa

definitions.definition: The great doer, the great enjoyer and the great renouncer: acting, enjoying and renouncing without ego, preference or notions of merit.

name: The three guṇas

definitions.definition: Sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas to action, tamas by negligence, sloth and sleep (BhG 14.5–8); each prevails by overpowering the others; their signs, destinies and the classification of faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 14, 17, 18); no being is free of them (18.40).

Sattva, rajas and tamas, the constituents of prakṛti and all its products: of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion; illuminating, activating and restraining; light, mobile and heavy; they dominate, support and produce one another and work together for one purpose like the parts of a lamp (SK 12–13). Prakṛti is their equilibrium (SS 1.61); creation abounds in sattva above, rajas in the middle and tamas below (SK 54).

Sattva (illumination), rajas (activity) and tamas (inertia) (2.18) — mutually dependent, distinct in power, transforming; their conflicting activity makes everything suffering for the discerning (2.15); all things are arrangements of them (4.13); the mind has three guṇas and its states depend on their mix (YBh 1.2).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva bound to the guṇas and 'three-guṇa'd' (ŚU 5.7); in MaiU 5.2 darkness (tamas), impelled, becomes rajas and then sattva, with Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu as their parts; MaiU 3.5 lists the marks of tamas and rajas.
Māyā/ignorance consists of sattva, rajas and tamas: sattva pure (adjunct of Īśvara) or impure (of jīva); tamas veils, rajas projects.
Sattva, rajas and tamas are qualities (non-substances) of prakṛti, mixed in all bodies and worlds; the Lord and the eternal realm are free of them.

notes: U05's contribution; classical Sāṃkhya's account is given by U09.

definitions.definition: Sattva (knowledge), rajas (attraction and aversion), tamas (ignorance) as qualities of the self determining whether one goes to the state of gods, men or animals, each in three grades (MDh 12.24–51).

name: The three kinds of insentient reality

definitions.definition: Pure sattva (śuddha-sattva), mixed sattva (prakṛti with the three guṇas and its twenty-three evolutes — mahat, ahaṃkāra, mind, ten senses, five subtle and five gross elements) and that devoid of sattva (time).

Discussion (vāda) for truth; wrangling (jalpa) using quibbles and futile rejoinders; cavilling (vitaṇḍā) without a counter-thesis (NS 1.2.1–3); the last two are allowed to protect truth like a thorn fence (NS 4.2.50); vāda is held with teachers and fellow-seekers (NS 4.2.48).
Faith born of one's nature is sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic, accordingly worshipping gods, yakṣas and rākṣasas, or ghosts and spirits; a person is made of faith (BhG 17.2–4).

Sāttvic food increases life, vitality, strength, health and happiness and is savoury and wholesome; rājasic food is bitter, sour, salty, hot and burning and brings pain and disease; tāmasic food is stale, tasteless, putrid, leftover and impure (BhG 17.7–10).

Giving because it ought to be given, to one who makes no return, at the right place and time to the worthy, is sāttvic; for a return or grudgingly, rājasic; at the wrong place and time, to the unworthy, with contempt, tāmasic (BhG 17.20–22).
The absolute (pāramārthika) jīva, in truth Brahman; the empirical (vyāvahārika) jīva, the reflection in the intellect; the illusory (prātibhāsika) jīva of dream.
Accumulated (burnt by knowledge), to come (does not cling) and begun (exhausted by experience, like a potter's wheel's momentum).
Cañcitam (stored), pirārattam (begun, which forms this body) and ākāmiyam (being made): dīkṣā and grace burn the first, the second is exhausted by experience, the third does not bind the freed.
Verses addressed indirectly, directly, or spoken of oneself (ādhyātmika) (Nirukta 7.1).

name: The three kinds of souls: puṣṭi, maryādā, pravāha

definitions.definition: Souls are created of three kinds, with different natures and destinies: grace-souls for loving service, rule-souls for scriptural liberation, stream-souls for worldly life.

name: Texts of difference, non-difference and mediation

definitions.definition: Scripture speaks of difference (bheda), of non-difference (abheda) and of the body–self relation (ghaṭaka); the last reconciles the first two, so that no text need be set aside as figurative or lower.

Being struck by the three sufferings prompts the inquiry (SK 1); the commentators name them internal (bodily and mental), from other beings, and from the divine (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati). Seen and Vedic remedies do not end them certainly and finally (SK 1–2); their complete cessation is the supreme goal (SS 1.1). Suffering from old age and death belongs to embodied existence until the subtle body ceases (SK 55); the discriminating count even pleasure as suffering (SS 6.6–8).

name: The three krāntās (Viṣṇukrāntā, Rathakrāntā, Aśvakrāntā)
notes: From memory; not verified. Owner of doctrine: U24.

definitions.definition: A later Śākta division of India into three regions, each with its own sixty-four tantras (192 in all), recorded in texts such as the Mahāsiddhasāra.

Inner (kuṇḍalinī, inner sound, blue light between the eyes), outer (colours and lights in space before the nose and above the head) and intermediate (the sequence of voids) — the objects of tāraka-yoga in the Advayatāraka and Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa.
Devotion is threefold: practice, emotion and love; practice aims at the manifestation of the eternally perfect bhāva.

relations.note: prema is then graded further in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi

definitions.definition: Ultimate (pāramārthika: Brahman, never sublated), empirical (vyāvahārika: the waking world, sublated only by Brahman-knowledge) and apparent (prātibhāsika: dream, rope-snake, sublated by waking cognition).
Āṇava (innate, one, beginningless), kārma (the stream of deeds) and māyīya (the bond of māyā's products); each a real substance.
Mummalam: āṇavam, kaṉmam, māyai — eternal; in release their power is quelled, not their existence ended.
Āṇava: loss of freedom or awareness; māyīya: the appearance of separate knowables; kārma: agency in an unconscious agent; all through the power of māyā (ĪPK 3.2.4-5).
The root impurity is ignorance, not a substance; knowledge alone liberates (TĀ 1.22-26).
Śiva is free of the three impurities; the soul is atomic through impurity and is freed when the bond of impurity is shaken off.

relations.note: the three plus māyeya and tirodhāna

name: The three transformations of the mind

definitions.definition: Stilling (impressions of stilling overpower those of emergence, 3.9, with a peaceful flow, 3.10), samādhi (all-objectness dwindles, one-pointedness rises, 3.11) and one-pointedness (subsiding and arising cognitions alike, 3.12).
Action, knowledge and devotion lead to liberation; devotion is the easiest, being mental and paining neither body nor mind.
Mahāviṣṇu (Kāraṇodakaśāyin), from whose pores the universes emerge; Garbhodakaśāyin within each universe; Kṣīrodakaśāyin as the Paramātman in every being.

name: The perishable, the imperishable and the highest person

definitions.definition: The perishable (all beings), the imperishable (the unchanging) and the highest person (Puruṣottama) beyond both, who sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).

relations.note: the Gītā's three persons and the Mokṣadharma's 24/25/26 both set a supreme above the knower of prakṛti

name: The three realities: cit, acit, Īśvara (Nimbārka)

definitions.definition: Souls (cit), the non-conscious (acit: aprākṛta, prākṛta, time) and the Lord (Īśvara), all established by scripture.

name: The three powers: will, knowledge, action

definitions.definition: Icchā, jñāna and kriyā, identified with the goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā (TĀ 1.271-272); knowing and acting are the life of the living (ĪPK 1.1.4).
Parā (Viṣṇu-śakti), aparā (kṣetrajña) and avidyā-karma, which veils the kṣetrajña and causes saṃsāra; the world as the śakti of Brahman like the light of a fire.
Internal (svarūpa/cit), marginal (the souls) and external (māyā) powers; the basis of acintya-bhedābheda.
Momentum, memory-impression (in the self), elasticity (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Outer, inner and supreme self (Ātma Upaniṣad); inner self Brahmā, supreme self Maheśvara, eternal self of all Viṣṇu (Rudrahṛdaya); the inner controller whose body is the elements (Subāla 7).
Consciousness-space, mind-space and elemental space; the latter two arise from consciousness-space.

name: The three states and the fourth (avasthā-traya, turīya)

definitions.definition: Waking (viśva), dream (taijasa) and deep sleep (prājña) come and go; the self as the fourth (turīya) pervades and transcends them, non-dual; analysis of the three states is a means to know the self.

Earth, atmosphere and heaven, formed from the Puruṣa's feet, navel and head (RV 10.90.14), each with its gods — Agni on earth, Vāyu or Indra in the atmosphere, Sūrya in heaven (Nirukta 7.5) — and named by the utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ (VS 36.3).

Knowledge, action and devotion are the only means; knowledge suits those disgusted with action, action those still desirous, devotion those with faith in the Lord's stories who are neither disgusted nor over-attached; action is done until disgust or faith arises.

relations.note: the Devī Gītā also names action, knowledge and devotion as the three paths and calls devotion the easiest

name: The threefold austerity (tapas) of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Austerity of body (worship of gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, non-harm), of speech (non-agitating, truthful, pleasant, beneficial speech and recitation) and of mind (serenity, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of being); each again sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (BhG 17.14–19); self-tormenting austerity not enjoined by scripture is demonic (17.5–6).
The world binds a person as body (seat of experience), senses (instruments) and objects (what is experienced); release is its absolute dissolution.

Bondage is threefold: to prakṛti (absorption from taking the eight prakṛtis as highest), to the modifications (domination by the senses and objects), and through gifts (giving with conceit); release is threefold: by increase of knowledge, by calming of the senses' passion, and by total exhaustion (of virtue and non-virtue), whence isolation (Tattvasamāsa 19–20 with the Kramadīpikā). Strictly, prakṛti is bound and released (SK 62).

name: The threefold consciousness (Rāma-hṛdaya)
