definitions.definition: As space is threefold — the whole, the space delimited by a pond and the sky reflected in it — consciousness is the whole, the consciousness delimited by the intellect, and its reflection; agency belongs to the intellect with the reflection and is superimposed on the witness.

notes: Combines the Advaita 'limitation' and 'reflection' accounts in one image.

name: The threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata

definitions.definition: The Bhārata has three levels of meaning: the narrative of the Pāṇḍavas with Kṛṣṇa (āstīka), the teaching of dharma, devotion and conduct (manvādi), and the reading of all its words as names of Nārāyaṇa (auparicara).

'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds' (BhG 11.32); 'Time takes all and gives all' (MBh 12.217.25); in Vidura's parable time is the serpent, days and nights the rats (11.5–6); all accumulations end in exhaustion (Rāmāyaṇa 2.105.16).

name: Time as the condition of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: The Vedas exist for the sacrifices, which are enjoined for fixed times; hence the science of time is needed and stands at the head of the limbs (VJ Ṛk 3, 35; Yajus 3); fires are set up under the Kṛttikās because they keep to the east (ŚB 2.1.2.3).
Time and space (direction) are single, all-pervading, eternal substances inferred from the notions 'earlier/later, simultaneous, quick' and 'this from here' (VS 2.2.6, 2.2.12 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Pilgrimage places and their inner meaning

definitions.definition: Earthly tīrthas are holy by the power of earth and water and the presence of sages; seven cities give liberation; but the virtues are inner tīrthas, purity of mind the highest, and devotees themselves make tīrthas holy.

An ancient tree made of karma with two seeds, a hundred roots, three trunks, five branches, five saps, eleven boughs, a nest of two birds, three barks and two fruits, cut down with the axe of knowledge sharpened by devotion to the teacher.

The goddesses Parā, Parāparā, Aparā (with Bhairava; Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī above them in Abhinavagupta's Trika); Śiva, Śakti and Nara; will, knowledge and action; non-difference, difference-in-non-difference, difference.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): MaiU 5.2 names Brahmā, Rudra and Viṣṇu as the foremost forms of the one, being its rajas-, tamas- and sattva-parts; MaiU 5.1 hails the one as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and all the gods.

One Lord takes the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in the Devī Māhātmya and Devī Bhāgavata the three receive their bodies and powers from the Goddess.
The Lord's transcendent three quarters beyond māyā, as distinct from the one quarter that is the world (Tripādvibhūti-Mahānārāyaṇa, developing Ṛgveda 10.90.3).
Every cognition is self-luminous and manifests the knower, the known and itself; the self appears only as subject.
The soul in three modes across the six sthalas: tyāgāṅga (bhakta, māheśvara), bhōgāṅga (prasādi, prāṇaliṅgi), yōgāṅga (śaraṇa, aikya), facing iṣṭa-, prāṇa- and bhāva-liṅga.
The liṅga is threefold: gross (the iṣṭaliṅga worn on the body), subtle (the prāṇaliṅga of inner contemplation) and beyond the highest (the tṛptiliṅga).
The vacanas speak of iṣṭaliṅga, prāṇaliṅga and bhāvaliṅga, and the manuals correlate them with the gross, subtle and causal bodies and with the three aṅgas (tyāga, bhōga, yōga).

relations.note: correlation found in the vacana/manual tradition, not stated in SSM 6.49–50

name: The tripartition (trivṛt) of heat, water and food

definitions.definition: Being made heat, water and food each threefold (ChU 6.3.3); the red, white and black forms of fire, sun, moon and lightning are those of heat, water and food, and the thing itself is only a name (ChU 6.4); eaten food, water and heat divide threefold into body and mind (ChU 6.5).

relations.note: later readers relate the three colours (and the red, white and black ajā of ŚU 4.5) to the three guṇas; the ChU does not name guṇas

definitions.definition: Beyond waking, dream and deep sleep: not inward- or outward-knowing, not a mass of cognition, unseen, ungraspable, whose essence is the certainty of the one self, the stilling of the world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual — 'that is the self, that is to be known' (MāU 7); the measureless (amātra) of Om (MāU 12); 'the fourth is greater than these' (MaiU 7.11).

name: The fourth and beyond the fourth (turīya, turīyātīta)

definitions.definition: The minor Upaniṣads extend the Māṇḍūkya's four states to five (waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth, beyond the fourth), place them in the body (navel/heart, throat, palate, brows, crown) and in the heart lotus, and in the sixteen-measured praṇava map sixteen states; the turīyātīta is also the name of the highest renouncer.

name: The twelve Kālīs of the Krama

definitions.definition: Twelve goddesses as the phases of cognition: Sṛṣṭikālī, Raktakālī, Sthitināśakālī, Yamakālī, Saṃhārakālī, Mṛtyukālī, Rudrakālī, Mārtaṇḍakālī, Paramārkakālī, Kālāgnirudrakālī, Mahākālakālī, Mahābhairavacaṇḍograghorakālī (TĀ 4.148-172; Kramastotra 15-27).

notes: The first six names and the phases are confirmed by TĀ 4.148-154 and the Kramastotra; the forms of names 7-12 (esp. Rudrakālī vs Bhadrakālī, and the full name of the twelfth) are reconstructed - moderate confidence.

name: The twelve topics (lakṣaṇas) of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra

definitions.definition: Means of knowledge, distinction, subsidiarity, prompting, sequence, eligibility, general and specific transfer, modification, cancellation, single performance and incidental benefit — the subjects of the twelve adhyāyas.

Self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, fruit, pain and liberation (NS 1.1.9) — the objects whose true knowledge liberates and whose false knowledge binds (NBh 1.1.9).

name: Twelve yamas and twelve niyamas (Uddhava Gītā)

definitions.definition: Yamas: non-violence, truth, non-stealing, non-attachment, modesty, non-accumulation, faith in dharma, celibacy, silence, steadiness, forbearance, fearlessness. Niyamas: purity (outer and inner), recitation, austerity, fire-offering, faith, hospitality, worship of the Lord, pilgrimage, acting for others, contentment, service of the teacher.

relations.note: different counts and members

name: The twenty-eight Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas (mūlāgamas)
notes: Member order is the Kāmika's. Variant lists: the Kiraṇa has Nārasiṃha (= Sarvokta slot), Bhadra (= Vimala), Candrabhāsa (= Candrajñāna), Vīraja (= Vīra), Saurabheya (= Vātula); the Śrīkaṇṭhīya puts Maukuṭa among the Śivabhedas and has Madgīta, Nārasiṃha, Candrāṃśu, Vīrabhadra, Visara, Vimala and Saurabheya among the Rudrabhedas. Scholarly note: most titles survive, if at all, as later South Indian ritual redactions; early texts survive for the Niśvāsa, Kiraṇa, Svāyambhuva and Raurava (sūtrasaṅgrahas) and some upāgamas.

definitions.definition: Ten Śivabheda and eighteen Rudrabheda root scriptures of the upper stream, each revealed to a Śiva or Rudra and handed down; they are the limbs of Sadāśiva's mantra-body.
The 'ten' and 'eighteen' of Śiva's teaching, whose essence is the Trika (TĀ 1.18).
In each Dvāpara of the Vaivasvata manvantara Śiva incarnates as a yoga-teacher with four disciples; the twenty-eighth and last is Lakulīśa/Nakulīśa at Kāyāvatāra.

The twenty-fifth is the knower, the self that is 'awakening' (budhyamāna), which on knowing itself becomes alone; the twenty-sixth is the ever-awakened (buddha), stainless and eternal, which the twenty-fifth does not know until it awakens to it and attains its state (MBh 12.294.43, 12.296.7–12; Yājñavalkya 12.306).

name: The twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva)

definitions.definition: Reality enumerated as twenty-five principles: puruṣa; mūlaprakṛti, which is not a product; seven principles that are both products and producers — mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra and the five subtle elements; and sixteen that are products only — manas, the five sense capacities, the five action capacities and the five gross elements (SK 3, 22; SS 1.61; Tattvasamāsa 1–3). 'The knower of the twenty-five principles is liberated in any stage of life' (verse quoted by Gauḍapāda and the Jayamaṅgalā).

members: 5–9 the five tanmātras (sound, touch, form, taste, smell) — producers and products
11–15 the five buddhīndriyas (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose) — products only
16–20 the five karmendriyas (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) — products only
21–25 the five mahābhūtas (space, air, fire, water, earth) — products only

relations.note: Śaiva schemes of thirty-six principles include these twenty-five as their lower principles (the Śaiva account; interpretive link)

definitions.definition: Seventeen named in VS 1.1.5 (colour, taste, smell, touch, number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, nearness, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort) and seven more included by 'ca' (heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, impression, merit, demerit, sound) (Praśastapāda).

relations.note: Vaiśeṣika guṇa = quality residing in substance; Sāṃkhya guṇa = constituent of prakṛti. Same word, different concept.

definitions.definition: Objections resting on mere similarity or dissimilarity (NS 1.2.18), listed in NS 5.1.1.

name: The twenty-four principles (epic Sāṃkhya)

definitions.definition: The Sāṃkhyas enumerate twenty-four principles together with prakṛti (the unmanifest), the twenty-fifth being beyond them (MBh 12.294.42); the Gītā's field lists the great elements, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, the ten organs and mind, and the five objects (BhG 13.5).

notes: The epic's lists vary between dialogues (e.g. 'eight prakṛtis and sixteen modifications'); the member list here follows BhG 13.5.

name: The avadhūta's twenty-four teachers

definitions.definition: The twenty-four teachers from whose ways the avadhūta brāhmaṇa learned freedom, told to King Yadu: earth (forbearance; its mountains and trees: living for others), air (content with bare sustenance; unattached among objects), sky (the self pervasive and untouched), water (purity that purifies), fire (taking all without taint; the Lord in all forms), moon (changes belong to the body), sun (taking and giving without attachment; one appearing many), pigeon (ruin by excessive attachment), python (accepting what comes), ocean (unmoved by gain and loss), moth (lured by forms to ruin), honeybee (begging a little from many; taking the essence of all scriptures; not hoarding), elephant (bound by touch of the female), honey-gatherer (hoarded wealth enjoyed by others), deer (lured by song), fish (the tongue), Piṅgalā (hope is misery, hopelessness bliss), osprey (possession invites attack), child (carefree bliss), maiden with bangles (live alone), arrow-maker (one-pointed absorption), serpent (homeless solitude), spider (the Lord emits and withdraws the world), wasp (one becomes what one dwells on). His own body is a further teacher of dispassion; knowledge from one teacher alone is not firm, for Brahman is sung in many ways.
Bodhya names six teachers — Piṅgalā, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden (Mahābhārata 12.171.61).

notes: List verified in the local Bhāgavata e-text (11.7.33-34). The six teachers of Bodhya are a subset (Piṅgalā, osprey, serpent, bee, arrow-maker, maiden).

definitions.definition: Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha (YS 1.4–5).

name: The twenty-one kinds of pain

definitions.definition: The pain whose absolute cessation is the goal is divided into twenty-one kinds (Vācaspati); later manuals list them as the body, the six senses (with mind), their six objects, the six cognitions, pleasure and pain itself; birth itself is pain (NS 4.1.55).

notes: The number is confirmed in the Tātparyaṭīkā e-text; the member list is recalled from later manuals.

name: The twenty-six qualities of a Vaiṣṇava

definitions.definition: Kindness, truthfulness, equality, mildness, freedom from pride, dependence on Kṛṣṇa alone and the rest.
Listed in NS 5.2.1 and defined in 5.2.2–25.

name: The virtues called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11)

definitions.definition: Absence of pride and pretence, non-harm, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control, dispassion, absence of ego, seeing the evil of birth, death, age, disease and pain, non-attachment, evenness, unswerving devotion, love of solitude, constancy in self-knowledge and insight into the goal of truth — these are called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11).

notes: Commentators count the items as twenty; the count is not in the text.

name: The two birds on one tree

definitions.definition: Two birds, companions, on one tree: one eats the sweet fig, the other looks on without eating (RV 1.164.20); the lord, guardian of the world, has entered 'me the simple one' (1.164.21).

Two birds, companions, cling to the same tree; one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating; the one who grieves, seeing the other, the Lord, and his greatness, is freed from sorrow (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7, quoting RV 1.164.20); KU 1.3.1 speaks of two, 'shadow and light', drinking in the cave. Later schools read the two birds as jīva and Lord distinct (Dvaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita) or as the reflected and the witness self (Advaita).

relations.note: the image distinguishes two where the mahāvākyas state identity; see dsp:souls-one-or-distinct

notes: The Upaniṣads (Muṇḍaka 3.1.1, Śvetāśvatara 4.6) read the birds as the individual self and the Lord; the Ṛgveda does not name them.

definitions.definition: Brahman has two forms: formed and formless, mortal and immortal (BAU 2.3.1; MaiU 6.3); time and the timeless (MaiU 6.15); sound and non-sound, the word-brahman and the highest (MaiU 6.22); Om is the higher and lower brahman (PrU 5.2).

name: The two natures of the Lord (aparā and parā prakṛti)

definitions.definition: The Lord's lower nature is eightfold — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego — and his higher nature is the life-element that upholds the world; both are the womb of all beings (BhG 7.4–6); he sends forth beings resting on his prakṛti (9.8).

members: aparā prakṛti: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego

name: The two paths after death (bright and dark)

definitions.definition: The bright path (fire, light, day, bright fortnight, northern course) leads knowers of Brahman to non-return; the dark path (smoke, night, dark fortnight, southern course) to the lunar light and return (BhG 8.23–26); Bhīṣma waits for the northern course to die (MBh 6.114).

notes: U05's contribution; the Upaniṣadic doctrine is covered by U03.

name: The two paths: of the fathers and of the gods

definitions.definition: 'I have heard of two paths for mortals, of the fathers and of the gods' (RV 10.88.15); death is sent off by its own path, other than the path of the gods (10.18.1).

notes: The Upaniṣads (BĀU 6.2; ChU 5.10) develop the two paths; that development is U03's.

definitions.definition: Projection (vikṣepa), which creates the world, and veiling (āvaraṇa), which covers knowledge (Rāma to Lakṣmaṇa).
Perception and inference; verbal knowledge is explained by inference (VS 9.18–19 C); testimony, comparison and presumption are included in inference (Praśastapāda).

name: The two seeds of the mind

definitions.definition: The tree of mind grows from two seeds, the vibration of prāṇa and firm conception (vāsanā); stilling either stills the mind, so yogins restrain the breath and give up vāsanās.

Saṃnyāsa is laying aside desire-prompted actions, tyāga relinquishing the fruit of all actions (BhG 18.2); obligatory acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned (18.5); relinquishment is threefold by the guṇas (18.7–9); the true renouncer is the one who acts without depending on the fruit (6.1).

name: Brahman's twofold mark (ubhaya-liṅga): free of all defect, full of auspicious qualities

definitions.definition: Brahman is at once opposed to all that is evil and the sole abode of infinite auspicious qualities; 'nirguṇa' texts deny only prākṛta, defiling qualities, so Brahman is both 'nirguṇa' and 'saguṇa' in these two senses.

relations.note: the Lord is free of prakṛti's guṇas

definitions.definition: The Āḻvārs' Tamil hymns, above all the Tiruvāymoḻi, are a Veda in Tamil equal to the Sanskrit; the teachers comment on both.
The Tamil Veda reveals the heart of the Sanskrit and, by its author's lowly birth, the Lord's accessibility.

name: The two realms of the Lord (nitya-vibhūti and līlā-vibhūti)

definitions.definition: The Lord's domain is twofold: the eternal realm of pure sattva (Vaikuṇṭha), a quarter beyond, and the realm of play made of prakṛti and time, where the world is created and souls transmigrate.
The remainder of the sacrifice praised as the ground in which name and form, the world, the gods and the rites rest (AVŚ 11.7).

name: Udayana's proofs of Īśvara (NK 5.1)

definitions.definition: The all-knowing maker is proved from: (1) the world's being an effect (kārya); (2) the combining of atoms at creation (āyojana); (3) the support of the world (dhṛti) and (4) its destruction ('ādi'); (5) traditional skills and usage of words (pada); (6) the validity of the Veda (pratyaya); (7) scripture (śruti); (8) the Veda's consisting of sentences (vākya); (9) special number — the magnitude of dyads, which requires an enumerating cognition at creation (saṃkhyāviśeṣa). The five clusters first answer five objections.

notes: Counted as eight or nine depending on whether 'ādi' is taken separately; glosses follow the usual explanation.

name: Enumeration, definition, examination (the method of the śāstra)

definitions.definition: The śāstra proceeds by naming (uddeśa), defining (lakṣaṇa) and examining (parīkṣā) (NBh 1.1.3); book 1 of the sūtra enumerates and defines, books 2–5 examine.

name: Unmanī / manonmanī — the state beyond mind

definitions.definition: The state in which mind has dissolved (unmanībhāva); reached by nāda and tāraka; beyond merit and sin; the supreme state of Viṣṇu (Amṛtabindu 4; Nādabindu 48; Yogaśikhā 6.61; Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa).

name: The upāgamas (upabhedas) of the Siddhānta
members: Mṛgendra (classed under the Kāmika by tradition)
Kālajñāna / Uttara (Vātula; cf. the Kālottara corpus)
notes: Only the better-known upāgamas are listed here; the full per-Āgama lists are in the structure.upabhedas_kamika field of each src entry.

definitions.definition: Subsidiary scriptures attached to the 28 root Āgamas; the Kāmika names them one by one (206 by its stated counts; tradition usually says 207); the Kiraṇa calls any division within a division an upabheda and says the divisions differ in knowledge, not in fruit.
Knowledge produced by similarity: seeing the gavaya, one knows the remembered cow as similar to it.
The teacher becomes pregnant with the pupil and brings him forth with the Sāvitrī on the third night (ŚB 11.5.4.12).
The Vedic birth in which the Sāvitrī is mother and the teacher father (MDh 2.170); the best birth, given by knowledge (ĀpDh 1.1.1.16–17); due at eight, eleven or twelve (MDh 2.36; ĀśGS 1.19).

name: Teacher and pupil in the Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The pupil approaches 'with fuel in hand' (MuU 1.2.12; PrU 1.1; ChU 8.7.2; KauU 1.1); the teacher must be learned in the Veda and established in brahman (MuU 1.2.12); pupils are tested — a year of austerity (PrU 1.2), truthfulness (ChU 4.4), 101 years of study (ChU 8.7-12); knowledge from a teacher leads most surely (ChU 4.9.3); 'one who has a teacher knows' (ChU 6.14.2); lineage lists (vaṃśa) trace teachings back to brahman (BAU 2.6, 4.6, 6.5; ChU 3.11.4, 8.15; MuU 1.1.1-2); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).

Secondary Purāṇas told by sages or by Vyāsa's disciples (VP 3.6.23; KūP 1.11.280); the Kūrma lists eighteen (Sanatkumāra, Nārasiṃha, Skānda, Śivadharma, Āścarya, Nāradīya, Kāpila, Mānava, Auśanasa, Brahmāṇḍa, Vāruṇa, Kālikā, Māheśvara, Sāmba, Saura, Pārāśara, Mārīca, Bhārgava); the Matsya adds that every Purāṇa apart from the eighteen issued from them (53.64).

Venerating something as brahman or as the self: name, speech, mind and the rest (ChU 7), the sun (ChU 3.19), mind and space (ChU 3.18), the six teachers' views (BAU 4.1), 'as the self' (BAU 1.4.7); each has a stated fruit. Kena 1.5 denies that brahman is 'this that people venerate here'.

Meditation on the qualified Brahman or a symbol, seated and one-pointed, until death, purifies and steadies the mind and leads to the Brahma-world; meditation on the attributeless leads to knowledge (Pañcadaśī 9).

name: The four Upavedas

definitions.definition: Sciences attached to the four Vedas: medicine (āyurveda), archery/warfare (dhanurveda), music (gāndharvaveda) and statecraft or architecture (arthaśāstra / sthāpatyaveda), as listed in the Caraṇavyūha.

notes: Assignments vary between sources; not verified here.

name: Samādhi from means and from birth (upāya-pratyaya, bhava-pratyaya)

definitions.definition: For the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti the state has becoming as its cause (1.19); for yogins it arises from means — faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight (1.20).
At death the tip of the heart lights up and the knower leaves through the crown channel by the power of knowledge and remembrance, helped by the grace of Hari in the heart.

name: Departure of the soul at death

definitions.definition: The knower or surrendered soul leaves through the channel of the head, the Lord in the heart illuminating the way; others leave by other channels to further births.
Favourable cultivation of Kṛṣṇa free of other desires, uncovered by knowledge and works; causeless (ahaitukī).
Speech was Prajāpati's own and his second, which he sent forth to pervade all (PB 20.14.2); speech is the consecration (KB 7.1); correct speech distinguishes gods from Asuras (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24).
The grammarians read the 'four horns' verse as speech, 'the great god who entered mortals', identity with whom grammar aims at (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā).

Speech is a goddess and cosmic power: she moves with all the gods, is queen and first of the worshipful, the power by which beings eat, see, breathe and hear, who makes whom she loves a seer (RV 10.125); she was found entered into the seers and reveals her body to some like a bride (10.71); gods begot her and animals speak her (8.100.11); the syllable in highest heaven bears the verses (1.164.39); she has four quarters, three hidden (1.164.45).

relations.note: The four quarters are the Saṃhitā's analysis of speech.

name: The vacana as speech of experience

definitions.definition: The vacana is spontaneous speech from experience in the mother tongue, sealed with the aṅkita; speech must be pure as a string of pearls and matched by deeds.
Practice impelled by scriptural command where spontaneous attraction is absent.
Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta and Aniruddha, invoked in worship (Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha placed in the directions).

name: Four forms of liberation in the Vaikhānasa tradition
notes: Recalled from Vaikhānasa literature (Vimānārcanakalpa); correlation of these with particular means is not recorded here (unverified).

definitions.definition: Attaining Viṣṇu's world (sālokya), nearness (sāmīpya), likeness of form (sārūpya) and union (sāyujya).

Lower dispassion is the consciousness of mastery of one free of thirst for seen and scriptural objects (1.15); higher dispassion is freedom from thirst for the guṇas, from discernment of the puruṣa — the utmost limit of knowledge, inseparable from kaivalya (1.16, YBh 1.16); dispassion even toward the highest powers yields kaivalya (3.50). Vācaspati divides the lower into four stages (see pth:vacaspati-four-stages-of-vairagya).

name: The self common to all men (vaiśvānara)

definitions.definition: The self conceived as the whole cosmos — sky its head, sun its eye, wind its breath, space its trunk, water its bladder, earth its feet — of which each partial meditation grasps only one part (ChU 5.11-18); the waking quarter of the self (MāU 3); the digestive fire (BAU 5.9).

A group of words is one sentence when it serves one purpose and its parts need each other if separated; otherwise the sentence splits (MS 2.1.46–47); arthavādas are one sentence with injunctions (MS 1.2.7).
Validity is intrinsic (svataḥ) both in arising and in being known; invalidity is extrinsic, due to a defect in the cause or a sublating cognition.
Every experience is valid; error is a pair of cognitions not distinguished, not a false cognition.

Lists at the ends of Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka sections naming the teachers from whom a teaching was received, traced back through seers and gods to Prajāpati and Brahman the self-existent (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 14.9.4.33; Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa; JUB).

name: The varṇas by guṇa and action

definitions.definition: The fourfold order is created by the Lord according to guṇa and action (BhG 4.13), each varṇa's duties arising from its nature (18.41–44); yet the epic also teaches that varṇa arose from actions in a world wholly of Brahman (MBh 12.181.10) and that conduct makes the brāhmaṇa (3.177.16); service is the śūdra's dharma (12.60.27–28).

notes: See dsp:varna-by-birth-or-conduct-epic for the recorded tension.

name: The four varṇas in the Puruṣa Sūkta

definitions.definition: The brāhmaṇa was the Person's mouth, the rājanya his arms, the vaiśya his thighs; from his feet the śūdra was born (RV 10.90.12) — the one Saṃhitā verse naming the four varṇas together.

notes: Its later use and the debates about it are recorded in dsp:varna-origin-purusa-sukta.

definitions.definition: Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes declared by Svayambhū (PŚ 3), produced at eight places (PŚ 13); vowels are selves of Indra, sibilants of Prajāpati, stops of Death (ChU 2.22.3); stops, sibilants and vowels correspond to earth, atmosphere and sky (AA 3.2.5).

name: Varṇa — the four classes, as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas correlate the classes with Prajāpati's limbs, metres, gods and animals, declaring the śūdra unfit for sacrifice (TS 7.1.1.4–6), with the three Vedas (TB 3.12.9.2), and call learned brāhmaṇas 'human gods' (ŚB 2.2.2.6).

Four classes, three of them twice-born (MDh 10.4), created from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet (MDh 1.31), with duties — teaching and sacrificing; protecting; trade and farming; service (MDh 1.88–91); each earlier class superior by birth (ĀpDh 1.1.1.4–8); a lower class rises and a higher falls in the next birth by conduct (ĀpDh 2.5.11.10–11); a brāhmaṇa who neglects the Veda sinks to a śūdra's state (MDh 2.168); penalties for a śūdra hearing the Veda (GDh 12.4–6).

notes: Recorded faithfully as the Brāhmaṇa and Dharmaśāstra traditions state it; the bhakti, Siddha, Buddhist, Jain and Upaniṣadic critiques are recorded by other units and in dsp:women-caste-liberation.

name: Varuṇa and Mitra, guardians of order

definitions.definition: Varuṇa, all-seeing sovereign, knows the paths of birds and ships and the months, is 'the third' when two conspire, counts the blinkings of men, and his spies never close their eyes; with Mitra he guards ṛta; he binds with fetters and releases.

Latent tendencies, laid down by the experience of afflictions, karma and fruition, manifest only when suited to the ripening karma (4.8), stay connected across births, places and times (4.9), are beginningless because the will to be is eternal (4.10), and cease when their cause, result, substrate and support cease (4.11); the mind, though variegated by them, exists for another (4.24).

name: Destruction of vāsanā, dissolution of mind and knowledge of truth

definitions.definition: The Muktikā's triad (shared with the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka): the three must be practised together for liberation while living; the mind-tree has two seeds, prāṇa-vibration and vāsanā, and stopping one stops the other.

name: Knowledge, destruction of tendencies, dissolution of mind

definitions.definition: Vidyāraṇya's triad, practised together for the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.

name: The wind-girdled seers (vātaraśana ṛṣayaḥ)

definitions.definition: Ascetic seers called śramaṇas who kept their seed drawn upward and were found by the other seers through faith and austerity (TA 2.7.1).

notes: Related to the long-haired sage of RV 10.136 (U01).

definitions.definition: Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), of the ṛju class and equal in rank with Brahmā, is the highest of souls; no soul equals him; by Viṣṇu's permission he gives liberation, and grace reaches lower beings through him.

name: Vāyu's three avatāras: Hanumān, Bhīma, Madhva

definitions.definition: The tradition holds, on Madhva's own statements reading Ṛgveda 1.141, that Vāyu descended as Hanumān, as Bhīma and, in Kali 4300, as Madhva, to proclaim the truth about Hari; the hagiographies' feats are told as signs of this.

name: Equal authority of Veda and Śaiva Āgama

definitions.definition: Both proceed from Śiva; Śrīkaṇṭha sees no difference between them.

name: The Veda as authored by a reliable speaker

definitions.definition: The Veda is valid like mantra and medicine because its seers and teachers are reliable (NS 2.1.69; NBh); its validity rests on its being rooted in the Lord's perception (Gaṅgeśa); all Vedic sentences are valid because spoken by the Lord (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by understanding (VS 6.1.1 C); its authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).

Vedic recitation distinguishes the raised (udātta), low (anudātta) and falling (svarita) accents; a mantra wrong in accent or letter does not convey its meaning and harms the sacrificer, as 'Indra-śatru' did (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 52).

name: The Vedic afterlife: Yama and the fathers

definitions.definition: The dead go by the ancient paths, past Yama's two four-eyed dogs, to Yama and the fathers in the highest heaven, where they are rejoined with their iṣṭāpūrta and a radiant body and rejoice in svadhā (RV 10.14); the fathers are lower, middle and higher (10.15.1); those who reached heaven by tapas, battle or great gifts are there (10.154); Kaśyapa asks for the immortal world of light and bliss (9.113).

name: Scripture and its authority in Viśiṣṭādvaita

definitions.definition: The Veda is authorless and eternal, re-promulgated by the Lord in each creation; it alone makes the Lord known; the Itihāsa–Purāṇas (above all the Viṣṇu Purāṇa) and the Pāñcarātra, spoken by the Lord, are authoritative, and the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs are a Veda in Tamil.

name: The named breaths in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās name in-breath, out-breath and diffused breath (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna) with life (asu) among the goods of the Camaka (TS 4.7) and in long-life charms (AVŚ 8.1); the Vrātya has seven prāṇas, seven apānas and seven vyānas identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures (AVŚ 15.15–17).

members: (udāna and samāna appear in later Vedic lists)

name: Time, the year and the wheel of ṛta

definitions.definition: The year is the twelve-spoked unaging wheel of ṛta with 720 sons (days and nights) (RV 1.164.11, 1.164.48); it was born from the ocean after ṛta and satya (10.190.2); the Disposer fashioned sun and moon 'as before' (10.190.3); generations pass while the dawns return (1.113.11); in the Atharvaveda Time itself is the first god (19.53–54).

name: The plurality of Vedic creation accounts

definitions.definition: The Saṃhitās give several accounts side by side: the Nāsadīya (10.129), the Puruṣa sacrifice (10.90), the Golden Germ (10.121), Viśvakarman the All-maker (10.81–82), Brahmaṇaspati smelting the worlds and being born from non-being (10.72), ṛta and satya from tapas (10.190), Vāc giving birth to the father (10.125.7), Indra's slaying of Vṛtra (1.32); in the Atharvaveda Skambha, Kāla, Kāma, Ucchiṣṭa, Virāj and Prāṇa.

name: The funeral as the hymns present it

definitions.definition: The corpse is burned by Agni asked not to consume it utterly; eye goes to sun, breath to wind, limbs to plants and waters; the unborn part is carried to the world of the well-doers; the flesh-eating fire is sent away; the widow lying beside the dead is bidden to rise to the world of the living; the living set a boundary against death and go back to dancing and laughter; the bones are laid in mother earth (RV 10.16–18); the Atharvaveda includes those buried, cast out, burned and exposed (AVŚ 18.2.34).

Disease is caused by demons, worms, sorcery, the anger of gods, sin or inheritance, and is driven out by plants, waters, amulets, fire and sun, and by the healer's verses and touch; Rudra and the Aśvins are divine physicians; 'the waters are the remedy for all' (RV 10.137.6); the physician is one among whom plants gather (10.97.6).
The metres (gāyatrī, triṣṭubh, jagatī, anuṣṭubh and others) were born from the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.9) and are recorded for every verse in the Anukramaṇīs.

Metres defined by syllable count and feet — gāyatrī (24), uṣṇih (28), anuṣṭubh (32), bṛhatī (36), paṅkti (40), triṣṭubh (44), jagatī (48) — described by Piṅgala with light/heavy syllables and three-syllable groups; the gods covered themselves with them against death (ChU 1.4.2); in the Brāhmaṇas each metre corresponds to a god, a class, a season and an animal (TS 7.1.1.4–6).

name: The person and the self in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The person comprises body (tanū, śarīra), life-breath (asu, prāṇa), mind (manas), breath-self (ātman) and, in one reading, an 'unborn part' (RV 10.16.4); at death eye goes to the sun and breath to the wind (10.16.3); the immortal is of one origin with the mortal (1.164.30, 38); the seer does not know what he is (1.164.37) yet can say 'I was Manu and the Sun' (4.26.1); Sūrya is the self of all (1.115.1); the wise, ageless self is known without fear of death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

The Veda is kept by exact oral transmission from teacher to pupil in several parallel recitations (continuous, word-by-word, step and the eight 'modified' ones), with attention to accent and quantity; reading from a written text is a fault (PŚ 32); memorization without understanding is 'dry fuel without fire' (Nirukta 1.18); the Vedas are endless (TB 3.10.11).

name: The recitation modes that guard the text

definitions.definition: The text is learned in the continuous form (saṃhitā), word by word (pada), in overlapping pairs (krama) and in the eight modified recitations (jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha, ghana), with hand gestures marking the accents; understanding the meaning is also enjoined (Nirukta 1.18; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 32–33, 54–55).

name: The fivefold division of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Veda consists of injunction (vidhi), mantra, name (nāmadheya), prohibition (niṣedha) and explanatory praise (arthavāda); all are meaningful through injunctions directly or indirectly.
The sūtra divides the Veda into mantra and brāhmaṇa (MS 2.1.32–33) and treats injunction, arthavāda, mantra, smṛti and name in adhyāya 1.

name: Waking, sleep and dream in the Saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The mind goes far from the waking and likewise returns to the sleeper (VS 34.1); prāṇa stays awake upright among sleepers (AVŚ 11.4.25); Sleep (svapna) is 'neither living nor dead', child of Yama, and bad dreams are warded off (AVŚ 6.46); even sleep does not keep away wrong (RV 7.86.6).

notes: The Upaniṣadic scheme of three states and the fourth is contributed by U03; any correspondence is interpretive and not asserted here.

name: Transmission of the Veda: teacher, śākhā and oral recitation

definitions.definition: The Veda passes from the seers by instruction (Nirukta 1.20) to pupils who repeat the teacher's words (RV 7.103.5); the teacher initiates the student and bears him as an embryo (AVŚ 11.5.3); Vyāsa divided the one Veda into four and his pupils' lines branched into śākhās (Bhāgavata 1.4.19–23; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4–5); each śākhā preserves its text by exact recitation.

The Lord as the best in each class — among lights the sun, among words Oṃ, among sacrifices japa, among sages Vyāsa, and so on — every glory springing from a fragment of his splendour; he sustains the world with one fragment (BhG ch. 10; 7.8–11).

Saṃyama on particular objects yields powers: knowledge of past and future, of the cries of beings, of former births, of other minds; invisibility; knowledge of death; strengths; knowledge of the worlds, stars, the body; freedom from hunger; steadiness; sight of siddhas; intuition; knowledge of the mind and of the puruṣa; divine senses; entering another body; levitation and departure at death; radiance; divine hearing; movement through space; mastery of elements and senses; the eight powers; omnipotence and omniscience (3.16–49).

name: The bodiless and those merged in prakṛti

definitions.definition: Beings who experience a state 'like kaivalya' but return: the bodiless (gods, per Vyāsa) pass through the ripening of their impressions; those merged in prakṛti remain until the mind returns by force of its unfinished task (YBh 1.19); they are placed outside the worlds, 'in the state of liberation' (YBh 3.26). Bhoja identifies the bodiless with those who rest content in the bliss-samādhi and the prakṛtilayas with those content in the I-am-ness samādhi (RM 1.17).

Liberation at the fall of the body when prārabdha is exhausted — like pot-space merging with space or wind becoming still (Muktikā 1 prose, 2.76; Yogakuṇḍalī 3.34); the dissolution of mind 'without form'.

Sāṃkhya's final isolation: 'when separation from the body is attained and pradhāna ceases, its purpose fulfilled, he attains isolation both certain and final' (SK 68). The SK does not use the word videhamukti.
At the fall of the body the knower's prāṇas do not depart; he merges, nothing new being attained.
The Vedic statement that impels to action; the sole means of knowing dharma, able to make known the future, subtle and remote.
What it conveys is bhāvanā, the prompting force (Kumārila); for Maṇḍana, that the act is a means to the desired (iṣṭasādhanatā).
What it conveys is the command / what is to be done (niyoga, kārya).

relations.note: the injunction presupposes the apūrva

name: Renunciation of the knower and of the seeker

definitions.definition: The knower (vidvat) renounces having realized; the seeker (vividiṣā) renounces in order to realize and keeps the insignia (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; developed in Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka).

Knowledge and ignorance lead to different ends (KU 1.2.4); fools in ignorance wander like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 says both those who worship ignorance and those who delight in knowledge enter darkness, and that one knowing both crosses death by ignorance and gains immortality by knowledge; ŚU 5.1 calls the perishable ignorance and the immortal knowledge; what is done with knowledge is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10).

Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin: vijñānākala souls raised to office in the pure universe, who act on Śiva's behalf and are liberated at the end of their office.

name: The six means of determining subsidiarity

definitions.definition: Direct statement, indicative power, syntactic connection, context, position and name — each later one weaker when they conflict, being more remote from the meaning (MS 3.3.14).

name: The fruition of karma: birth, life-span, experience

definitions.definition: Karma ripens as the kind of birth, the length of life and experience (2.13), bearing joy or anguish according to merit or demerit (2.14).
Error apprehends something as other than it is; the relation alone is unreal (Śāstradīpikā, following Kumārila; also Maṇḍana's Vibhramaviveka).
Separation (vipralambha) intensifies love; Caitanya's last years and Śikṣāṣṭaka 7–8.
Love in separation is the highest state; renunciation is fitting only when viraha makes home impossible.
The gopīs' longing when Kṛṣṇa vanishes or departs, which Kṛṣṇa says he causes so that their minds dwell on him; Uddhava wishes to be the dust of their feet.

Virāj, born from the Puruṣa and giving birth to him (RV 10.90.5), was all this in the beginning and entered the fires, the assembly and the council; gods, men and others milked their foods from her (AVŚ 8.10).

The vacanas refuse caste among devotees: Basava calls himself the son of a cobbler's house and asks to say of every devotee 'he is ours'; the intercaste marriage at Kalyāṇa is remembered as the occasion of the upheaval.

The SSM makes devotion, not birth, the mark of the bhakta (9.4–5), tells the māheśvara to drop jāti-dharmas opposed to the liṅga (10.30–31) and sees brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike at union (14.19–20), but also prescribes eating with twice-born of one's own jāti on the path (9.29) and distinguishes Śiva's and Brahmā's orderings of varṇa and āśrama (10.34–36).

name: Conduct: inner and outer purity, word and deed

definitions.definition: Do not steal, kill, lie, rage, despise others, praise yourself or blame others — inner and outer purity; compassion is the root of dharma; deeds must match words; equanimity under praise and blame.

name: Consciousness, samādhi and the void of mental activity

definitions.definition: The liṅga is consciousness (cit, saṃvit) shining within; śivayoga-samādhi is undivided attention on the supreme self as 'I am He'; in aikya the yogin abides in a heart empty of mental activity, dissolved in Śiva; the realized abides in the self through all dealings of knower, known and knowing.

notes: Waking/dream/deep sleep/fourth are not treated in the passages recorded here — gap.

name: Cosmology: Śiva, Śakti and the world

definitions.definition: The thirty-six tattvas are the waves and bubbles of Śiva's ocean of consciousness; Śiva emits the pramathas; the world arises from Śiva and is not different from him; the five ācāryas appear in every yuga; the descent of Reṇuka at Kollipāki is placed in the Kali age.

name: Inner centres and the liṅga of light

definitions.definition: The liṅga of light shines at the base (mūlādhāra), in the heart and between the brows — gold, coral-red and crystal; the prāṇaliṅga rises from the navel-bulb where prāṇa and apāna meet; six centres from the base to the brows, and above them the thousand-petalled lotus with the moon-disc and the subtle aperture called Kailāsa, from which nectar cools the heart.
The manual tradition places the six liṅgas in the six centres (low confidence).

The one consciousness-brahman is imagined as enjoyer, enjoyed and impeller through the three guṇas; tamas and rajas are removed at the śaraṇa stage; earth and the other elements are Śiva's eight forms, his body and effect; the thirty-six tattvas are waves of Śiva's ocean.

name: The guru: how he is found, tested and honoured

definitions.definition: The disciple, discerning and dispassionate, seeks a guru free of greed, versed in self-inquiry and the Śiva-siddhānta, righteous, of good conduct, wearing ash, rudrākṣa and the liṅga, knowing the yoga of liṅga and aṅga (6.1–6); without a perfected guru there is no end to saṃsāra, and such gurus are rare (13.24–27); the guru is Śiva and is not to be regarded as an ordinary man (11.19–24).
Allama tests every aspirant, including Akka Mahādēvi and Siddharāma, by questioning in the assembly.

Born by karma into castes and burned by threefold suffering, the soul becomes pure-minded when karma ripens and Śiva's grace arises; those who bear the inner liṅga do not return; liberation while living belongs to the one who knows the liṅga as liberation; the knower's karma-seeds are burnt, his acts leave no fruit and every act is worship.
Liberation is liṅgaikya, union with the liṅga, open to all who wear it.
The mind is a mirror soiled by ignorance that the guru cleanses; serenity of mind is grace; outer impressions (vāsanā) project the world, inner ones reveal the self's bliss.
Māyā is not gold, woman or land but the desire standing before the mind.

name: Powers and the warning against them

definitions.definition: Gorakṣa's indestructible body is surpassed by Allama's void body; attainment of powers is not the goal.
The five-syllable mantra is said to give all powers when uttered (8.36–43); the Śivayogin's sight gives accomplishment (11.37–43).
Women receive the liṅga, compose vacanas and sit in the assembly; Akka Mahādēvi is examined and acknowledged by Allama; Dāsimayya teaches that the self is neither man nor woman.

name: Brahman as the locus of contradictory attributes

definitions.definition: Contradictory scriptural statements about Brahman are all literally true; it is not necessary to relegate saguṇa statements to a lower level.

relations.note: Vallabha rejects assigning the qualified statements to a lower level

definitions.definition: The endless particularities residing in eternal substances (atoms, selves, minds) that make each distinct from every other (Tarkasaṅgraha); traditionally linked with the name Vaiśeṣika.

A thing has no real difference from its lasting properties (and God none from his qualities, acts and forms), yet they can be spoken of distinctly by virtue of viśeṣa; with temporary properties there is difference-and-identity. (Distinct from the Vaiśeṣika category viśeṣa.)

relations.note: viśeṣa accounts for distinctions where there is no real difference

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu measured the worlds in three strides; his highest step, where there is a well-spring of honey and where god-seekers rejoice, the wise ever see like an eye stretched in heaven (RV 1.22.20, 1.154).

The sovereign form shown to Arjuna by grace through a divine eye: the whole universe in one body, as bright as a thousand suns, and as Time devouring the warriors (BhG 11.5–34); seen only by undivided devotion (11.52–54); a similar self-manifestation occurs in the Kaurava court (MBh 5.129) and Mārkaṇḍeya sees the worlds within a divine child (3.186).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's real transformation of prakṛti; Advaita accepts pariṇāma only for māyā
vivarta speaks of appearance; ajāti denies any origination at the highest level

definitions.definition: The world is an apparent, not a real, transformation of Brahman, as the snake of the rope; effects are non-different from the cause, mere names (BS 2.1.14).

The discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2), accomplished by buddhi (SK 37) and culminating, through repeated practice of the principles, in the complete, pure and single knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64); it is the direct realization of the distinctness of sattva and puruṣa (Vācaspati). Liberation comes from it alone (SS 3.23–25); it is reached by renouncing each principle with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

The cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa (YBh 2.26); unwavering, it is the means of liberation (2.26); limbs of yoga make knowledge shine up to it (2.28); from it come sovereignty and omniscience (3.49); complete, it yields the cloud of dharma (4.29); the discerning mind bends toward kaivalya (4.26).

relations.note: non-discrimination is removed by discrimination

name: Vrata: the gods' ordinance and the human vow

definitions.definition: Varuṇa is 'of firm ordinances' (RV 1.25); one prays to be sinless under his vrata (1.24.15); the sacrificer undertakes a vow before Agni, lord of vows (VS 1.5).

A self-imposed observance for a day or period (fast, vigil, worship, gifts), bound to a lunar date and deity, with a story and a promised fruit; Ekādaśī, Śivarātri, Navarātra and the Kātyāyanī vow are examples.

The vow-bound wanderer of Atharvaveda 15 who stirs Prajāpati into creation, becomes the one, the great, brahman, tapas and truth, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, stands upright a year, is seated on a throne of seasons and Vedas, has seven prāṇas identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures, and is to be honoured above the king when he comes as guest.

name: Pervasion by the mode but not by its result

definitions.definition: Ordinary objects are pervaded by both the mental mode and the reflected consciousness (its 'result'); Brahman, being self-luminous, only by the mode, which removes ignorance.

The manifest is caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, dependent, merging, composite and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite (SK 10); both consist of the three guṇas and are non-discriminating, objects, common, unconscious and productive, unlike puruṣa (SK 11).

The invariable concomitance of probans with probandum ('wherever smoke, there fire'), known through observation of co-presence and absence of deviation, aided by tarka and extraordinary contact through the universal; defined exactly after rejecting five provisional definitions.

name: The five provisional definitions of pervasion (Vyāptipañcaka)

definitions.definition: Five definitions of pervasion in terms of non-occurrence in loci of the probandum's absence, each rejected chiefly because it fails for a probandum present everywhere (kevalānvayin).

Spaces seen in the intermediate target: ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa and paramākāśa (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 4.1), or the guṇa-less space, supreme space, great space, space of principles and space of the sun (Advayatāraka) — order and names differ.

name: The fourfold form of the Lord (the vyūhas)

definitions.definition: Vāsudeva (the knower of the field), Saṃkarṣaṇa (the jīva), Pradyumna (mind) and Aniruddha (ego, source of Brahmā), each arising from the prior; the liberated pass back through them into Vāsudeva (MBh 12.326.38, 12.326.68–69, 12.327.26, 12.332.13–18).

relations.note: the vyūhas are correlated with jīva, mind and ego in the Nārāyaṇīya

name: The weighing of deeds after death

definitions.definition: In the other world a man is placed on a balance and follows whichever side prevails, good or evil; the knower mounts the balance here and escapes it there (ŚB 11.2.7.33); Bhṛgu sees retribution in kind (ŚB 11.6.1; JB 1.42–44).
Not the jīva, body, birth, learning, action or dharmic deeds, but one who has realized the non-dual Self and is free of faults (Vajrasūci); caste is imagined for convention (Nirālamba).

Eligibility rules: dispassion, the fourfold means, freedom from certain defects and statuses; the ineligible may renounce when at the point of death; texts differ on whether the unmarried may renounce and on consent of kin.

The puruṣa is the witness (pratisaṃvedin) of the buddhi (YBh 2.17, 2.20); the mind's activities are always known to it (4.18); Vijñānabhikṣu explains its knowing through the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi (YV 1.7).

A word means the universal (ākṛti), since action concerns it (MS 1.3.33); meanings follow the śāstra where usages differ (MS 1.3.9) and accept current usage of non-Āryas where uncontradicted (MS 1.3.10); the Buddhist 'exclusion' (apoha) is rejected.

Word, object and cognition are confused through mutual superimposition; saṃyama on their distinction gives knowledge of the cries of all beings (3.17). The word is a single unit grasped by the buddhi from the letters (YBh 3.17); the relation of word and meaning is held eternal (YBh 1.27); savitarkā coalescence is mixed with these constructions (1.42).

name: Word, meaning and their relation as established (siddha)

definitions.definition: Kātyāyana's first vārttika: word, meaning and relation are established (eternal, per Patañjali); grammar only restricts usage for the sake of dharma; the word is that by which the meaning is understood (Mahābhāṣya).

notes: The fuller philosophy of language (sphoṭa, śabda-brahman) belongs to lin:vyakarana (U31).

definitions.definition: Word-meaning is the individual, form and universal together (NS 2.2.68); the relation of word and meaning is conventional (NS 2.1.56–57; NBh).
Understanding meaning from words is conventional (VS 7.2.24 C).
The denotative power is the Lord's convention (Tarkasaṅgraha); analysed in detail in the Śaktivāda and Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā.

name: The world as the mind's projection

definitions.definition: The seen does not exist apart from consciousness; worlds arise from the mind's conceiving (saṅkalpa, manorājya) like dreams, whole lives occurring in a moment, worlds within a room, a rock or an atom; wiping away the seen is nirvāṇa.
All grasped by mind and senses is māyā, a mental creation; the three states are the mind's play like a whirling firebrand.

name: Yajña: the sacrifice that sustains the world

definitions.definition: Ritual action is the Vedic paradigm of effective action: the gods first sacrificed the Person and 'sacrificed to the sacrifice with the sacrifice — these were the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16); the sacrifice is woven like a cloth by the fathers (10.130.1); through it the petitions of the Camaka are 'made fit'.

The Gītā keeps the wheel of sacrifice between gods and men (3.10–16) but widens sacrifice to austerity, yoga, study, sense-restraint, breath and knowledge (4.25–30), declares the sacrifice of knowledge highest (4.33) and sees offering, oblation, fire and offerer as Brahman (4.24); sacrifice is to be done without desire for fruit (17.11; 18.5); the Anugītā describes an inner sacrifice of the senses (14.20).

Yama (Dharmarāja), king of the ancestors, judges the dead by their deeds under the Lord's command; the sinful see him terrible, the virtuous gentle; he has no power over the Lord's devotees; the Ekādaśī vow can empty his realm.

The dead, bound by Yama's messengers in a body for suffering, is dragged south over thorns, stones and burning ground to Yama's city: in MkP in twelve days, in the Garuḍa over a year past sixteen cities where he eats the monthly piṇḍas, crossing the Vaitaraṇī; in the Bhāgavata in two or three muhūrtas. Gifts made in life (umbrellas, sandals, food, the Vaitaraṇī cow) ease the road.
Non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possessiveness (2.30); universal and unlimited they are the great vow (2.31); non-harming is their root (YBh 2.30).

name: The body for torment after death

definitions.definition: For evil-doers another body arises after death from the five subtle elements, in which they suffer Yama's torments, then dissolves (MDh 12.16–22).

name: The year as Prajāpati and as Death

definitions.definition: Prajāpati is the year (saṃvatsara); the Veda's syllables are arranged to equal its moments (ŚB 10.4.2.22–25); the year is also Death, wearing away mortals' lives by days and nights (ŚB 10.4.3.1).
The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa opens in homage to Prajāpati as lord of the five-year age whose limbs are days, seasons, half-years and months (Ṛk 1).

name: Yoga as the stilling of the mind's activities (citta-vṛtti-nirodha)

definitions.definition: Yoga is the stilling of the mind's activities (YS 1.2), after which the seer abides in its own form (1.3); Vyāsa equates yoga with samādhi and admits it only in the one-pointed and stilled mind (YBh 1.1); commentators describe stilling as the inward dissolution of the activities into their cause.

relations.note: stilling is achieved by these means

definitions.definition: Seven worlds from the Avīci hell to the world of Brahmā (bhūr, the intermediate world, Mahendra's heaven, Prajāpati's mahar, and Brahmā's jana, tapas and satya), with hells and seven netherworlds below, the earth of seven continents around Meru, and classes of gods whose highest members enjoy the meditations with reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness; the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti are outside the worlds (YBh 3.26). Known by saṃyama on the sun (3.26–28).

Breath-control with Oṃ and the utterances, fixation, withdrawal and meditation burn away faults, sin, attachment and ungodly qualities (MDh 6.70–74); the removal of the fifteen faults is rooted in yoga (ĀpDh 1.8.23); seeing the self by yoga is the highest dharma (YS 1.8); the Yājñavalkyasmṛti describes yogic powers (3.202–203) and liberation through music (3.115).

The claim of the Yogatattva and Yogaśikhā that knowledge without yoga and yoga without knowledge cannot liberate, and that both must be practised; contrasted with the Muktikā and Mahāvākya, where knowledge alone liberates.

name: Karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga and bhakti-yoga in sequence

definitions.definition: As read from the Gītā by Yāmuna and Rāmānuja: karma-yoga (with self-knowledge) purifies and leads to the vision of the self, which jñāna-yoga also yields; this prepares bhakti-yoga, the direct means to the Lord; the three are done as his worship.
When the mind abides in the self (and does not join the senses), the embodied one has no pleasure or pain: that is yoga (VS 5.2.16–17 C).

relations.note: the Nyāya prescription of samādhi as the means to knowledge of truth

definitions.definition: At death the yogin fixes the breath between the brows (BhG 8.10) or, closing the gates and holding the mind in the heart and the breath in the head, utters Oṃ remembering the Lord (8.12–13); Bhīṣma chooses his time and his self breaks through the crown (MBh 6.114; 13.154.5); Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira (15.33.25); Śuka rises by yoga (12.318–320).

name: Departure through the crown and the path to brahman

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): of the 101 channels one goes to the crown; going up by it one reaches immortality (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); the person made of mind goes out through the indrayoni at the parting of the hair (TU 1.6); the self entered through the vidṛti (AU 1.3.12); through the suṣumṇā, joined with breath, Om and mind, one goes upward (MaiU 6.21); the path of the gods leads to the brahma-worlds from which there is no return (BAU 6.2.15).

The yogin may leave the body at will through the crown (BhP 2.2.15-21) and either be liberated at once or rise by the suṣumnā through Agni, Śiśumāra, Mahar- and Satyaloka and be liberated with Brahmā at the dissolution (2.2.22-31); the Vāyavīya also speaks of departure at will (ŚiP 7.2.37.26).
Leaving the body with the breath through the crown so as not to return (Amṛtanāda 39; Kuṇḍikā); recorded summary-only.
No perception, however heightened, can know dharma: perception grasps only what is present, and any excellence of a sense stays within its own domain (seeing far or subtle, not hearing colours).

name: Yogic perception and seers' knowledge

definitions.definition: The self is perceived through a special conjunction of self and mind, as are other substances (VS 9.13–17 C); yogins in concentration and out of it perceive the subtle, hidden and distant (Praśastapāda); seers' knowledge and the vision of the perfected arise from merit (VS 9.28).
The perception of one engaged in yoga arises from samādhi (NBh 1.1.3).

notes: The root texts give no warnings about such powers comparable to YS 3.37; none are recorded here.

name: Yogic powers in the epic

definitions.definition: Yogins with yoga-power enter other beings at will (MBh 12.289.24); Sulabhā enters Janaka's mind (12.308); Jaigīṣavya moves unseen between the worlds (9.49); Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira's body at death (15.33.25); Śuka rises into the sky (12.318–320).

notes: The epic's warnings: the path of yoga is hard and dangerous (12.289, low confidence on the exact images); the Gītā warns against self-tormenting austerities (17.5–6).

name: Vision limited by fitness — the warning against striving for an unfit vision

definitions.definition: One may see God only in the manner one's fitness allows; one who strives for a vision (or office) he is unfit for falls even from what he had; so service is to be rendered according to fitness.

relations.note: the limits of vision follow from intrinsic fitness

name: The means proper to each age

definitions.definition: Meditation in Kṛta, sacrifice in Tretā, worship in Dvāpara, singing the name in Kali (BhP 12.3.52; VP 6.2.17).

Dharma declines by a quarter in each age and its chief form changes — austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, giving (MDh 1.81–86); each age has its code — Manu, Gautama, Śaṅkha-Likhita, Parāśara (Parāśarasmṛti 1.24); litigation arose with that decline (Nāradasmṛti Mātṛkā 1.1–2); later authorities list practices forbidden in Kali (kalivarjya).
Using things in Kṛṣṇa's service without attachment rather than renouncing them as worldly.
